# Quba Mosque

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

The Quba Mosque, Masjid Quba (مَسْجِد قُبَاء‎), is a historic mosque located on the outskirts of Medina, Saudi Arabia. Also spelled as _Masjid e Quba_ or _Masjid al-Quba_ is believed to have been built in the lifetime of the Islamic prophet Muhammad in the seventh century CE. The current _Masjid Quba_ either stands on the site of _Masjid al-Dirar_ (see notes) or close to it.

#### Overview

Initially, when the mosque was first built, it was situated some six kilometres (3.7 miles) south of Medina in the village of _Quba_, before Medina (known as [_Yathrib_](https://madainproject.com/yathrib "Yathrib") at the time) expanded to include this village. According to one tradition it is believed, this is the mosque, where first Friday Prayer (_Salat al-Jummah_) was offered. Depending on whether the [Mosque of the Companions](https://madainproject.com/as_sahaba_mosque_(massawa) "as-Sahabah Mosque") in the Eritrean city of Massawa is older or not, it may be the first mosque in the world that dates to the lifetime of Prophet Muhammad in the early seventh century CE.

The current structure was designed by the Driehaus Prize winner and New Classical architect _Abdel-Wahed El-Wakil_. Initially it was planned that the older structure will be incorporated in the new one, but this idea was abandoned and the older building was torn down entirely. When the Masjid al-Quba was rebuilt in 1986 CE, the Medinan architecture was retained, characterised by the ribbed white domes, and basalt facing and modest exterior, qualities that recalls the simple Arabian architecture of Madinah.

One of the gates of Masjid an-Nabawi, the [_Bab Quba_](https://madainproject.com/quba_gate_(masjid_al_nabawi) "Bab-i Quba, Masjid al-Nabawi") (built during the second Saudi expansion of the Prophet's Mosque), is named after the village where this mosque is located.

[![Image 2: Masjid al-Quba](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_22837.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_22837.jpg "Masjid al-Quba")

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

#### Brief History

circa 622 CE

[![Image 3](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_11829.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_11829.jpg)

When prophet Muhammad arrived here, the area was inhabited by the tribe of _Bani Amr bin Auf_. According to a tradition, at the time, there was a water well at the site as well, probably owned by _Abu Ayub Ansari_.

According to tradition, its first stones (foundation-stones) were positioned by prophet Muhammad as soon as he arrived on his emigration from the city of Mecca to Medina, and the mosque was completed by his companions. Prophet Muhammad is said to have spent some fourteen days in this mosque praying _qaṣr_ (a short prayer) while waiting for Ali to arrive in Medina.

After it was first constructed during the lifetime of prophet Muhammad, it has been renovated quite often, subsequently. The third Caliph Uthman ibn Affan made the first renovations. Then again Caliph Omar bin Abdul Aziz built the mosque’s first minaret. It was renovated again in 1043 CE (435 Hijri) by _Abu Yali al-Husaini_ who constructed a prayer niche known as the "Mihrab". In the year 1160 CE (555 Hijri), several additions were made to the mosque by _Kamal al-Din al-Isfahani_. Successive renovations of the mosque took place in the years 1272, 1332, 1436, 1476 CE (671, 733, 840, 881 Hijri respectively), and the latest changes were made in the era of Sultan _Abdulmajid_ in the year 1830 CE (1245 Hijri) during the era of the Ottoman Empire.

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

#### Architecture

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 4](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_22661.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_22661.jpg)

**Domes and Minarets**  
 It total the mosque has 54 domes of three sizes, out of which 48 are small domes, five mid-sized domes and one is the large one built over the mihrab area. Mosque building has four minarets, one on each corner. Originally, there was one minaret, the new renovations included the addition of the other three minarets, they rest on square bases, have octagonal shafts which take on a circular shape as they reach the top.

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 5](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_44889.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_44889.jpg)

**Central Courtyard**  
 The courtyard of this mosque is constructed out of black, red, and white marble. The courtyard, is flagged with black, red and white marble. The courtyard of the Masjid Quba is covered by fabric screens during the day to protect the pilgrims and visitors from the scorching heat with shades. Arabesque latticework (a type of projecting window enclosed with carved wood latticework) filters the light of the palm groves outside. Elements of the new building include work by the Egyptian architect _Abdel-Wahed el-Wakil_, Pakistani architect _Hassan Khan Sayyid_ and the Stuttgart tensile architect _Mahmoud Bodo Rasch_, a student of _Frei Otto_.

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 6](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_55681.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_55681.jpg)

**Minbar and Mihrab**  
 Along with majority of the internal architecture, the minbar and mihrab are all composed of white marble as well.

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 7](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_interior_118201.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_interior_118201.jpg)

**Prayer Hall**  
 The mosque has two main prayer areas one in the south and the other in the north connected by two roofed colonnades on the eastern and the western sides, arranged around a central courtyard. The main prayer hall (pictured here) is situated on the southern end of the mosque's central building. The southern prayer hall is topped by six larger domes, norther prayer area is topped with 32 smaller domes, and the colonnades are topped by even smaller domes.

The one-bayed portico which borders it on the north, separates the main body of the mosque from the women's prayer area. The women's prayer area, which is surrounded by a screen, is divided into two parts as a passageway connects the northern entrance with the courtyard.

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

#### Notable Landmarks in the Vicinity

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 8](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/unavailable.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/unavailable.jpg)

**House of _Kulthum bin al-Hedm_**  
 The house of noble companion _Kulthum bin al-Hedm_ (موضع دار كلثوم بن الهدم), from the _Banu 'Amr bin 'Awf_ of the _Aws_ tribe, was situated on the southern side of the current structure of the _Masjid Quba_. He died shortly after the prophet Muhammad's migration to _Madinah_ from Mecca. Today nothing remains of the historic residential structure, but it was situated south-east of the _Saad bin Khaithamah_'s house. This is where prophet Muhammad is believed to have resided during his stay in Quba before arriving in the ancient city of Yathrib. During the migration to _Madinah_ a number of other _Sahaba_ (companions) are also known to have stayed in the same house, including _abu Bakr al-Siddiq_, _Ali ibn abi Talib_, _al-Miqdad bin Amr_, _Khabbab bin al-Aratt_, _abu Ubaidah bin al-Jarrah_, _Saad bin Khawla_ among others.

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 9](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/unavailable.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/unavailable.jpg)

**House of _Saad bin Khaythamah_**  
 The site associated or maked as the house of _Saad bin Khaythamah_, who belonged to the _Bani al-Salam_ from the _Aws_ tribe, was situated adjacent to the south-western corner of the modern _Masjid Quba_. _Saad bin Khaythamah_ was martyred in the Battle of _Badr_. Prophet Muhammad is said to have hosted his visitors and coducted meetings with delegates in _Saad_'s house since it was situated close to the house of _Kulthum_.

_Saad_ also hosted several of the companions during their migration from Mecca, including _Hamza ibn Abdul Muttalib_, _Zaid bin Haritha_, _abu Marthad al-Ghanawi_, _Abdullah bin Mas'ud_, _Dhu al-Shamalayn bin abd Amr_, _Suhaib al-Rum_, _Bilal ibn Rabaha_ (commonly known as the _Bilal Habashi_, literally meaning _Bilal the Abyssinian_) among others.

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 10](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bir_khatim_quba_181032.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bir_khatim_quba_181032.jpg)

**_Bir Khatim_**  
 Also known as the _Bir al-Arees_ (also spelled as _Bir al-Aris_ literally meaning the "Well of the Ring") the _Bir al-Khatam_ is one of the historical wells dating back to the pre-Islamic period, located south-west of the modern Masjid al-Quba. The name of the historic well comes from the incident of prophet Muhammad's ring falling in to this well during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan.

The well holds significance due to its affiliation with the prophet Muhammad, as mentioned in his biographies. It is said that the prophet once sat in the water basin with two horns of the well (_qif_) with the first caliph Abu Bakr to his right and secon caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab to his right and Uthman ibn Affan (the third caliph) in front. It was here that the _Bisharah_ (glad tidings) of the _Jannah_ (paradise) to the three. Today a roundel inside a square marks the spot

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

#### Gallery [Want to use our images?](javascript:;)

[![Image 11](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_22881.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_22881.jpg)

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

#### Notes

*   The destruction or burning of _Masjid al-Dirar_, literally meaning the Mosque of Dissent, is recorded in the Quran. Situated near the Quba Mosque in _Madinah_, _Masjid al-Dirar_ initially gained approval from Prophet Muhammad but was later demolished upon his return from the Expedition to Tabouk in October 630 CE. According to most scholars, the mosque was constructed by 12 hypocrites, following the directives of _Abu 'Amir al-Rahib_, a _Hanif_ who rejected Muhammad's call to Islam and allied with the Meccan non-Muslims in the Battle of Uhud. _Abu 'Amir_ encouraged his followers to fortify the mosque and gather arms, suggesting plans for an army, purportedly supported by Heraclius, to oust Muhammad from Medina (known as Yathrib at the time). _Ahmad ibn Yahya al-Baladhuri_ further recounts that those behind the construction and operation of _Masjid al-Dirar_ aimed to cause discord among the believers and refused to pray at the Quba Mosque, asserting it was built where a donkey had once been tethered. Prophet Muhammad prepared himself to go to the Masjid Dirar, but was prevented by a revelation about the hypocrisy and ill designs of the builders of the Mosque. Upon learning that these men were hypocrites (_munafiqeen_) and had ulterior motives for building the _Masjid al-Dirar_, he ordered the companions to burn it down. According to the Islamic tradition, prophet Muhammad was requested to lead prayer there but received a revelation (mentioned in the Qur'anic verses 9:107 and 9:110) after which the mosque was destroyed by fire. Henceforth, it was known as the "Mosque of Opposition".

[](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque)

#### See Also

# Mataf

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

Mataf (Arabic: المطاف, al-maṭāf) is the designated circumambulatory area surrounding the Kaʿba within [al-Masjid al-Ḥarām](https://madainproject.com/gates_of_masjid_al_haram "Gates of Masjid al-Haram (Great Mosque of Mecca)") (the Sacred Mosque) in modern day [Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Mecca"), [Saudi Arabia](https://madainproject.com/saudi_arabia "Saudi Arabia"). It is the space in which ṭawāf—the ritual circumambulation of the [Kaʿba](https://madainproject.com/kaaba "Kabah") performed seven times counterclockwise—is carried out as a central rite of the [ḥajj](https://madainproject.com/hajj "Hajj") and [ʿUmrah](https://madainproject.com/mataf "Umrah") pilgrimages.

#### Contents Hide / Show

*   [Overview](https://madainproject.com/mataf#overview)
*   [Historic Structures](https://madainproject.com/mataf#historic-structures)
    *   [Bab Bani Shaibah and Zamzam](https://madainproject.com/mataf#bab-bani-shaibah-and-zamzam)

#### Overview

Total area of current Mataf's ground floor is about 14,000 square meters. The [Ka'ba](https://madainproject.com/kaaba "Kabah") (الكعبة) is located in the center of Mataf area, along with [Hateem](https://madainproject.com/mataf "Hateem") (_Hajr Ismaeel_) and [Maqam Ibrahim](https://madainproject.com/station_of_abraham "Maqam e Ibrahim"). The Mataf area was originally just sands, and was first plastered by 'Abdullah ibn Zubayr, since then Mataaf has seen countless, building and rebuilding developments. Current Mataf floor is paved with Carrara marble.

Although, during its long history the Mataf area has seen several renovations, major changes were made during [Ottoman Empire](https://madainproject.com/mataf "Ottoman Empire") period and subsequent Saudi era. During 1940s and 1950s CE it was extended from 40 meters to 50 meters in a circular shape. In the interests of the pilgrims performing Hajj and Umrah, the Ottoman pulpit, the platform used for Adhaan and some pathways were removed from the Mataf.

Other than the _Shia Madhab_ who specify the maximum extent of Mataf to the _Maqam Ibrahim_, no other schools of thought restrict the outer limit of Mataf.

[![Image 2](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_83274832.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_83274832.jpg)

[](https://madainproject.com/mataf)

#### Historic Structures

[](https://madainproject.com/mataf)

circa 1930 CE

[![Image 3](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/kaaba_8248299.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/kaaba_8248299.jpg)

**Bab Bani Shaibah and ZamZam**  
 Previously the Mataf area had several structures built within, including Zam Zam building, [Bab Bani Shaybah](https://madainproject.com/bab_bani_shaiba "Bab Bani Shaiba") (باب بني شيبة), an Ottoman era pulpit (minbar), Mukkabariya (Adhan platform). Some of the these were removed during the first Saudi expansion of Masjid al-Haram and some were removed late on to allow the Hajis (pilgrims) perform Tawaf with ease.

[](https://madainproject.com/mataf)

circa 1920 CE

[![Image 4](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mataf_maqamat_66278.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mataf_maqamat_66278.jpg)

**_Maqāmāt_**  
 Up until the first Saudi expansion of Masjid al-Haram, there used to be four stations ([identify](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mataf_maqamat_66279.jpg)) dedicated to the Imams of four _Madhahibs_. These four "_[Maqamat](https://madainproject.com/maqamat\_of\_the\_four\_imams "Maqamat of the Four Imams")_" were established some time before 1326 CE (726 Hj.). Each shrine was a chapel for the imams to lead prayer of followers of each doctrine (Madhhab) of the four schools (Shafali, Hanafi, Hambali, Maliki).

[](https://madainproject.com/mataf)

circa 1920 CE

[![Image 5](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mataf_00362.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mataf_00362.jpg)

**List of Structures in Mataf**  
 During the Ottoman era a large number of structures, stood in the _al-Mataf_ around the Kabah. Some of these are pictured here, from left to right:   
 1. [Bab Bani Shaibah](https://madainproject.com/bab_bani_shaiba "Bab Bani Shaiba"),  
 2. [Hateem](https://madainproject.com/mataf "Hateem") (not pictured),  
 3. [Zamzam well](https://madainproject.com/zam_zam "Zam Zam Well") building,  
 4. [Kabah Staircase](https://madainproject.com/kabah_stairway "Access Staircase of Kabah"),  
 5. Older set of [staircase of Kabah](https://madainproject.com/kabah_stairway "Access Staircase of Kabah"),  
 6. [Maqam Ibrahim](https://madainproject.com/station_of_abraham "Maqam e Ibrahim"),  
 7. Ottoman pulpit.

[](https://madainproject.com/mataf)

#### Construction Plaque of Jaffar al-Mansur

circa 1254 CE   
(631 Hj.)

[![Image 6](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mosques_exhibit_2738.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mosques_exhibit_2738.jpg)

Inscription on a marble slab, today preserved in the [Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques' Architecture](https://madainproject.com/exhibition_of_the_two_holy_mosques_architecture "Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques' Architecture") (معرض عمارة الحرمين الشريفين), marking the date for the construction of the Mataf during the reign of Abbaid caliph abi Ja'far al-Mansur al-Muntasir Billah in the year 611 Hj. The Mataf area has been rebuilt, redeveloped and expanded over the centuries.

[](https://madainproject.com/mataf)

#### Third Saudi Expansion

circa 2020 CE

[![Image 7](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/tawaf_distance_23483288.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/tawaf_distance_23483288.jpg)

After the [King 'Abdullah Expansion](https://madainproject.com/king_abdullah_expansion "King Abdullah Expansion") the Mataf area is at its largest in its over 1500 year history. Performing tawaf closest to the Kaba constitutes about 75-80 meters per tawaf. And a total seven tawafs around Kaabah would make about 525-600 meter (about half a kilo meter). The circle of tawaf begins and ends at the [Black Stone](https://madainproject.com/black_stone_(hajar_al_aswad) "Black Stone (Hajar al-Aswad)") (_al-Ḥajar al-'Aswad_) on the corner of the Kaaba. If possible, [Muslims](https://madainproject.com/mataf "Muslims") are to kiss or touch it, but this is often not possible because of the large crowds, so it is acceptable for them to simply point or hold up their hand to the Stone on each circuit.

[](https://madainproject.com/mataf)

#### Notable Incidents

[](https://madainproject.com/mataf)

circa 2020 CE

[![Image 8](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mataf_74832.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mataf_74832.jpg)

**COVID-19 Closure**  
 The Mataf, (area for circumambulation around the Kaaba) at the Grand Mosque in Makkah was closed down for about two days during the 2019-20 COVID-19 outbreak. The Mataf along with [Mas'a](https://madainproject.com/al_masaa_(masjid_al_haram) "Masa'a (Masjid al-Haram)") (area for sa’i between Safa and Marwah) and the [Rawdah al-Sharifah](https://madainproject.com/tomb_of_prophet_muhammad "Tomb of Muhammad") was closed down for about two days, from 5th till 7th March 2020, to be disinfected over fears of the coronavirus. It is one of the rarest events, as the [Great Mosque of Mecca](https://madainproject.com/gates_of_masjid_al_haram "Gates of Masjid al-Haram (Great Mosque of Mecca)") (Masjid al-Haram) remains open round the clock.

The Madain Project is an online archive of Abrahamic History and Archaeology.

Abrahamic History & Archaeology is the study of history and archaeology with respect to the three Abrahamic Faiths without considering the religious and theological aspects. The goal of Abrahamic History is to understand how and why the religious doctrines and behaviours have evolved and changed over time. Searching for patterns in the evolution of significant cultural events such as the development of farming, the emergence of cities, or the collapse of major civilizations for clues of why and how these have influenced the three major Abrahamic religions.

# Mecca

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

Mecca also spelled Makkah (مكة المكرمة), is a city in the [Hejazi region](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Hejaz") of Saudi Arabia. As the birthplace of prophet [Muḥammad](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Prophet Muhammad") and the site of first revelation of the [Quran](https://madainproject.com/quran "Quran"), Mecca is regarded as the holiest city in [Islam](https://madainproject.com/islamic_archaeology "Islam"). According to Islamic tradition, the history of Mecca goes back to prophet [Abraham](https://madainproject.com/abraham "Abraham") (_Ibrahim_), who built the holy sancturay of [Kaaba](https://madainproject.com/kaaba "Kabah") with the help of his elder son [Ishmael](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Ishmael") in circa 2000 BCE, when the inhabitants of the site then known as Bakkah had fallen away from the original monotheism of Abraham through the influence of the [Amalekites](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Amalek / Amalekites").

Back to [Saudi Arabia](https://madainproject.com/saudi_arabia "Saudi Arabia") / [Arabia](https://madainproject.com/arabia "Arabia") / [Middle East](https://madainproject.com/middle_east "Middle East") / [Asia](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Asia")

[![Image 2: Ancient Mecca](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mecca_timeline_478718.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mecca_timeline_478718.jpg "Ancient Mecca")

[](https://madainproject.com/mecca)

### Brief History of Mecca

According to Islamic tradition, the origins of Mecca can be traced back to figures from the [Bible](https://madainproject.com/bible "Bible"), namely [Abraham](https://madainproject.com/abraham "Abraham"), [Hagar](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Hagar"), and [Ishmael](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Ishmael"). They were eventually joined by some members of the Yemeni tribe of [Jurhum](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Jurhum") and the settlement began to grow. It is recounted that a member of the Jurhum tribe assisted Ishmael and his father in constructing the _Ka'bah_. This act held profound social, religious, political, and historical significance for the site and the broader region. With time, the city of Makkah, nestled amidst the desolate landscapes of the [Arabian Peninsula](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Arabin Peninsula"), was inhabited by various Arabian tribes and developed in to a significant center for trade and commerce due to its strategic location along important caravan routes.

In the pre-Islamic era, Mecca was already a bustling hub of commerce and spirituality. The city served as a prominent center of Arabian paganism, with the Ka'bah housing numerous idols revered by various tribes across the Arabian Peninsula. Mecca's status as a pilgrimage site attracted pilgrims from far and wide, contributing to its economic significance. However, Mecca's history during this period is marked by tribal rivalries, nomadic lifestyles, and a diverse tapestry of cultural and religious beliefs, all of which would undergo a profound transformation with the [advent of Islam](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Advent of Islam") in the seventh century CE.

[History of Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca "History of Mecca")

[](https://madainproject.com/mecca)

### Archaeology of Mecca

[![Image 3: Bab Bani Shaybah](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_23842231.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/bab_bani_shaiba "Bab Bani Shaiba")
### Bab Bani Shaybah

The _Bab Bani Shaybah_ was a symbolic gate dating back to the time of prophet Muhammad, located on the north-eastern side of the Kaaba. It was named after the _Bani Shaybah_ tribe, one of the Arab tribes residing in the area adjacent to the entrance. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/bab_bani_shaiba "Bab Bani Shaiba")

[![Image 4: Wadi Muhassar](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/elephant_year_823.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/wadi_muhassar "Wadi e Muhassar")
### Wadi Muhassar

Wadi Muhassar, located east of the Great Mosque of Mecca (Masjid al-Haram), is believed to be the stage of destruction of Abraha's army, when he tried to march on the Kaaba with the intention of destroying it. Though identified with the historic event, its location is not certain. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/wadi_muhassar "Wadi e Muhassar")

[![Image 5: Masjid Bay'ah](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bayah_masjid_3283.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/bayah_mosque "Bayah Mosque")
### Masjid Bay'ah

Also known as the Mosque of Pledge, it is believed to be located on the site where the prophet Muhammad met with the two delegations (first in the 11th and second in the 13th year of Nabawi) from Yathrib (later called Medina) and took oath of allegiance from them. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/bayah_mosque "Bayah Mosque")

[![Image 6](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mecca_timeline_162937.jpg) ### Pictorial Timeline of Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca_through_time "Mecca Through Time")

## Featured[Pictorial Timeline of Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca_through_time "Mecca Through Time")

In the Islamic view, the beginnings of Mecca are attributed to Ishmael's descendants. The Old Testament chapter Psalm 84:3–6, and a mention of a pilgrimage at the Valley of Baca, that Muslims see as referring to the mentioning of Mecca as Bakkah in Quran's Surah 3:96. Some time in the 5th century, the Kaaba was a place of worship for the deities of Arabia's pagan tribes.

[Explore](https://madainproject.com/mecca_through_time "Mecca Through Time")

[![Image 7: al-Malik 'Abdullah Expansion of Masjid al-Haram](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_82373848.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/king_abdullah_expansion "King Abdullah Expansion")
### al-Malik 'Abdullah Expansion

The Malik 'Abdullah Expansion (توسعة الملك عبدالله) of Masjid al-Haram was launched in 2011 CE, by the then King 'Abdullah bin Abdulaziz al-Saud. It is the third Saudi expansion and by far the largest, covering an area of approximately 300,000 square metres (3,200,000 sq ft). [Read more](https://madainproject.com/king_abdullah_expansion "King Abdullah Expansion")

[![Image 8: Jabal Thawr](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jabal_thawr_00182.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/mount_thawr "Jabal Thawr")
### Mount Thawr

Mount Thawr, situated to the south of Mecca's city center, is one of the notable geographic features in the region. It is inside one of its caves that the Prophet Muhammad, along with Abu Bakr, sought refuge during the migration from Mecca to Medina in the year 622 CE. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/mount_thawr "Jabal Thawr")

[![Image 9: Masjid al-Haram](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_83247332.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram "Masjid al-Haram")
### Masjid al-Haram

Masjid al-Haram (Great Mosque of Mecca) is situated in the city center of Mecca, in the Hejaz region of Saudi Arabia. It is the focal point for Islamic pilgrimage (Hajj) and lesser pilgrimage (Umrah), rituals that date back to the time of the Prophet Ibrahim and his family. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram "Masjid al-Haram")

[![Image 10: Mosque of Ascension, Jerusalem](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jannat_mualla_00128.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_mualla_before_demolitions "Jannat ul-Mualla before Demolitions")
### Pre 1926 Jannat ul-Mualla

Jannat al-Mu'alla is known for being the final resting place of several prominent figures in early Islamic history, including many members of the Prophet Muhammad's family, notably, of Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, and Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib, his uncle and guardian. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_mualla_before_demolitions "Jannat ul-Mualla before Demolitions")

[![Image 11: Masjid al-Taneem](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_taneem_66827.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_taneem "Masjid e Tan'eem")
### Masjid al-Taneem

Masjid al-Taneem, also known as the Masjid Aisha, is situated approximately 7 kilometers from the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca. It is located to the south of the city and is one of the points of entry (_miqat_) for pilgrims coming to Mecca from outside the Haram area. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_taneem "Masjid e Tan'eem")

[![Image 12: Safa and Marwah](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/safa_2384723.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/safa_and_marwah "Safa and Marwah")
### Safa and Marwah

Safa and Marwah are two small hills, now incorporated inside the Masjid al-Haram complex. According to Islamic tradition, the hills of Safa and Marwah are associated with Hagar (Hajar in Arabic), the wife of the Prophet Abraham (Ibrahim in Arabic), and their son Ismail. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/safa_and_marwah "Safa and Marwah")

## Featured[Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques' Architecture](https://madainproject.com/exhibition_of_the_two_holy_mosques_architecture "Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques' Architecture")

The "Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques' Architecture" is a showcase of the architectural splendor and historical significance of two of the holiest sites in Islam, namely the Masjid al-Haram (the Grand Mosque) in Mecca and the Masjid al-Nabawi (the Prophet's Mosque) in Medina. It is located on the north-western edge of Makkah. Discover how the Great Mosque of Mecca and Masjid Nabawi in Madinah have transformed over the centuries. Explore a plethora of historical and archaeological exhibits.

[Explore](https://madainproject.com/exhibition_of_the_two_holy_mosques_architecture "Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques' Architecture")

[![Image 13](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mosques_exhibit_2726.jpg) ### Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques' Architecture](https://madainproject.com/exhibition_of_the_two_holy_mosques_architecture "Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques' Architecture")

[![Image 14: Masjid al-Jinn (Makkah)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jinn_masjid_13729.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/jinn_mosque_(mecca) "Jinn Mosque (Mecca)")
### Masjid al-Jinn

According to Islamic tradition, the Prophet Muhammad was once reciting the Quran during Salah at this site, when a group of jinn came to listen. This event is described in Surah al-Jinn (Chapter 72) of the Quran. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/jinn_mosque_(mecca) "Jinn Mosque (Mecca)")

[![Image 15: Masjid al-Shajarah (Makkah)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/shajarah_masjid_11738.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/masjid_shajarah_(mecca) "Masjid Shajarah (Mecca)")
### Masjid al-Shajarah

It is a small mosque in the neighbourhood of _Shi'b 'Aamir_ (Valley of _'Aamir_), it marks the spot where the "miracle of the tree" is believed to have happened. It is located close to the historic _Masjid al-Jinn_ and _Masjid al-Rayah_. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/masjid_shajarah_(mecca) "Masjid Shajarah (Mecca)")

[![Image 16: Masjid al-Rayah (Makkah)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/alrayah_masjid_11829.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/al_rayah_mosque_(mecca) "Rayah Mosque (Mecca)")
### Masjid al-Rayah

Islamic historic accounts relate that prophet Muhammad entered the city of Mecca on the day of the Fateh Makkah from here. The mosque is believed to have been first built by 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/al_rayah_mosque_(mecca) "Rayah Mosque (Mecca)")

[![Image 17: Jannatul Mualla](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jannat_mualla_37267.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_mualla "Jannat ul-Muallah")
### al-Mualla Cemetery

Jannat al-Mu'alla is known for being the final resting place of many important figures in Islamic history, including several close relatives of the Prophet Muhammad. This includes his wife Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, his grandfather Abdul Muttalib, and many others. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_mualla "Jannat ul-Muallah")

[![Image 18: Jabal Nour](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jabal_noor_10289.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/jabal_al_nour "Jabal al-Nour (Mount Hira)")
### Jabal Nour

The Cave of Hira is situated on the slopes of Jabal al-Nour. It was in this cave that the Prophet Muhammad used to retreat for meditation and reflection even before the advent of Islam, and then received first _Wahi_ through Angel Gabriel. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/jabal_al_nour "Jabal al-Nour (Mount Hira)")

[![Image 19: Masjid Nimrah Mashar Arafat](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_nimrah_mashar_arafat_hejaz_saudi_arabia_makkah_history_924512.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nimrah_(arafat) "Masjid Nimrah Bi-Mashar Arafat")
### Masjid al-Nimrah

Masjid al-Namirah plays a central role during the Hajj pilgrimage. On the ninth day of Dhul-Hijjah, known as the Day of Arafah, the annual Hajj sermon is delivered from its pulpit to hundreds of thousands of pilgrims who gather around the site. The combined Dhuhr and Asr prayers are performed here, following the practice established by the Prophet during his Farewell Pilgrimage. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nimrah_(arafat) "Masjid Nimrah Bi-Mashar Arafat")

[![Image 20](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ashab_alfil_3782.jpg) ### Companions of the Elephant](https://madainproject.com/companions_of_the_elephant "Compaions of the Elephant")

## Featured[Companions of the Elephant](https://madainproject.com/companions_of_the_elephant "Compaions of the Elephant")

Historically, in Islamic tradition the companions or the people of the elephant are identified with an army of Abraha, so-called because it included a number of war elephants. He felt slighted by the Quraysh, and planned to exact revenge by destroying the kaaba. The principal source on Abraha outside of Islamic tradition is a series of six inscriptions, of which four were written by the sovereign himself.

[Explore](https://madainproject.com/companions_of_the_elephant "Compaions of the Elephant")

#### Overview

According to non-Muslim scholars, Islam started during the lifetime of prophet Muhammad in the early 7th century (circa 610 CE), and so did architectural components such as the mosque. In this case, either the [Mosque of the Companions](https://madainproject.com/as_sahaba_mosque_(massawa) "as-Sahabah Mosque") in the Eritrean city of Massawa, or the [Quba Mosque](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque "Masjid al-Quba") in the Hejazi city of Medina (the first structure built by Muhammad upon his emigration from Mecca in 622 CE), would be the first mosque that was built in the history of Islam.

After the Quba Mosque, prophet Muhammad went on to establish another mosque in Medina, which is now known as al-Masjid an-Nabawi (The Prophet's Mosque). prophet Muhammad participated in the construction of the mosque himself and this structed became the social and cultural focal point of the ancient city of Medina. From then onwards a large number of mosques were built across the entire city, and more were added as the city expanded outwards.

[![Image 2](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_nabawi_0002366.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_nabawi_0002366.jpg)

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

#### List of the Mosques

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa 709 CE

[![Image 3](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/dhul_hulaifah_77928.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/dhul_hulaifah_77928.jpg "Masjid u Shajarah (one of the miqat), Dhul Hulaifah, Medina")

**as-Shajarah Mosque**  
 The [Masjid as-Shajarah](https://madainproject.com/miqat_dhul_hulaifah_mosque "Miqat Dhul Hulaifah Mosque") (مسجد الشجرة), also known as the Miqat Dhu al-Ḥulayfah, is located in the area of Abyar Ali, west of Wadi al-Aqiq some twelve kilometers from the Prophet's Mosque. It is one of the Miqaat stations (places where ihram is put on), situated [in Dhul Hulaifah](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Dhul Hulaifah"). It is the place where pilgrims coming from Medina wishing to perform Umrah or Hajj enter into ihram before they set for Mecca. The current mosque building was built during the reign of King Fahd. It is in the shape of a square of an area of approximately 6,000 square meters (65,000 ft2) inside a 36,000 m2 (388,000 ft2) square-shaped enclosure.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 4](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ijabah_masjid_2838.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ijabah_masjid_2838.jpg "Ejabah Mosque")

**Ijabah Mosque**  
 The [Masjid Ijabah](https://madainproject.com/al_ijabah_mosque "Ijabah Mosque (Medina)") (مسجد الإجابة) also known as _Masjid Bani Muawiya_ or _Masjid al-Mubahalah_ is approx 385 meters to the north of [Jannat ul-Baqi](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_baqi "Jannat ul Baqi"). It is known as Masjid e Ijabah (the mosque of approval/acceptance) and is approx. 600 meters away from Masjid al-Nabawi in the Bani Muawiya district. This particular mosque derives its significance from an account mentioned in a Hadith of Sahih Muslim, relating that once Prophet Muhammad passed the Bani Muawiyah Mosque, entered there and offered two rakats, and his companions also followed him.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 5](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/fatah_masjid_4782.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/fatah_masjid_4782.jpg "al-Fatah Mosque, built at the place where command post of prophet Muhammad was located during Ahzab battle.")

**al-Fatah Mosque**  
 The [al-Fatah Mosque](https://madainproject.com/al_fatah_mosque_(seven_mosques)) (مسجد الفتح) is the most significant one of the [Seven Mosques](https://madainproject.com/seven_mosques "Seven Mosques"), situated at the site of the [Battle of Ahzab](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of the Trench"). Largest of the seven mosques the masjid al-Fath is situated on a small hilltop near the western side of Sal’ mountain. It was first built when Umar ibn Abd Al-Aziz was governor of Madinah in the years 87 to 93 after Hijrah (705 CE to 711 CE). It was rebuilt in 1179 CE (575 Hj.) again. It was then rebuilt again during the reign of the Ottoman Sultan Abd Al-Majid I in 1851 CE. The modern structure is nearly square with a roofed hall towards the south fronted by a small courtyard towards the north. A large flight of stairs leads to the entrance, situated in the eastern wall of the courtyard.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 6](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/manaratain_mosque_8283.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/manaratain_mosque_8283.jpg "Masjid al-Manaratain, The Mosque of the Two Minarets")

**al-Manaratain Mosque**  
 The [Masjid al-Manaratain](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Masjid al-Manaratain") (مسجد المنارتين), mosque of the two towers or minarets, (also known as the _Masjid e Bani Dinaar_) originally a crude basalt structure it was rebuilt and expanded during the reign of Fahad bin Abdul 'Aziz in 2003 CE (1424 Hj.). It is situated on the main highway going towards Mecca near al-Anbariya. Another reason for the name is attributed to its location; because it is located in between two mountains which were dubbed as two towers.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 7](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_nabawi_3842939.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_nabawi_3842939.jpg "Masjid al-Nabawi (The Mosque of the prophet)")

**Masjid Nabawi**  
 The [Masjid al-Nabawi](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi") (مسجد النبوي) often called the Prophet's Mosque, is a historic mosque situated in the city of al-Madinah, Saudi Arabia. As the final resting place of Prophet Muhammad, it is considered the second holiest site in the world after Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, ([al-Aqsa](https://madainproject.com/al_aqsa_mosque "al-Aqsa Mosque") in Jerusalem comes in at third). It is a major pilgrimage site and many people who perform the Hajj also go on to al-Madinah before or after Hajj to visit the mosque.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 8](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/salman_farsi_masjid_823782.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/salman_farsi_masjid_823782.jpg "Mosque of Salman the Persian")

**Salman Farsi Mosque**  
 The [mosque of Salman Farsi](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Mosque of Salman the Persian") (مسجد سلمان الفارسي), another one of the _Masajid Saba'_, is located south of the al-Fath Mosque, 20 meters from the base of Sal' mountain. It is named after Salman, the companion of the Prophet Muhammad who recommended digging a trench to fortify the city during [Ghazwa-i Ahzab](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of the Trench"). It has one hall at 7 meters long and 2 meters wide. Originally built when Umar ibn Abd Al-Aziz was governor of Madinah. In 575 H (1179 CE) it was rebuilt on the orders of minister Said Al-Deen Abu Al-Haija. It was rebuilt again during the reign of the Ottoman Sultan Abd Al-Majid I.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 9](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_233288.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_233288.jpg "Masjid-e Quba")

**Quba Mosque**  
 The site of [Masjid Quba](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque "Masjid al-Quba") (مَـسْـجِـد قُـبَـاء), back then a small town on the outskirts of Medina, was the last stop made by the prophet Muhammad during his [Hijrah](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Hijrah") from [Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Mecca") before reaching the city of Medina. It's construction was initiated by prophet Muhammad and was completed by the companions, it was left in ruins by 1905 CE, rebuilt as a simple structure and renovated by the mid of the twentieth century. Depending on whether the [Mosque of the Companions](https://madainproject.com/as_sahaba_mosque_(massawa) "as-Sahabah Mosque") in the Eritrean city of Massawa is older or not, it may be the first mosque in the world that dates to the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad, 7th century CE.

circa

# Masjid al-Qiblatain (Medina)

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

The Masjid al-Qiblatayn (مَسْجِد ٱلْقِبْلَتَیْن‎), 'Mosque of the Two Qiblas', is a mosque in [Medina](https://madainproject.com/medina "Medina tu-Nabi") that is historically important for [Muslims](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Muslims") as the place where, after [prophet Muhammad](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Prophet Muhammad") received the command to change the [_Qiblah_](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Qibla") (Direction of Prayer) from [Jerusalem](https://madainproject.com/jerusalem "Jerusalem") to [Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Mecca"), the entire congregation led by a companion changed direction in prayer. The name of the mosque goes back to the lifetime of Muhammad, when his [companions](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "List of Sahabah") named it after an event that took place.

#### Overview

The Qiblatayn Mosque is among the earliest mosques that date to the time of Muhammad, along with the [Quba Mosque](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque "Masjid al-Quba"), [Prophet's Mosque](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi") and possible the [Masjid as-Sahaba](https://madainproject.com/as_sahaba_mosque_(massawa) "as-Sahabah Mosque"), considering that the Great Mosque of [Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Mecca") and the [Haram as-Sharif](https://madainproject.com/haram_al_sharif_(al_quds) "Haram al-Sharif (al-Quds)") in [Jerusalem](https://madainproject.com/jerusalem "Jerusalem") are associated with earlier [Prophets](https://madainproject.com/prophets_of_abrahamic_religions "Prophets of Abrahamic Religions") in Islamic thought. Most recently it was renovated, circa 1988 CE, during the reign of Malik Fahad bin 'Abdulaziz al-Sa'ud.

[![Image 2](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_7382.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_7382.jpg)

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain)

#### Tradition of the Change of the Qibla

circa 622 CE

[![Image 3](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_9027.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_9027.jpg)

Prophet Muhammad received revelation from [Allah](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain) instructing him to take the holy [Kaaba](https://madainproject.com/kaaba "Kabah") as the Qibla in the early morning hours of the day, instead of the Qibla of the [Jews](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Jews"), that is the [Temple Mount](https://madainproject.com/temple_mount "Temple Mount") in the [Old City](https://madainproject.com/old_city_of_jerusalem "Old City of Jerusalem") of [Jerusalem](https://madainproject.com/jerusalem "Jerusalem"). He announced this to his companions in his own mosque, after which the news began to spread. A companion who heard this went to Masjid al-Qiblatayn to share this news. Upon arriving, he noticed the congregation were already engaged in the afternoon prayer.

He called out from the back of the mosque that the change of direction has been ordained, and upon hearing this, the imam (leader of the prayer) immediately turned around to face Mecca, and those praying behind him also did so. Another tradition recounts that it was the prophet himself who was leading the prayer, and the revelation came during the _Salah_. There's another mosque in Zeila, Somali which is also known as the [Masjid al-Qiblatayn](https://madainproject.com/masjid_qiblatayn_(somalia) "Masjid Qiblatain (Somalia)"), after the same tradition.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain)

#### Architecture

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 4](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_9064.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_9064.jpg)

**_Mihrab al-Quds_**  
 Before the most recent renovation the Qiblatain Mosque uniquely contained two Mihrabs (Prayer niches), one facing Mecca and one facing Jerusalem, hence the name "Mosque of the two Qiblas". During modern renovations the Mehrab facing Mecca was left but the Mehrab facing al-Quds (Jerusalem) was removed and a small marker mihrab was installed overhead. It is located below a false dome which is linked to the first by a small cross-vault to symbolise the transition from one qibla to another. The design is a reproduction of the mihrab Suleimani ([inspect](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/well_of_souls_277371.jpg)) found in the [lower chamber](https://madainproject.com/well_of_souls_(temple_mount) "Well of Souls") of the [_Qubbat al-Sakhara_](https://madainproject.com/dome_of_the_rock "Dome of the Rock") in Jerusalem reminds onlookers of the oldest extant mihrab of [Islam](https://madainproject.com/islamic_archaeology "Islam").

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 5](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_0946.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_0946.jpg)

**Main Prayer Hall**  
 The main prayer hall adopts rigid orthogonal geometry and symmetry which is accentuated by the use of twin minarets and twin domes. The prayer hall consists of a series of arches which support barrel-vaults running parallel to the qibla wall. These vaults are interrupted by two domes which establish an axis in the direction of Mecca. The main dome to the south is raised on a drum of clerestory windows ([inspect](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_4832.jpg)) which allow light to filter into the interior directly above the mihrab.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 6](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_8843.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_8843.jpg)

**Exterior**  
 Externally, the architectural vocabulary is inspired by traditional elements and motifs in a deliberate effort to offer an authentic image for an historic site. The mosque is located on the north-west of the city of Medina, on Khalid bin al-Waleed road. The mosque was initially maintained by Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattāb. By the rise of the [Ottoman Empire](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Ottoman Empire") the mosque was maintained by Sultan [Suleiman the Magnificent](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Sultan Suleiman the Magnificient") who renovated and reconstructed it.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain)

circa 622 CE

[![Image 7](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_8415.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_8415.jpg)

**Underground Facilities**  
 Entry to the prayer hall is from the raised courtyard, also to the north, which can be reached by stairs and ramps from the main directions of approach. A sub-basement level is incorporated in the southeast corner of the mosque, which serves as the ablutions area for worshippers.

The Madain Project is an online archive of Abrahamic History and Archaeology.

Abrahamic History & Archaeology is the study of history and archaeology with respect to the three Abrahamic Faiths without considering the religious and theological aspects. The goal of Abrahamic History is to understand how and why the religious doctrines and behaviours have evolved and changed over time. Searching for patterns in the evolution of significant cultural events such as the development of farming, the emergence of cities, or the collapse of major civilizations for clues of why and how these have influenced the three major Abrahamic religions.

## **2.0 Information We Collect and How We Use It**[](https://support.scribd.com/hc/articles/210129366-Privacy-policy#h_01KCM3H9JBTRD7ZP3WYGCWWXY3)

The information that we collect and how we use or disclose it depends on your relationship with us and any applicable laws and regulations. In this section, we describe some of the ways that we collect and use information and the legal bases for doing so. We endeavor to collect only the limited amount of information that is relevant for the purposes of Processing as described in this Policy and its related policies as noted in Section 1.0.

If you apply for a job with Scribd or otherwise engage with us in connection with employment (including as an employee, contractor, or other personnel), the personal information we process in that context is subject to our Employee and Applicant Privacy Policy, which is available [here](https://support.scribd.com/hc/en-us/articles/49754646187284-Employee-and-Applicant-Privacy-Policy-and-Notice-at-Collection).

### **2.1 How We Collect Information**[](https://support.scribd.com/hc/articles/210129366-Privacy-policy#h_01KCM3H9JC66RCD2P270VWE3W6)

The data that we collect from or about you depends on how you use the Services or interact with us. Some of the ways that we Process your personal information (“Personal Information”) may include when you:

*   Register for an account; register for or attend an event;
*   Subscribe to or purchase a product;
*   Participate in a contest, promotion, or survey;
*   Sign up to receive information, including marketing, from us;
*   Use our Services, including submitting content or feedback to us or otherwise contact Us; or
*   Visit or engage with our Sites, Apps, Services.

### **2.2 Information You Provide to Us**[](https://support.scribd.com/hc/articles/210129366-Privacy-policy#h_01KCM3H9JEXSVNMW7D6P7MMNEH)

We collect the following information that you provide to us directly:

*   Contact information such as your name, e-mail address, street address, and phone number;
*   Payment information such as your credit card number (processed by our third-party payment processor) and expiration date, where appropriate to process a financial transaction that you have requested;
*   Transaction information such as your order (e.g., subscription) information;
*   User-Generated Content such as documents, comments, images, photos, videos, or other content you provide to the Services;
*   Profile Information if you choose to provide it, such as a profile picture, professional information (like job title and company), general location (like city and state);
*   Engagement with Interactive Content on the Service such as responses to questions, surveys; searches for recommendations; and clicks on such interactive content; and
*   Contents of communications with us,such as comments, requests, feedback and questions you submit through customer service interactions with us and recordings of calls when you call customer service.

We may use the information you provide, along with the information we collect automatically and from third parties, to make inferences about you, including your preferences and interests.

### **2.3 Information We Collect Automatically**[](https://support.scribd.com/hc/articles/210129366-Privacy-policy#h_01KCM3H9JGTW1YMNNMQ6694K2C)

We and service providers on our behalf automatically collect certain information about your use of the Services or your device. For example, we collect:

*   Device information such as hardware model, IP address, device identifiers, operating system, browser type and settings (like language and available font settings) and settings of the device you use to access the Services.
*   Usage information, including, but not limited to, your use of the Services, navigational data, the name of the domain and host from which you access the Internet, the date and time you access the Services, customer service interactions, and how you interact with our emails.
*   Location information such as general location derived from your computer’s IP address.

We and our service providers use cookies, web beacons, and other tracking technologies to collect such information.

### **2.4 Information from Third Party Sources**[](https://support.scribd.com/hc/articles/210129366-Privacy-policy#h_01KCM3H9JHHJG1SPE5W6DCAFDR)

[](https://support.scribd.com/hc/articles/210129366-Privacy-policy)We may process supplemental information about you from third parties in order to verify the information that you have provided to us and to enhance our ability to provide you with customer support and information about our businesses, products and Services. We may also occasionally offer optional service features by means of a third party application or service. We may receive information about you from these third parties if you choose to accept such offers. We may receive information about you from:

*   Publicly and commercially available data sources, as permitted by law, including contact information, demographic data, and interests.
*   Social media services,if you interact with us through a social media service or log in using social media credentials. Depending on your social media settings, we may have access to your information from that service, such as your name, email address, friend or followers/following list, profile and demographic information, current city, comments about or reactions to our Services, and the people/sites you follow.
*   Data analytics providers and advertising partners,including usage information, demographic information, information about your activity and transactions on other websites or platforms or with other companies, and inferred interests about You.

### **2.5 How We Use Your Information**[](https://support.scribd.com/hc/articles/210129366-Privacy-policy#h_01KCM3H9JJ7TM4FGWPCMMSGCEZ)

Depending on how you use the Services, we and our service providers may use your information as follows:

*   Provide Information and Services that You Request. We may use the information about you to provide you with Services or information that you request (such as information about a product or service) including to: (a) manage your account information and settings; (b) process payments; (c) ; (c) verify your identity (d) provide access to certain areas and features; and (e) permit you to register for, and participate in, online and in-person events.
*   Improve and Personalize the Services.We may use the information about you to improve and personalize the Services, including, without limitation, to: (a) measure and analyze your interest in our Sites, Apps, programs or Services; (b) perform internal quality control; and (c) personalize the Services for you.
*   Communicate with you.We may use the information about you to communicate with you, including to (a) respond to your questions, comments and requests (e.g. customer support requests and legal requests) and (b) send you communications regarding the Sites, Apps, programs, Services, your Account(s) and/or Subscription, or any changes to any company policy, terms, or agreement.
*   Market and Advertise Products and Services. We may use the information about you to provide you with materials about offers, products, and our Services. We may provide you with these materials by notification via the Services, postal mail, email, or other electronic notification as permitted by applicable laws. We may work with third parties to provide you with personalized ads on the Services through the automatic collection of information (e.g. cookies) or to advertise the Services on other sites and services. You can opt out of marketing communications at any time by clicking the unsubscribe link in any commercial communication from us. Please note that, even if you opt out of marketing communications, we may continue to send you transactional communications related to your account or use of the Services.
*   Research and Development. We may use your information to create de-identified, anonymous, or pseudonymous information that we may use, alone or in the aggregate, along with information obtained from other sources, for any purpose, including to help us to optimally deliver our existing products and services or develop new products, processes and services.
*   Surveys. We may occasionally engage third parties to conduct voluntary surveys on our behalf. Responses may be utilized to determine the effectiveness of the Services, the Company's communications, advertising campaigns, and/or promotional activities. If you participate in a survey, the information given will be used along with that of other study participants. The information collected will be used to help us to learn more about your needs and the quality of the products and services that we provide to you. We may occasionally disclose de-identified and aggregated data to third parties for research and analysis purposes.
*   Sharing Content with Friends or Colleagues. We may offer various tools and functionality that will allow you to forward or share certain content.
*   To Protect the Rights of the Services and Others and Comply with Law.We use your information if we, in good faith, believe it is necessary or appropriate to secure, protect, enforce, or defend the legal rights, privacy, safety, or property of the Services, its employees or agents, or other users, and to comply with applicable law and legal process. This includes using your information in order to prevent fraud and to protect the accuracy and integrity of financial transactions made throughout the Services and enforcing our Global Terms of Use, this Policy, and other related policies.
*   With Consent. We use your information with your consent or at your direction.
*   Deidentified and Aggregated Data. We may use your information and other information about you to create de-identified and aggregated data. Our use and disclosure of de-identified information is not subject to any restrictions under this Privacy Policy, and we may use de-identified data for research, analysis, analytics, and any other legally permissible purposes.

A **[prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/prophet "w:prophet")** is an [individual](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Individual "Individual") who, in [religious](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Religious "Religious") terms, is claimed to have been contacted by [divine](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Divine "Divine") or supernatural [entities](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Entities "Entities"), or to speak for such, serving as an intermediary with [humanity](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Humanity "Humanity"), delivering [knowledge](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Knowledge "Knowledge") or [information](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Information "Information") of such entities to others. The [message](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Message "Message") that the prophet conveys is called a **[prophecy](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Prophecy "Prophecy")**. The English word "prophet" comes from the Greek προφήτης (_profétés_) meaning advocate, and has become applied generally to anyone who makes [predictions](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Predictions "Predictions") based on nearly any means of [analysis](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Analysis "Analysis") or assessment, whether correct or not.

### [Xi'an](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Xi'an "Xi'an")

[China's ancient capital is the home of the Terracotta Warriors and has a history going back several millenia.](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Xi'an "Xi'an")

![Image 10: Xi'an](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikivoyage/en/4/45/XianBanner1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikivoyage.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)[![Image 11: Xi'an](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikivoyage/en/4/45/XianBanner1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikivoyage.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Xi'an "Xi'an")

![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Interactive_icon.svg/250px-Interactive_icon.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikivoyage.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

[![Image 13: OtBP](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8d/Right_turn_icon_white.svg/40px-Right_turn_icon_white.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikivoyage.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Previously_Off_the_beaten_path "Previously Off the beaten path")

### [Gjakova](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Gjakova "Gjakova")

[Famous for its restored Grand Bazaar, Gjakova is a cultural centre of Kosovo.](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Gjakova "Gjakova")

![Image 14: Gjakova](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikivoyage/en/6/63/BannerGjakova1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikivoyage.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)[![Image 15: Gjakova](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikivoyage/en/6/63/BannerGjakova1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikivoyage.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Gjakova "Gjakova")

### [Broadway](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Broadway "Broadway")

[One of the world's most famous streets connects many of Manhattan's top attractions to the much less busy town of Sleepy Hollow.](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Broadway "Broadway")

![Image 18: Broadway](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikivoyage/en/b/b8/BroadwayBanner1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikivoyage.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)[![Image 19: Broadway](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikivoyage/en/b/b8/BroadwayBanner1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikivoyage.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Broadway "Broadway")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Senftenberger_See.JPG/250px-Senftenberger_See.JPG?utm_source=en.wikivoyage.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/File:Senftenberger_See.JPG)

*   Fura de nono, made of cow milk and millet dough, is referred to as the **local yoghurt of [Gembu](https://en.wikivoyage.org/wiki/Gembu "Gembu")**.

## Already a donor?

Thank you for your generous support. It really makes a difference. For information on how to manage your recurring donation, please click below, or contact [donate@wikimedia.org](mailto:donate@wikimedia.org).

[Manage your donation](https://wikimediafoundation.org/give/manage-your-donation/)

## What your donation makes possible

Wikipedia is not funded through advertising, and we don’t sell your data for profit. Instead, we rely on donors — people who find value in the free knowledge and resources we provide. This means Wikipedia remains neutral, trusted, and free from commercial interests. Watch our video to learn more.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1Q8s16b39q8)

## Where your donation goes

Accountability and transparency are core values at the Wikimedia Foundation. We manage funds and resources to ensure that every contribution supports our mission. We have earned the Platinum Seal of Transparency from Candid (formerly GuideStar), and Charity Navigator awarded us its highest rating. You can [read our most recent annual report](https://wikimediafoundation.org/annualreports/current/) for more information about our financial health.

### Investment in Technology 45%

Nearly half of our budget goes toward supporting the technology that powers Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects. We are constantly working to enhance the user experience for both contributors and readers, improve site security, and ensure reliable access to our websites globally. This infrastructure and product support sustain one of the top ten most visited websites in the world, all at a fraction of the cost of popular for-profit websites.

### Support for Volunteers 32%

The global reach of Wikimedia projects is made possible by the hard work of volunteers from across the globe. We provide grants, legal support, and other resources to help build vibrant volunteer communities. Additionally, we promote community engagement through outreach initiatives and advocate for the growth and protection of free knowledge.

### General and Administrative Expenses 11%

Operational costs are essential for the smooth management and governance of the Wikimedia Foundation. These expenses help us recruit top talent and support staff around the world, empowering them to carry out the mission of the Wikimedia Foundation.

### Allocation to Fundraising Efforts 12%

Donor support is crucial to sustaining Wikipedia and our other free knowledge endeavors. Our team is committed to efficient and effective fundraising throughout the year, ensuring that every contribution helps advance our mission.

* * *

We appreciate each and every person who chooses to become a Wikimedia Foundation donor! You are the key to making this important work possible. Thank you. We also offer a special acknowledgement to our Benefactors — people who give $1,000 or more. We proudly list our [Benefactors here](https://wikimediafoundation.org/give/benefactors/).

## Still have questions?

Please find answers to our most frequently asked questions below. If you’re unable to find what you are looking for there, you can browse our [general FAQs](https://wikimediafoundation.org/who-we-are/frequently-asked-questions/), or get in touch using [donate@wikimedia.org](mailto:donate@wikimedia.org).

### Are my donations tax deductible?

The Wikimedia Foundation has 501(c)(3) tax exempt status in the United States. Our tax-exempt status varies according to the laws of each country. Donations to the Wikimedia Foundation are likely not tax-deductible outside the USA. Please see our [tax deductibility](https://wikimediafoundation.org/give/donor-frequently-asked-questions/#tax-deductibility) page for more details.

### What is your donor privacy policy?

We are committed to protecting the privacy rights of our supporters and will never sell, trade, or rent your nonpublic personal information. Please see our [Donor privacy policy](https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Donor_privacy_policy) for full details.

### How secure is an online donation?

The Wikimedia Foundation donation pages are extremely secure and powered by [GlobalSign](https://www.globalsign.com/). After clicking on a fundraising banner or following a donation link, the page you’re taken to is on a secured site (https); all information is encrypted and handled following the highest standard of data protection.

We would also like you to know that we neither process nor store credit card details or bank information. Instead, we work closely with third party payment processors affiliated with banks to process donations. Please also note that when you transfer to a partner site – if you are donating via Apple Pay, Google Pay, or PayPal, for example – we do not store your login credentials and the full donation process is done from your account on their secure site.

### How can I update my recurring gift?

You may pause, update, or cancel your recurring donation via your donor portal. [Please click here](https://donorpreferences.wikimedia.org/index.php?title=Special:DonorPortal&wmf_medium=wmfSite&wmf_source=113#/login) to log in with the email address you used to set up your donation.

If you donate by credit/debit card, in some cases credit card processors will notify us when card details (including expiration date) are updated, to ensure the donation is not interrupted. If you have questions about this, please contact your credit card provider for more information.

Please note that if you donate via PayPal, you may need to manage your donation directly via your PayPal account.

If you encounter any issues or have any questions, please reach out to our Donor Relations team at [donate@wikimedia.org](mailto:donate@wikimedia.org) and they will be happy to assist. **Please do not include your credit card number or other financial information when contacting us.**

Due to the volume of inquiries we receive, we use Zendesk as a donor response platform. By emailing [donate@wikimedia.org](mailto:donate@wikimedia.org), you understand that your information will be processed by the Zendesk Group in accordance with Zendesk’s terms. Users from the following countries should consult Section A of Zendesk’s privacy policy for more information about Zendesk’s country-specific practices: Australia, Brazil, Canada, Japan, New Zealand, and Singapore.

[View all frequently asked questions](https://wikimediafoundation.org/give/donor-frequently-asked-questions/)

# History of Masjid Nabawi

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

The history of Masjid Nabawi (the [Prophet's Mosque](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi")), in [Medina](https://madainproject.com/medina "Medina tu-Nabi"), spans over fourteen centuries, tracing a continuous narrative of spiritual centralization, geopolitical shifts, and cultural synthesis that mirrors the trajectory of [Islamic civilization](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Islamic Civilization") itself. Initially built in 622 CE (1 Hijri) as an all-encompassing institution but as a modest communal structure, the historical trajectory of the site is characterized by its transition from the socio-political capital of the early [Caliphate](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Caliphate") to a monumental locus of dynastic legitimacy during the [middle ages](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Middle Ages") and global pan-Islamic pilgrimage in to the modern period.
