#### Overview

While the physical boundaries of the mosque expanded across successive imperial eras, its historical legacy remains anchored in its role as the premier theater of early Islamic governance, theological discourse, and institutional evolution. Crucially, the history of Masjid al-Nabawi must not be conflated with its mere [physical construction phases](https://madainproject.com/expansion_chronology_of_masjid_al_nabawi "Chronology of Masjid e Nabawi's Expansions"). While its structural chronology tracks the material evolution of stone, mortar, and spatial expansions, its true historical narrative is defined by a profound institutional transition. If we could apply modern terminology, the mosque evolved from a universal social, economic, political, and legal hub of early Islamic society into a specialized, universally venerated sacred religious complex and global pilgrimage destination.

The historical documentation of the Prophet's Mosque relies on a robust tradition of classical Islamic historiography, urban chronicles, and travel literature (_Rihla_). Early developments and territorial disputes are preserved in the 8th- and 9th-century works of historians such as [_Ibn Ishaq_](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Ibn Ishaq") and [_al-Waqidi_](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "al-Waqidi"). Detailed architectural and social histories of the mosque emerged premarily during the [medieval period](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Medieval Period"), most notably in [_Ibn Zabala_](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Ibn Zabala")'s now lost 9th-century CE chronicle of Medina which is only largely preserved in later texts. [al-Samhudi](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "al-Samhudi")'s definitive 15th-century CE work, _Wafa al-Wafa bi Akhbar Dar al-Mustafa_ also provide distinct and descriptions of how the mosque and its role eveolved over the centuries. These narrative texts, supplemented by epigraphic evidence and the eyewitness accounts of medieval travelers like _Ibn Jubayr_ and [_Ibn Battuta_](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Ibn Battuta"), provide a granular record of how the mosque functioned as a living institution through centuries of political developments, fires, and reconstructions.

[![Image 2](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_nabawi_qadeem_182918.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_nabawi_qadeem_182918.jpg)

[](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi)

#### Concise History

[](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi)

circa 622–632 CE

[![Image 3](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/unavailable.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/unavailable.jpg)

**The Prophetic Era**  
 Following the Hijrah in 622 CE (circa 1 Hijri), the [establishment of a meager stone-mud-brick structure](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi_at_the_time_of_prophet_muhammad "Masjid an-Nabawi at the Time of Prophet Muhammad") served as the primary location for the social and urban fabric of [ancient Yathrib](https://madainproject.com/yathrib "Yathrib"), which was subsequently renamed [_al-Madinah al-Munawwarah_](https://madainproject.com/medina "Medina tu-Nabi").

According to tradition the she-camel, named _al-Qaswa_, of Prophet Muhammad on the command of [Allah](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi) demarcated the location of the mosque, on the same day prophet arrived in [Medina](https://madainproject.com/medina "Medina tu-Nabi") from [Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Mecca") in 621/622 CE. The selected site was a _mirbad_, a commercial plot used for drying dates, belonging to two Banu Najjar orphans, _Sahl_ and _Suhayl_, under the guardianship of _As'ad ibn Zurarah_. In one tradition, the Prophet Muhammad is said to have himself purchased the land directly; in another, the funds were provided by _Abu Bakr al-Siddiq_ on prophet's behalf to legitimize the land's public title. Structurally, the initial almost square enclosure measured approximately 70 by 60 cubits. The outer walls were constructed with unbaked mud bricks (_labin_) resting on stone foundations. The enclosure was partially roofed on the north with palm fronds (_jarid_) supported by palm-trunk columns (_juda'_).

The first adhan was pronounced from a private house adjacent to the Masjid Nabawi, however, later on a small circular elevated platform. This may have been a precursor to the minaret.

In Rajab 2 Hijri (January 624 CE), the congregation at Masjid al-Nabawi underwent a physical reorientation of qibla direction. Prior to this date, the mosque had been built with its prayer direction (_qibla_) oriented northward toward [_Bayt al-Maqdis_](https://madainproject.com/haram_al_sharif_(al_quds) "Haram al-Sharif (al-Quds)") ([Jerusalem](https://madainproject.com/jerusalem "Jerusalem")), a direction the Prophet and his [companions](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "List of Sahabah") had observed since before the [Hijrah](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Migration to Medina"). Following the Quranic revelation of verse 2:144 — which commanded the reorientation of prayer toward the [Masjid al-Haram](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram "Masjid al-Haram") in Mecca, the congregation at Masjid al-Nabawi turned southward mid-prayer. A hadith in [Sahih al-Bukhari](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Sahih Bukhari") records that revelation was received at the [Masjid Qiblatain](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Masjid Qiblatain, Medina") but the Prophet's first Asr prayer facing the [Ka'bah](https://madainproject.com/kaaba "Kabah") was performed at Masjid al-Nabawi following this revelation. The physical fabric of the mosque was subsequently restructured: the original northern prayer wall became the rear wall of the enclosure, a new southern wall was constructed to anchor the direction toward Mecca, and the roofed portion of the mosque was extended to support three rows of palm-trunk columns. This event is unique in the mosque's architectural history as the only instance in which a divine liturgical command produced an immediate, irreversible physical reorganization of the building's orientation during its foundational era.

The stark paradox of this foundational but meager structure lies in the extreme disproportion between its physical humility and the concentrated complexity, diversity and significance of its institutional operations. It operated as a legislative assembly where constitutional decrees, such as the _Mithaq al-Madinah_ ([Constitution of Medina](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Constitution of Medina"): see [note 1](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi#note-1)), were enacted, and as a supreme judicial court where the Prophet adjudicated inter-tribal and civil disputes. Military logistics and strategic deployments, including the mobilizations for the Battles of [Badr](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Battle of Badr") and Uhud, were planned within the courtyard, which also housed a defensive armory. In modern terms, the Prophet's Mosque functioned much like a "town hall", but one that simultaneously housed every branch of governance the nascent Islamic state needed. Despite having a physical footprint that would represent a fraction of a modern religious complex, the mudbrick enclosure functioned simultaneously as legislature, judiciary, military command center, diplomatic reception hall, residential academy as well as a charity institution (see [note 2](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi#note-2)).

The mosque's role as the primary diplomatic reception space of the nascent Islamic state is documented across multiple attested encounters, most densely in the period following the conquest of Mecca in 8 Hijri, when tribal delegations from across the [Arabian Peninsula](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Arabin Peninsula") arrived to negotiate terms of allegiance. The year 9 Hijri became known in the Islamic historical tradition as the _'Am al-Wufud_ (the [Year of Delegations](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Year of Delegations")) and the mosque served as the primary site for their reception. The Prophet would receive these groups leaning against a palm trunk at what later became known as the [_Ustuwanah al-Wufud_](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Ustwana e Wufud (Delegations' Column), Riyad ul-Jannah") (Pillar of Delegations), a structural memory sufficiently significant that the pillar retained its designation across subsequent centuries of expansion. Among these encounters, the Banu Tamim chieftains arrived and requested a contest of tribal oratory and poetry within the mosque, an established form of Arab precedence-claiming that the Prophet engaged directly by appointing Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas as his respondent, with the encounter recorded in both [Ibn Ishaq's Sira](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (Ibn Ishaq)") and Sahih al-Bukhari. The Banu Thaqif of Ta'if, also in 9 Hijri, were accommodated within a tent pitched inside a corner of the mosque for the duration of their negotiations, allowing them to observe Muslim prayer as a deliberate component of their reception, another well attested instance of the mosque being physically adapted to serve a processual diplomatic function. In 10 Hijri, al-Ash'ath ibn Qays arrived with a delegation of eighty Kinda riders from southern [Arabia](https://madainproject.com/arabia "Arabia"); Ibn Ishaq records explicitly that "they went in to the apostle in the mosque", their formal submission within the congregational space concluding the principal phase of peninsular consolidation.

The mosque also served as the site of the most formally documented inter-religious encounters of the Prophetic era, occasions on which its spatial boundaries were extended to accommodate non-Muslim visitors in ways that later jurisprudential tradition would engage with extensively. In 9 Hijri, Adi ibn Hatim al-Ta'i, chief of the Tayy tribe and son of the poet Hatim al-Ta'i, entered the mosque wearing a gold cross, was received by the Prophet, and engaged in a theological exchange recorded in [Ibn Kathir](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Ibn Kathir")'s [Tafsir](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Tafsir ibn Kathir") via chains traced to [Ahmad ibn Hanbal](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Ahmad ibn Hanbal") and [al-Tirmidhi](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "al-Tirmidhi"); his conversion within the mosque drew the Tayy tribe as a whole into the Islamic polity. Another of these well known encounters was the arrival of the Christian delegation from [Najran](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "Najran") in 10 Hijri — bishops and scholars who came to engage the Prophet in theological disputation concerning the status of Jesus, recorded in Ibn Ishaq's Sira and referenced in Surah al Imran (3:61). When the time for the delegation's prayer arrived, the Prophet permitted them to perform it within the mosque facing east according to their own rite. The encounter concluded not with the proposed Mubahala — a mutual invocation of divine curse to settle the dispute — but with the Treaty of Najran, making the mosque the site of both inter-religious theological disputation and formal treaty negotiation between the Islamic state and a non-Muslim community.

The northern section of the mosque accommodated the [Suffah](https://madainproject.com/suffah_(masjid_al_nabawi) "Suffah Platform of Masjid Nabawi"), a dedicated raised platform that institutionalized Islam's first residential academy for disenfranchised companions who had no family, home, or income in Medina. Under the instruction of teachers such as Ubai ibn Ka'b, the ahl al-Suffah were housed, fed, and educated within the mosque's physical fabric on a permanent basis. Their sustenance was drawn from alms brought directly to the Prophet within the Masjid Nabawi's congregational space, which he redistributed among them; wealthier companions would additionally send food and provisions directly to the platform. The Suffah thus embedded a formal welfare institution within the mosque's spatial economy — one in which the congregational floor served simultaneously as a site of worship, charitable distribution, and residential shelter for the community's most vulnerable members.

Architecturally integrated into the eastern perimeter were the Hujurat (domestic quarters), constructed with wattle-and-daub walls and mud-brick for the Prophet's wives, Aisha bint Abi Bakr and Sawda bint Zam'a. # Medina

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

Ancient Medina, also transliterated as _Madīnah_, is a city in the Hejazi region of the Arabian Peninsula and administrative headquarters of the _al-Madinah_ Region of Saudi Arabia. At the city's heart is _al-Masjid an-Nabawi_ ('The Prophet's Mosque'), which is the burial place of the Islamic prophet, Muhammad, and it is one of two holiest cities in Islam, the other being the city of [Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Mecca").

Medina is generally considered to be the "cradle of Islamic culture and civilization". The city is considered to be the second-holiest of three key cities in Islamic tradition, with Mecca and Jerusalem serving as the holiest and third-holiest cities respectively. The original name of the city before the advent of Islam was [_Yathrib_](https://madainproject.com/yathrib "Yathrib") (Hebrew: יתריב; Arabic: يَثْرِب), and it is referred to by this name in Chapter 33 (_Al-Aḥzāb_, literally meaning 'The Confederates') of the Quran. It was renamed to _Madīnat an-Nabī_ (literally 'the City of the Prophet' or 'The Prophet's City') after Muhammad's death.

Medina is home to several distinguished sites and landmarks, most of which are mosques and hold historic significance. These include the three aforementioned mosques, _Masjid al-Fath_ (also known as _Masjid al-Khandaq_), the Seven Mosques, the _Baqi'_ Cemetery where the graves of many famous Islamic figures are presumed to be located; directly to the southeast of the Prophet's Mosque, the _Uhud_ mountain, site of the eponymous Battle of Uhud and the King Fahd Glorious _Qur'an_ Printing Complex where most modern Qur'anic Mus'hafs are printed.

### Brief History

[](https://madainproject.com/medina)
#### Yathrib (Pre-Islamic Era)

During antiquity the city of Medina was known as _Yathrib_ (يثرب). In historiography, the term "_Yathrib_" or "ancient _yathrib_" describes the periods of occupation starting with early Arab-Jewish settlements in the area during the fourth or fifth century CE. Though it is uncertain how far back the settlement history of _Yathrib_ Oasis goes, it is believed that the area was inhabited at least for over 1,500-1,700 years (circa 900-700 BCE) before prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca. The Yathrib region received peoples from various regions who formed its pre-Islamic community and fomulate history.

[History of Ancient Yathrib](https://madainproject.com/history_of_ancient_yathrib "History of Ancient Yathrib")

[](https://madainproject.com/medina)
#### Medina (Islamic Period)

Much like most of the Hejaz, the historic city of Medina has seen numerous exchanges of power within its comparatively short existence in the recorded history. The history of Medina starts with the advent of Islam, after the Hijrah of prophet Muhammad, the event that marked the beginning of the Islamic calendar. Today, Medina continues to be a vital center for Islam, attracting millions of pilgrims and visitors from around the world. It remains a city of historical and religious significance, deeply embedded in the cultural and spiritual heritage of Saudi Arabia and the broader Islamic world.

[History of Medina](https://madainproject.com/history_of_medina "History of Medina")

### List of Mosques in Medina

One of the most remarkable aspects of Medina is its rich religious heritage, embodied by a multitude of mosques that dot its landscape. These mosques not only serve as places of worship but also hold stories that resonate with the profound history of Islam, making them integral to the identity of this enchanting city. ### Masjid an-Nabawi

The Prophet's Mosque, second only in significance to the Kaaba in Mecca, is a place of profound veneration for Muslims worldwide. Beyond its historical and architectural splendor, it is a living testament to the teachings and compassion of the Prophet Muhammad, who, more than 1,400 years ago, laid its first stones. ## Featured[Expansions History of Masjid an-Nabawi](https://madainproject.com/expansion_chronology_of_masjid_al_nabawi "Chronology of Masjid e Nabawi's Expansions")

Over the centuries Masjid an-Nabawi has under gone various expansions and reconstructions. After an expansion during the reign of the Umayyad caliph al-Walid I, it now incorporates the final resting place of Muhammad and the first two Rashidun caliphs Abu Bakr and Umar. These expansions aimed to accommodate the growing Muslim population and provide a larger space for worship. Today, Masjid an-Nabawi remains a revered pilgrimage site, symbolizing the rich heritage and spiritual significance of Islam.

[Explore](https://madainproject.com/expansion_chronology_of_masjid_al_nabawi "Chronology of Masjid e Nabawi's Expansions")

[![Image 7: Masjid Qiblatain](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_masjid_7382.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Masjid Qiblatain, Medina")
### Masjid Qiblatain

Its name, which translates to the "Mosque of the Two Qiblas," hints at the remarkable event that unfolded within its sacred walls. This mosque's significance lies in its role as the place where the Prophet Muhammad received divine revelation to change the direction of prayer (qibla) from Jerusalem to Mecca. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Masjid Qiblatain, Medina")

[![Image 8: Jannat ul-baqi Before Demolitions of the Tombs](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jannat_baqi_0000377.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_baqi_before_demolitions "Jannat ul-Baqi before Demolitions")
### Pre-1926 Baqi al-Gharqad

The demolition of the tombs in Jannat al-Baqi took place around 1925 CE when the cemetery was extensively razed by the Saudi authorities. Before the destruction of Jannat al-Baqi, the cemetery contained a variety of structures and mausoleums that served as markers for the graves of important figures from Islamic history. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_baqi_before_demolitions "Jannat ul-Baqi before Demolitions")

[![Image 9: Dar al-Medinah Museum](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/medina_museum_32782.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/dar_al_madinah_museum "Dar al-Madinah Museum")
### Dar al-Madinah Museum

This purpose built museum is designed to provide insight into the rich history of the Holy City of Madinah. Its exhibits chronicle the city's evolution from the era of the Prophet Muhammad to the present day. Additionally, the museum houses a collection of rare manuscripts and a variety of detailed models as well. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/dar_al_madinah_museum "Dar al-Madinah Museum")

[![Image 10: Palace of Urwah ibn Zubair](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/castle_urwah_7487.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/palace_of_urwah "Qasr Urwah")
### Palace/Castle of Urwah

The _Qasr_ of _Urwah ibn Zubair_, one of the renowned companions and religious leaders of Islam, was an agricultural estate that was built during the early Islamic eras and is famous for being a gathering and discussion place for the companions and scholars of that time. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/palace_of_urwah "Qasr Urwah")

[![Image 11: Masjid Ghamama](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ghamama_masjid_328788.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/ghamama_mosque "Ghamamah Mosque")
### Masjid Ghamama

_Masjid Ghamama_ (Mosque of Clouds) is a historic mosque located close to the Masjid an-Nabawi. It is believed that the Prophet Muhammad led a prayer for rain on this spot during a period of drought. After the prayer, a cloud miraculously appeared, and rain began to fall, ending the drought. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/ghamama_mosque "Ghamamah Mosque")

[![Image 12: Masjid al-Quba](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_22837.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque "Masjid al-Quba")
### al-Quba Mosque

The foundation of the al-Quba Mosque, situated on the outskirts of the radiant city of Medina, can be traced back to the time of the Prophet Muhammad. It is revered as the first mosque ever built in Islam by prophet Muhammad and his companions shortly after their migration (Hijra) to Medina in 622 CE. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque "Masjid al-Quba")

## Featured[Temple District of Mahlab al-Naqa](https://madainproject.com/mahlab_al_naqa "Mahlab al-Naqa")

The temple of Mahlab al-Naqa (Arabic: معبد محلب الناقة), also spelled Mahlib Annaqa, is a 6th-7th century BCE temple that was built by ancient Lihyanite people, located in the Khuraybah area of al-Ula Governorate, Saudi Arabia. The temple contains a purification basin carved in front of a Lihyanite temple. The current ruins of the ancient site, located in Khuraybah area of al-Ula Governorate, which date back to the fourth century CE, includes a number of well-preserved ruins, including a palace, tombs and a small mosque from the later Islamic period.

[Explore](https://madainproject.com/mahlab_al_naqa "Mahlab al-Naqa")

[![Image 13: The History of Masjid Nabawi](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mahlab_annaqa_32489.jpg) ### Temple District of Mahlab al-Naqa](https://madainproject.com/mahlab_al_naqa "Mahlab al-Naqa")

[![Image 14: Jannat ul-baqi Graveyard](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jannat_baqi_3783223.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_baqi "Jannat ul Baqi")
### Jannat ul-Baqi Cemetery

The Jannat al-Baqi, or the Jannat ul-Baqi or Baqi al-Gharqad, is a historic cemetery located adjacent to the Masjid Nabawi. It is renowned for being the final resting place of numerous companions of the Prophet Muhammad, members of his family, and other prominent figures from the early days of Islam. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_baqi "Jannat ul Baqi")

[![Image 15: Bab e Ambariya](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bab_anbariya_32.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/bab_anbariya "Bab Anbariya")
### Bab Anbariya

The Bab Anbariya ("Gate of Anbar") is known for its historical importance, as it is named after a prominent figure from Islamic history named Anbar ibn Abi Sufyan, a cheiftan in the Ottoman Empire, who donated the part of the land close to the gate for a military academy during the Ottoman period. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/bab_anbariya "Bab Anbariya")

[![Image 16: Site of the Battle of Badr](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/badr_masjid_areesh_182171.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/battlefield_of_badr "Battlefield of Badr")
### Site of the Battle of Badr

The site of the Battle of Badr holds immense historical significance in Islam. Located near the town of Badr in present-day Saudi Arabia, it was the site of a pivotal battle in March 624 CE. The exact location of the battlefield is approximately 80 miles (130 kilometers) southwest of Medina. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/battlefield_of_badr "Battlefield of Badr")

[![Image 17: al-Fatah Masjid, Medina](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/fatah_masjid_4782.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/al_fatah_mosque_(seven_mosques))
### Masjid al-Fatah

The small hill-top mosque, Masjid al-Fatah, marks the historic spot that is thought to have been used as the commanding post by the prophet Muhammad in the Battle of the Trench. It is one of the Seven Mosques built at the site of Ghazwa Khandaq. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/al_fatah_mosque_(seven_mosques))

[![Image 18: Lion Tombs of Dadan](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/dadan_tombs_3719.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/lion_tombs_of_dadan "Lion Tombs of Dadan")
### Lion Tombs of Dadan

This UNESCO World Heritage Site is renowned for its ancient rock-cut tombs and archaeological remnants, which date back to the Nabatean civilization. One of the standout features of the Lion Tombs is the intricate rock-cut facades of the burial niches. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/lion_tombs_of_dadan "Lion Tombs of Dadan")

[![Image 19: Miqat Dhul Hulaifah Mosque](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/dhul_hulaifah_77928.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/miqat_dhul_hulaifah_mosque "Miqat Dhul Hulaifah Mosque")
### Miqat Dhul Hulaifah Mosque

The Miqat Dhul Hulaifah Mosque is one of the five designated miqats (stations), around and oustide the boundary of Mecca, where pilgrims assume their state of Ihram (specific clothing), a sacred state of ritual purity, before proceeding to Mecca. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/miqat_dhul_hulaifah_mosque "Miqat Dhul Hulaifah Mosque")

[![Image 20: Madain Saleh (al-Hijr)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/madain_saleh_87238.jpg) ### Madain Saleh (_Hegra_)](https://madainproject.com/madain_saleh "Madain Saleh")

## Featured[Madain Saleh (_al-Hijr_)](https://madainproject.com/madain_saleh "Madain Saleh")

The _Mada’in Saleh_, also called _al-Hijr_ or _Hegra_, is a pre-Islamic archaeological site. A majority of the vestiges date from the Nabatean kingdom (1st century CE). The site constitutes the Saudi Kingdom’s southernmost and largest settlement after Petra, its capital. Traces of Lihyanite and Roman occupation before and after the Nabatean rule, respectively, can also be found in situ, while accounts from the _Qur’an_ tell of an earlier settlement of the area by the tribe of Thamud in the 3rd millennium BCE.

[Explore](https://madainproject.com/madain_saleh "Madain Saleh")

[![Image 21: Bir al-Ghars Well](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bir_ghars_118392.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/al_ghars_well "al-Gharas Well")
### Ghars Well (Bir al-Ghars)

The _Bir Ghars_ is the site where prophet Muhammad once made a stop drank and watered his camel. According to tradition, the water from this now defunct well was favoured by the prophet Muhammad so much that he made a request to be bathed with its water after his demise. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/al_ghars_well "al-Gharas Well")

[![Image 22: Wadi al-Aqeeq](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/wadi_aqiq_34788.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/al_aqeeq_valley "Wadi al-Aqeeq")
### al-Aqeeq Valley

The Wadi al-Aqiq, situated south of Medina, holds historical significance in Islamic history. It is believed that the Prophet Muhammad passed through this valley on his way to various battles and expeditions. The valley also served as a route for trade and commerce in ancient times. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/al_aqeeq_valley "Wadi al-Aqeeq")

[![Image 23: Well of Uthman (Well of Rumah)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/rumah_well_44058.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/well_of_rumah "Well of Rumah")
### Well of Uthman/Rumah

The Well of Uthman, or the Well of Rumah the Jew (who sold the well to Uthman ibn Affan), dates back to the time of the Prophet Muhammad and was one of the few sources of fresh water in the area. The "Well of Uthman" was located in the lower part of Wadi al-Aqiq, where the flood waters collected. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/well_of_rumah "Well of Rumah")

[![Image 24: Masjid al-Shumaisi](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_shumaisi_4788.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/al_shumaisi_mosque_(hudaybiyyah) "al-Shumaisi Masjid")
### al-Shumaisi Masjid (Hudaybiyya)

The _Masjid al-Shumaisi_, is a modern mosque located in the city of Hudaybiyya (also spelled Hudaybiyah or Hudaybiyyah), marks the historically believed site of the Treaty of Hudaybiyah signed between the Muslims of Medina and the Meccan Quraish in the year 628 CE. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/al_shumaisi_mosque_(hudaybiyyah) "al-Shumaisi Masjid")

[![Image 25: Masjid al-Shumaisi](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bayruhaa_madinah_581022.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/bayruhaa "Bayruhaa (بئر حاء)")
### Bayruhaa'

The _Bir Ha'_ was one of the seven renowned wells in Madinah during the time of the Prophet Muhammad. These wells served as crucial water sources for the early Muslim community, providing sustenance and facilitating daily life in the arid environment of the region. According to historical accounts, the well was owned by Abu Talha al-Ansari, a notable companion of the Prophet. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/bayruhaa "Bayruhaa (بئر حاء)")

### al-Madina Museum

The al-Madinah Museum exhibits history and heritage of city of Medina featuring different archaeological collections, visual galleries and rare photographs. The museum includes an exhibition presenting the evolution of Masjid Nabawi from its humble beginning to the modern complex. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/al_madinah_museum "al-Madinah Museum")

[![Image 27: al-Ijabah Masjid](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_ijabah_%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AC%D8%AF_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A5%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%A8%D8%A9_masjid_bani_umaiya_madinah_ejaba_mosque_medina_saudi_arabia_7378217.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/al_ijabah_mosque "Ijabah Mosque (Medina)")
### al-Ijabah Masjid

Masjid al-Ijabah, also known as Masjid Bani Muawiyah, was a historic mosque in Medina located north of the Prophet's Mosque. It is renowned as the site where Prophet Muhammad offered a long prayer and requested three things from Allah, two of which were granted, and one withheld. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/al_ijabah_mosque "Ijabah Mosque (Medina)")

[![Image 28: Masjid al-Anbariya](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/anbariya_masjid_117392.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/medina "Anbariya Mosque")
### Masjid al-Anbariya

The Anbariya Mosque, also referred to as the Hamidiye Mosque, is a historic mosque located in Medina, Saudi Arabia. It was constructed by the Ottoman Turks in 1908 during the reign of Sultan Abdülhamid II. The mosque is named after the Anbariya Gate, which was situated nearby. This religious structure is associated with the Hejaz Railway project and is located adjacent to the al-Muazzim Railway Station in Medina. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/medina "Anbariya Mosque")

[![Image 29: Saqifah Bani-Sa'ida](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/saqifah_bani_saidah_113392.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/medina "Saqifah Bani Sa'idah")
### Saqifah Bani-Sa'ida

The _Saqifa_ (a covered communal place for conversation) of the _Banu Sa'ida_ clan refers to the location of an event in early Islam where some of the companions of the prophet Muhammad pledged their allegiance to _Abu Bakr_ as the first caliph and successor to Muhammad shortly after his death in 11 Hijri. Today a beautiful garden marks the site on the north-western side of the Masjid Nabawi. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/medina "Saqifah Bani Sa'idah")

[![Image 30: Masjid Jummah](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jummah_masjid_medina_118392.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/medina "Masjid e Jummah")
### Jummah Mosque

Traditionally believed to mark the site where according to the tradition prophet Muhammad offered his first Jummah prayer while migrating to the Yathrib Oasis. It is located near _Wadi Ranuna'_, 900 metres (3,000 feet) north of Quba Mosque, and 6 km south of _Masjid Nabawi_. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/medina "Masjid e Jummah")

[![Image 31: Jabal Uhud](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jabl_uhud_118372.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/medina "Mount Uhud")
### Jabal Uhud

Jabal Uhud is most famous for being the site of the Battle of Uhud, which took place in the year 625 CE during the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad. This battle was fought between the Muslim community of Medina and the Quraysh tribe of Mecca. It was a pivotal moment in the early history of Islam. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/medina "Mount Uhud")

#### Overview

According to non-Muslim scholars, Islam started during the lifetime of prophet Muhammad in the early 7th century (circa 610 CE), and so did architectural components such as the mosque. In this case, either the [Mosque of the Companions](https://madainproject.com/as_sahaba_mosque_(massawa) "as-Sahabah Mosque") in the Eritrean city of Massawa, or the [Quba Mosque](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque "Masjid al-Quba") in the Hejazi city of Medina (the first structure built by Muhammad upon his emigration from Mecca in 622 CE), would be the first mosque that was built in the history of Islam.

After the Quba Mosque, prophet Muhammad went on to establish another mosque in Medina, which is now known as al-Masjid an-Nabawi (The Prophet's Mosque). prophet Muhammad participated in the construction of the mosque himself and this structed became the social and cultural focal point of the ancient city of Medina. From then onwards a large number of mosques were built across the entire city, and more were added as the city expanded outwards.

#### List of the Mosques

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa 709 CE

[![Image 3](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/dhul_hulaifah_77928.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/dhul_hulaifah_77928.jpg "Masjid u Shajarah (one of the miqat), Dhul Hulaifah, Medina")

**as-Shajarah Mosque**  
 The [Masjid as-Shajarah](https://madainproject.com/miqat_dhul_hulaifah_mosque "Miqat Dhul Hulaifah Mosque") (مسجد الشجرة), also known as the Miqat Dhu al-Ḥulayfah, is located in the area of Abyar Ali, west of Wadi al-Aqiq some twelve kilometers from the Prophet's Mosque. It is one of the Miqaat stations (places where ihram is put on), situated [in Dhul Hulaifah](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Dhul Hulaifah"). It is the place where pilgrims coming from Medina wishing to perform Umrah or Hajj enter into ihram before they set for Mecca. The current mosque building was built during the reign of King Fahd. It is in the shape of a square of an area of approximately 6,000 square meters (65,000 ft2) inside a 36,000 m2 (388,000 ft2) square-shaped enclosure.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 4](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ijabah_masjid_2838.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ijabah_masjid_2838.jpg "Ejabah Mosque")

**Ijabah Mosque**  
 The [Masjid Ijabah](https://madainproject.com/al_ijabah_mosque "Ijabah Mosque (Medina)") (مسجد الإجابة) also known as _Masjid Bani Muawiya_ or _Masjid al-Mubahalah_ is approx 385 meters to the north of [Jannat ul-Baqi](https://madainproject.com/jannat_ul_baqi "Jannat ul Baqi"). It is known as Masjid e Ijabah (the mosque of approval/acceptance) and is approx. 600 meters away from Masjid al-Nabawi in the Bani Muawiya district. This particular mosque derives its significance from an account mentioned in a Hadith of Sahih Muslim, relating that once Prophet Muhammad passed the Bani Muawiyah Mosque, entered there and offered two rakats, and his companions also followed him.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 5](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/fatah_masjid_4782.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/fatah_masjid_4782.jpg "al-Fatah Mosque, built at the place where command post of prophet Muhammad was located during Ahzab battle.")

**al-Fatah Mosque**  
 The [al-Fatah Mosque](https://madainproject.com/al_fatah_mosque_(seven_mosques)) (مسجد الفتح) is the most significant one of the [Seven Mosques](https://madainproject.com/seven_mosques "Seven Mosques"), situated at the site of the [Battle of Ahzab](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of the Trench"). Largest of the seven mosques the masjid al-Fath is situated on a small hilltop near the western side of Sal’ mountain. It was first built when Umar ibn Abd Al-Aziz was governor of Madinah in the years 87 to 93 after Hijrah (705 CE to 711 CE). It was rebuilt in 1179 CE (575 Hj.) again. It was then rebuilt again during the reign of the Ottoman Sultan Abd Al-Majid I in 1851 CE. The modern structure is nearly square with a roofed hall towards the south fronted by a small courtyard towards the north. A large flight of stairs leads to the entrance, situated in the eastern wall of the courtyard.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 6](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/manaratain_mosque_8283.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/manaratain_mosque_8283.jpg "Masjid al-Manaratain, The Mosque of the Two Minarets")

**al-Manaratain Mosque**  
 The [Masjid al-Manaratain](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Masjid al-Manaratain") (مسجد المنارتين), mosque of the two towers or minarets, (also known as the _Masjid e Bani Dinaar_) originally a crude basalt structure it was rebuilt and expanded during the reign of Fahad bin Abdul 'Aziz in 2003 CE (1424 Hj.). It is situated on the main highway going towards Mecca near al-Anbariya. Another reason for the name is attributed to its location; because it is located in between two mountains which were dubbed as two towers.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 7](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_nabawi_3842939.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_nabawi_3842939.jpg "Masjid al-Nabawi (The Mosque of the prophet)")

**Masjid Nabawi**  
 The [Masjid al-Nabawi](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi") (مسجد النبوي) often called the Prophet's Mosque, is a historic mosque situated in the city of al-Madinah, Saudi Arabia. As the final resting place of Prophet Muhammad, it is considered the second holiest site in the world after Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, ([al-Aqsa](https://madainproject.com/al_aqsa_mosque "al-Aqsa Mosque") in Jerusalem comes in at third). It is a major pilgrimage site and many people who perform the Hajj also go on to al-Madinah before or after Hajj to visit the mosque.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 8](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/salman_farsi_masjid_823782.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/salman_farsi_masjid_823782.jpg "Mosque of Salman the Persian")

**Salman Farsi Mosque**  
 The [mosque of Salman Farsi](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Mosque of Salman the Persian") (مسجد سلمان الفارسي), another one of the _Masajid Saba'_, is located south of the al-Fath Mosque, 20 meters from the base of Sal' mountain. It is named after Salman, the companion of the Prophet Muhammad who recommended digging a trench to fortify the city during [Ghazwa-i Ahzab](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of the Trench"). It has one hall at 7 meters long and 2 meters wide. Originally built when Umar ibn Abd Al-Aziz was governor of Madinah. In 575 H (1179 CE) it was rebuilt on the orders of minister Said Al-Deen Abu Al-Haija. It was rebuilt again during the reign of the Ottoman Sultan Abd Al-Majid I.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 9](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_233288.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/quba_mosque_233288.jpg "Masjid-e Quba")

**Quba Mosque**  
 The site of [Masjid Quba](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque "Masjid al-Quba") (مَـسْـجِـد قُـبَـاء), back then a small town on the outskirts of Medina, was the last stop made by the prophet Muhammad during his [Hijrah](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Hijrah") from [Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Mecca") before reaching the city of Medina. It's construction was initiated by prophet Muhammad and was completed by the companions, it was left in ruins by 1905 CE, rebuilt as a simple structure and renovated by the mid of the twentieth century. Depending on whether the [Mosque of the Companions](https://madainproject.com/as_sahaba_mosque_(massawa) "as-Sahabah Mosque") in the Eritrean city of Massawa is older or not, it may be the first mosque in the world that dates to the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad, 7th century CE.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 10](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_omar_017366.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_omar_017366.jpg "Mosque of Umer ibn al-Khattab, at the site of Battle of the Trench.")

**Umar Mosque**  
 The [Umar Mosque](https://madainproject.com/omer_mosque_(seven_mosques) "Mosque of Umer") (مسجد عمر), at the site of Ghazwa Khandaq, is traditionally believed to be located at the spot of the command post of Umer ibn Khattab was pitched during the [Battle of the trench](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of the Trench"). It is one of the Seven Mosques (المساجد السبعة) or _Sab'u Masajid_, a complex of six small historic and often visited mosques in the city of Medina, Saudi Arabia. In contrast to the other mosques this mosque is not situated on elevated gound rather in the valley below, and its look is corresponding to al-Fath Mosque, thus it is considered that they were built and renovated at the same time. The small mosque covers and area of about fifty square meters and resonates the construction style of other mosques in the area with a small roofed prayer hall fronted by an open courtyard.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 11](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_mosque_237237.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qiblatain_mosque_237237.jpg "Masjid al-Qiblatain, (The Mosque of the Two Directions)")

**Qiblatain Mosque**  
 The [Masjid e Qiblatain](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_qiblatain "Masjid Qiblatain, Medina") (مسجد القبلتين) is among the earliest mosques that dates to the time of Muhammad, along with Quba Mosque and al-Masjid al-Nabawi. The name, Mosque of the two Qiblas, refers to one of the most notable and important events in the history if islam, the changing of Qibla (_Tehweel Qibla_) from Jerusalem to Mecca. This event was directed through a revelation about changing the Qiblah and bowing towards [Kaaba](https://madainproject.com/kaaba "Kabah") in [Mecca](https://madainproject.com/mecca "Mecca") during a Zohar (noon) prayer to prophet Muhammad. The instruction to change the direction of the Qiblah is recorded in Surah al-Baqarah, verse 144.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 12](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/abu_bakr_masjid_002373.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/abu_bakr_masjid_002373.jpg "abu-Bakr al-Siddique Mosque in Medina.")

**abu Bakr al-Siddique Mosque**  
 The [abu-Bakr al-Siddique Mosque](https://madainproject.com/abu_bakr_al_siddique_mosque_(medina) "Abu Bakr al-Siddique Mosque (Medina)") (مسجد ابو بكر) is a small mosque in [Medina](https://madainproject.com/medina "Medina tu-Nabi"). It is situated some 450 meters to the south-west of the Masjid Nabawi's Bab as-Salam and some forty meters north-west of the [Masjid al-Ghamamah](https://madainproject.com/ghamama_mosque "Ghamamah Mosque"). According to a tradition prophet Muhammad prayed Eid prayer at this site, and since the first caliph abu Bakr continued this tradition during his era, the small mosque was attributed to him. Although, it is not certain, but it was most likely built during the reign of Umar ibn Abdulaziz to mark the location of the tradition. It is a small square mosque with one minaret and a large dome that covers nearly the entire roof. The entrance to the mosque is from the east. The current structure most likely dates back to the Ottoman era, with modern renocations during the Saudi era.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 13](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_ali_khandaq_272.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_ali_khandaq_272.jpg "Mosque of Ali ibn abi Talib at the site of Ghazwa-i Ahzab")

**Ali ibn Abu Talib Mosque**  
 The [Mosque of Ali ibn abu Talib](https://madainproject.com/ali_ibn_abi_talib_mosque_(seven_mosques) "Masjid e Ali") (مسجد علي بن أبي طالب) is a small memorial mosque at the site where the battle of Ahzaab was fought. It is believed to mark the sport from where Ali, the paternal cousine of prophet Muhammad, was commanding his battalion. The small mosque shares its architectural style with several other smaller mosques situated at the site, collectively known as the "Seven Mosques". A large flight of stairs leads to the main building of the Mosque, which consistes of a small prayer hall fronted by a samll courtyard. It is located east of the [Fatimah Mosque](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Fatimah Mosque (Masajid Sab'a)") on an elevated ridge. It is 8.5 meters long and 6.5 meters wide. It has one small step. It is likely to have been built and renovated with [al-Fath Mosque](https://madainproject.com/al_fatah_mosque_(seven_mosques)). It is narrated that Ali joined the Battle of the Trench here.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 14](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_abu_ayub_27333.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_abu_ayub_27333.jpg "Masjid abu Ayub Ansari")

**Abu Ayub Ansari Mosque**  
 The Masjid abu Ayub Ansari (مسجد أبو أيوب الأنصاري) was situated at the approximate location where once the house of prophet Muhammad's companion (_Sahabi_) abu Ayub stood. It was located towards the north-eastern direction from the House of Aiesha which later became the [Tomb of Prophet Muhammad](https://madainproject.com/tomb_of_muhammad "Rawdah e Rasool Section"). This area was incorporated in the Masjid al-Nabawi during the second [Saudi Expansion](https://madainproject.com/expansion_chronology_of_masjid_al_nabawi "Chronology of Masjid e Nabawi's Expansions") and today comprises the southern _Sahat_ (plaza) area.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 15](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_shaikhain_231.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_shaikhain_231.jpg "Masjid-e Shaikhain")

**Shaikhain Mosque**  
 The [Masjid Shaikhain](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Masjid e Shaikhain") (مسجد الشيخين), literally meaning the Mosque of the Two people/sardars, marks the spot where according to the tradition Prophet prayed salah on the eve of the [battle of Uhud](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of Uhud") in the year 625 CE (Islamic date is believed to be the 14th of Sha’ban 3 Hj.). It's name points towards a tradition of a wresteling match between two boys (_Rafe'y_ and _Jundub_) before Ghazwa-i uhud to prove their worthiness to participate in battle despite their young ages. The prophetic biography notes that when the prophet Muhammad offered prayer here at ash-Shaikhain, he also met some locals and denied meeting some. The mosque of Shaikhain is located some two kilometers directly north of of the Masjid Nabawi and some 1.5 kilometers south of the Sayyed ash-Shohada where the Battle of Uhud was fought.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 16](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/fasah_masjid_1728.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/fasah_masjid_1728.jpg "Remains of the exterior walls of the al-Fasah' mosque.")

**al-Fash' Mosque**  
 The [al-Fasa'h mosque](https://madainproject.com/al_fasah_mosque "al-Fas'h Mosque") (مسجد الفسح) is said to have been built where prophet Muhammad is believed to have offered noon prayer (_Zohar_) on the day of [battle of Uhud](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of Uhud"), after the fighting was over. Not much remains of this historic mosque, the current remains are undated though it is likely that this was also first constructed during the time of Umar ibn Abdulaziz. Today, only some of the wall structure and mehrab remains on east, south and west and is enclosed within iron railings. It is situated almost 4.5 kilometers north of the Masjid al-Nabawi, inline with the Shaikhain Mosque and ash-Shohada Mosque.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 17](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_mustarah_38782.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_mustarah_38782.jpg "Masjid Mustarah")

**Mustarah Mosque**  
 The [Masjid al-Mustarah](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Masjid e Mistarah") (مسجد المستراح) also known as _Masjid Bani Haritha_ (مسجد بني حارثة), is located where according to the tradition the Muslim army camped on its way back to Medina from the [Battle of Uhud](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of Uhud"). Whenever the Prophet used to visit the grave of Hamza and the other martyrs of Uhud he used to take rest here. The mosque was renovated during the time of the king Fahd, and the place was expanded to 491 square meters wide. Houses belong to the members of Bani Haritsah tribe are located nearby the mosque. It is also located north of the Masjid Nabawi and close to Masjid Shaikhain.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 18](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_umar_madina_3728381.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_umar_madina_3728381.jpg "Masjid e Omar ibn al-Khattab, Medina")

**Umar ibn al-Khattab Mosque**  
 The [Masjid Umar ibn al-Khattab](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Mosque of Umar (Medinah)") (مسجد عمر بن الخطاب), was most likely built by Shams al-Din Mohammed bin Ahmed Slaoui. This small mosque, according to tradition, is believed to mark the spot where the second caliph of Islam [Umar ibn Khattab](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Umar ibn al-Khattab") met prophet Muhammad and was blessed. Today it is flanked by modern urban development projects, large commecial plazas and hotels. It is located some 160 meters directly to the north of Masjid al-Ghamama. The small mosque has only one minaret and one dome, but recently its architecture has changed significantly due to the constructions around it and is usually inaccessible.

[](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina)

circa

[![Image 19](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_fatima_00372371.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_fatima_00372371.jpg "Mosque of Fatima al-Zahra, at the site of the Ahzab.")

**Fatima al-Zahra Mosque**  
 The [Mosque of Fatima al-Zahra](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Fatimah Mosque (Masajid Sab'a)") (مسجد فاطمة الزهراء), also known as _Mus'ad ibn Mo'az_ Mosque, is one of the "Seven Mosques" situated at the site of the [Ahzab](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of the Trench"). It is the smallest of the group and measures 4 meters by 3 meters. It has one small step. It has a similar structure to other mosques in the area and may have been built during the Ottoman era, most likely during the reign of Sultan Abd Al-Majid I in 1851.

**abi Bakr al-Siddique Mosque**  
 The [abu-Bakr Mosque](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "abi Bakr Mosque (Masajid Sab'a)") (مسجد أبي بكر) was a small memorial mosque built at the purported site of the [Battle of Ahzab](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of the Trench"). The mosque no longer exists as it was razed to make space available for the parking lot at the site.

**'Atban ibn Malik Mosque**  
 The [Mosque of 'Atban ibn Malik](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Masjid e 'Atban bin Malik") (مسجد عتبان بن مالك) is located at the site where prophet Muhammad offered Salah and supplicated on the request of one of his companions _Atban ibn Malik_ who was blind. The site was the location of his (Atban ibn Malik's) house. It was situated approx. 60km south of [al-Jum'a Mosque](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Masjid e Jummah").

**Ghamamah Mosque**  
 Facade of the [Masjid al-Ghamamah](https://madainproject.com/ghamama_mosque "Ghamamah Mosque") (مسجد الغمامة), situated close to the [Prophet's Mosque](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi"), is one of the oldest mosques in Medina. According to tradition it is believed to be located in the place where the prophet Muhammad performed an Eid prayer in the year 631 CE. The mosque was built during the reign of the Caliph Umar bin Abdul Aziz between the hijri calendar of 86 to 93, and renovated by the Sultan Hasan bin Muhammad bin Qalawan Ash-Shalihi in 1340 during the Sharifate of Mecca era.

**Ali ibn Abi Talib Mosque**  
[Masjid Ali ibn abi Talib](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Masjid Ali ibn abi Talib") (مسجد علي), it is situated 290 meters from the [Masjid al-Nabawi](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi") and 122 meters from [Masjid Ghamamah](https://madainproject.com/ghamama_mosque "Ghamamah Mosque"). **Imam al-Bukhari Mosque**  
[Masjid Imam al-Bukhari](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Masjid Imam Bukhari") (مسجد الإمام البخاري) is said to have been built where [Imam bukhari](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Imam Bukhari") stayed during his visit to Medina, but this is highly unlikely.

**Misbah Mosque**  
 The remains of [Masjid Misbah](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Misbah Mosque") (مسجد مصباح), also known as Masjid bani Harithah, according to the tradition is the first ever masjid where [Rasool Allah](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Prophet Muhammad") Prayed fajr in as he reached [Madina](https://madainproject.com/medina "Medina tu-Nabi"). Seen here the mehrab in the qiblah wall. Current structure dates back to the Ottoman era circa 1850 CE.

**Sajdah Mosque**  
[Masjid-e Sajdah](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "as-Sajadah Mosque") (مسجد سجدة), also known as the abu Zar al-Ghafari Mosque today, renovated in 1421 Hj./2000 CE it is situated 900 meters north of [Masjid an-Nabawi](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi"). According to a tradition it is called Masjid-e Sajdah because prophet Muhammad prostrated due to gratitude as he receieved news of Salwat from angel [Jibraeel](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Gabriel/Jibraeel").

**Thaniyat ul-Wada' Mosque**  
 The [Tahniyat ul Wada'a Mosque](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Thaniyat al-Wada Mosque") (مسجد ثنية الوداع), commemorates a historic event during the course of Hijrah. According to tradition it was believed to mark the site where prophet Muhammad and Abu Bakr were greeted when they reached close to Medina. The prophetic biography narrates that a large number of Medinians came out of their houses to welcome the prophet and when he arrived young kids greeted him with a _Nasheed_ poem. Also the valley of Wada' was the place where people would walk with their loved ones who were travelling and say goodbye. This mosque no longer stands, it was razed to make space for the commercial buildings and hotels to accommodate the burgeoning number of pilgrims. It was also known as the Mosque of Bani Khudara since it was located in the neighbourhoor of a sub-tribe of al-Khazarj, called Banu Khudara.

Ibn Shibah narrated on the authority of a sheikh from among the Ansar that the Prophet, may God’s prayers and peace be upon him, prayed in the mosque of Banu Khadara, and he shaved his head there.

**al-Saqiya Mosque**  
[Masjid-e al-Saqiya](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "al-Saqiya Mosque") (مسجد السقيا‎), near Bir al-Sakiye (Well of Saqiye), this is where prophet [Muhammad](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Prophet Muhammad") camped as he returned from [Battle of Badr](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of Badr"). The mosque has three domes, without minaret, originally built during Ottoman era, it was recently renovated by Fahad bin Abdul Aziz in 1423 Hj.

**Bani Haram Mosque**  
 The [Masjid Bani Haram](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Bani Haram Mosque") (مسجد بني حرام), located in al-Fath, west of [Jabl-e Sila'](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Mount Sela"), it situated where the dwellings of Bani Haram of al-Khazarj tribe were located. According to tradition [prophet Muhammad](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Prophet Muhammad") prayed at this site when the food was prolifirated by him while digging the [trench](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of the Trench").

**Jummah Mosque**  
 The [Masjid e Jumu'a](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Jummah Mosque"), Friday Mosque, (مسجد الجمعة) is according to the tradition the first mosque where the first [Jumua' prayer](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Friday Prayer") was offered by Muslims after the [Migration](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Hijrah"). Initially it was used only for the Friday prayers and remained close for others. Located on As Salam Road, Medina it was recently renovated from an older and much smaller Ottoman structure.

**Anbariya Mosque**  
 The [Masjid e Ambariye](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Amberiye Mosque") (مسجد العنبرية), also known as the Hamidiye Mosque, was built as a part of the Hejaz Railway project next to the el-Muazzem Railway Station. It was built in 1908 by the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II and is one of the few historic buildings which were not destroyed by the Saudi government. It is named after the Anbariya Gate, next to which the mosque was located.

**al-Fadhikh Mosque**  
 This is an old picture of [Masjid Al-Fadhikh](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Fadhikh Mosque") (مسجد الفضيخ) also known as the Masjid e Shams (Sun Mosque) was built at the location where prophet Muhammad offered Salah during the battle with Banu Nadir in Medina. It was extensively renovated during the third and fourth decade and stood until late 1960s, now there is a small cemetery at the location. Also the mosque is called al-Fadhikh, as it is a beverage made from palm fruit which is not ripe, and the verses containing the prohibition of alcohalic beverages are believed to have been revealed here as well. It is situated approx. 3.5 kilometers from [Masjid al-Nabawi](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi") and aprrox. 1 kilometer from [Masjid-e Quba](https://madainproject.com/quba_mosque "Masjid al-Quba").

**al-Khandaq Mosque**  
 The main courtyard of [Jameh al-Khandaq](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Jameh al-Khandaq") (جامع الخندق) or Masjid Ahzaab, the latest mosque built at the site of [Ghazwa Khandaq](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of the Trench"). This mosque lies at the foot or base of the Sal’ hill, on its western side. It signifies the scene of the Battle of Trench, or Khandaq, which is about three kilometers from the Prophet’s Mosque. Established in 2007, the mosque is surrounded by Jabl Sil'a from three sides and is accessible from north only. Madinah’s battle of the trench marked the consolidation of the Prophet’s tenure when he was faced with an attack on Madinah by an alliance of Jewish and non-Muslim Arab tribes.

**al-Areesh Mosque**  
 The facade and the main entrance to the [Masjid e Areesh](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Masjid Areesh, Medina") (مسجد العريش), situated at the site where during the [Battle of Badr](https://madainproject.com/mosques_in_medina "Battle of Badr") the command post of prophet Muhammad was pitched. The historic Battle of Badr (غزوة بدر), fought on Tuesday, 13 March 624 CE (17 Ramadan, 2 Hj.), was a key battle in the early days of Islam and a turning point in Muhammad's struggle with his opponents among the Quraish in Mecca.

**al-Sabaq Mosque**  
 The [as-Sabaq Mosque](https://madainproject.com/as_sabaq_mosque "Masjid as-Sabaq") (مسجد السبق‎), was a mosque located in Medina, south of al-Masjid an-Nabawi. The place was originally a place for horse racing during the time of the prophet Muhammad. There is an account in Hadith of al-Bukhari, that the prophet participating in a horse racing from Al-Hayfa to Tsaniyatul Wada' around six or seven miles, and from Tsaniyatul Wada' to the Bani Zuraiq Mosque for around one mile.

**al-Rayah Moque**  
 The al-Rayah Mosque (مسجد الراية), mosque of the flag, or Dzubab Mosque, is a small mosque historic situated on top of Mount Dzubab (Dzubab means "flies"), not far from Mount Sala'. According to a tradition the command post (tent/shade) was pitched for Prophet Muhammad here, hence it was named as Al-Rayah, which means battle flag. The mosque was first built during the reign of Umar ibn Abdul Aziz, with a small square with an area of 61 square meters and a height of 5 meters.

The **Prophet's Mosque** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): ٱلْمَسْجِد ٱلنَّبَوِي, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_al-Masjid al-Nabawī_, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'Mosque of the Prophet') is the [second mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_oldest_mosques "List of the oldest mosques") built by the Islamic prophet [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam") in [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina"), after the [Quba Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quba_Mosque "Quba Mosque"), as well as the second [largest mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_large_mosques "List of large mosques") and [holiest site in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiest_sites_in_Islam "Holiest sites in Islam"), after the [Masjid al-Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram "Masjid al-Haram") in [Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca "Mecca"), in the [Saudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") region of the [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-2) The mosque is located at the heart of Medina, and is a major site of [pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ziyarat "Ziyarat") that falls under the [purview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purview "Purview") of the [Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custodian_of_the_Two_Holy_Mosques "Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques").

[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad") himself was involved in the construction of the mosque. At the time, the mosque's land belonged to two young orphans, Sahl and Suhayl, and when they learned that Muhammad wished to acquire their land to build a mosque, they went to Muhammad and offered the land to him as a gift; Muhammad insisted on paying a price for the land because they were orphaned children. The price agreed upon was paid by [Abu Ayyub al-Ansari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Ayyub_al-Ansari "Abu Ayyub al-Ansari"), who thus became the endower or donor (Arabic: وَاقِف, romanized:_wāqif_) of the mosque, on behalf or in favor of Muhammad.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-3)

Originally an open-air building, the mosque served as a community center, a court of law, and a religious school. It contained a raised platform or pulpit (_[minbar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minbar "Minbar")_) for the people who taught the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") and for Muhammad to give the Friday sermon (_[khutbah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khutbah "Khutbah")_). Subsequent Islamic rulers greatly expanded and decorated the mosque, naming its walls, doors and minarets after themselves and their forefathers. After an expansion during the reign of the [Umayyad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate "Umayyad Caliphate") caliph [al-Walid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Walid_I "Al-Walid I") (r.705–715), it now incorporates the final resting place of Muhammad and the first two [Rashidun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate "Rashidun Caliphate") caliphs [Abu Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Bakr "Abu Bakr") (r.632–634) and [Umar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar "Umar") (r.634–644).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Syed-4) One of the most notable features of the site is the [Green Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Dome "Green Dome") in the south-east corner of the mosque,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Peterson-5) which was built above the site of the former house of [Aisha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aisha "Aisha"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Syed-4) where the graves of Muhammad, Abu Bakr and Omar are located.

In 1909, under the reign of [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire")[Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan "Sultan")[Abdul Hamid II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdul_Hamid_II "Abdul Hamid II"), it became the first place in the [Arabian Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula") to be provided with electrical lights.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-6) From the 14th century, the mosque was guarded by [eunuchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunuch "Eunuch"), the last remaining guardians were photographed at the request of then-[Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Saud#Third_Saudi_state "House of Saud")[Faisal bin Salman Al Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_bin_Salman_Al_Saud "Faisal bin Salman Al Saud"), and in 2015, only five were left.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-8) It is generally open regardless of date or time, and has only been closed to visitors once in modern times, as Ramadan approached during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Saudi_Arabia "COVID-19 pandemic in Saudi Arabia") in 2020.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-9)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [Muhammad in Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Medina "Muhammad in Medina")

See also: [History of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Islam "History of Islam")

### Under Muhammad and the Rashidun (622–660)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Under Muhammad and the Rashidun (622–660)")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Hadith_Masjid_an-Nabawi_Calligraphy_1.png/250px-Hadith_Masjid_an-Nabawi_Calligraphy_1.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hadith_Masjid_an-Nabawi_Calligraphy_1.png)

A [hadith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadith "Hadith") inscribed in the mosque which says "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers anywhere else, except for _Al-[Masjid al-Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid\_al-Haram "Masjid al-Haram")_."

The mosque was built by Muhammad in 622 after his arrival in Medina.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-10) Riding a camel called Qaswa, he arrived at the place where this mosque was built, which was being used as a burial ground.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200549-11) Refusing to accept the land as a gift from the two orphans, Sahl and Suhayl, who owned the land, he bought the land which was paid for by Abu Ayyub [al-Ansari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ansar_(Islam) "Ansar (Islam)"), and it took seven months to complete the construction of the mosque. It measured 30.5 m ×35.62 m (100.1 ft ×116.9 ft).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200549-11) The roof which was supported by palm trunks was made of beaten clay and palm leaves. It was at a height of 3.60 m (11.8 ft). The three doors of the mosque were the _Bāb ar-Raḥmah_ (بَاب ٱلرَّحْمَة, "Gate of the Mercy") to the south, _Bāb Jibrīl_ (بَاب جِبْرِيْل, "Gate of [Gabriel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel "Gabriel")") to the west, and _Bāb an-Nisāʾ_ (بَاب ٱلنِّسَاء, "Gate of the Women") to the east.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200549-11) At this time point in the history of the mosque, the wall of the _[qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla")_ was facing north to [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem "Jerusalem"), and the [Suffah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffah "Suffah") was along the northern wall. In the year 7 AH, after the [Battle of Khaybar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Khaybar "Battle of Khaybar"), the mosque was expanded[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200550-12) to 47.32 m (155.2 ft) on each side, and three rows of columns were built beside the west wall, which became the place of praying.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200551-13) The mosque remained unaltered during the reign of Abu Bakr.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200551-13)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Al-Masjid_al-Nabaw%C4%AB_Original_Schematic_Plan_1_AH_622_CE_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AC%D8%AF_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%8A_%E2%80%94_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%B7%D8%B7_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%B5%D9%84%D9%8A.svg/250px-Al-Masjid_al-Nabaw%C4%AB_Original_Schematic_Plan_1_AH_622_CE_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AC%D8%AF_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%8A_%E2%80%94_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%B7%D8%B7_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%B5%D9%84%D9%8A.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Al-Masjid_al-Nabaw%C4%AB_Original_Schematic_Plan_1_AH_622_CE_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AC%D8%AF_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%8A_%E2%80%94_%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%B7%D8%B7_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D8%B5%D9%84%D9%8A.svg)
