A miniature of the mosque in 628 CE (7 AH) after the first expansion

Umar demolished all the houses around the mosque, except those of [Muhammad's wives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad's_wives "Muhammad's wives"), to expand it.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-14) The new mosque's dimensions became 57.49 m ×66.14 m (188.6 ft ×217.0 ft). Sun-dried mud bricks were used to construct the walls of the enclosure. Besides strewing pebbles on the floor, the roof's height was increased to 5.6 m (18 ft). Umar constructed three more gates for entrance. He also added _Al-Buṭayḥah_ (ٱلْبُطَيْحَة) for people to recite poetry.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200554-15)

The third Rashidun caliph [Uthman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthman "Uthman") demolished the mosque in 649. Ten months were spent in building the new rectangular shaped mosque whose face was turned towards the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") in Mecca. The new mosque measured 81.40 m ×62.58 m (267.1 ft ×205.3 ft). The number of gates as well as their names remained the same.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200555-16) The enclosure was made of stones laid in mortar. The palm trunk columns were replaced by stone columns which were joined by iron clamps. [Teakwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teakwood "Teakwood") was used in reconstructing the ceiling filza.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200556-17)

### Umayyad era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Umayyad era")]

In 706 or 707, the [Umayyad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad "Umayyad") caliph [al-Walid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Walid_I "Al-Walid I") (r.705–715) instructed his governor of Medina, the future caliph [Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar_ibn_Abd_al-Aziz "Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz"), to significantly enlarge the mosque and carried out the fourth and most monumental expansion of the mosque.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:3-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHillenbrand199473-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMunt2014106-20) According to the architectural historian Robert Hillenbrand, the building of a large scale mosque in Medina, the original center of the caliphate, was an "acknowledgement" by al-Walid of "his own roots and those of Islam itself" and possibly an attempt to appease Medinan resentment at the loss of the city's political importance to [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilad_al-Sham "Bilad al-Sham") under the Umayyads.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHillenbrand199473-19)

It took three years for the work to be completed. Raw materials were procured from the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-21) Al-Walid lavished large sums for the mosque's reconstruction and supplied mosaics and Greek and [Coptic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copts "Copts") craftsmen.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBacharach199635-22) The area of the mosque was increased from the area 5,094 square metres (54,830 ft 2) of Uthman's time, to 8,672 square metres (93,340 ft 2).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200562-23) For the first time, [porticoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porticoes "Porticoes") were built in the mosque connecting the northern part of the structure to the sanctuary.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200562-23) The reconstruction preserved the location of the _qibla_ wall (in the direction of prayer), but Umar ordered the addition of a curved niche to it and this became the first concave [mihrab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihrab "Mihrab") in [Islamic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_architecture "Islamic architecture").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:0523-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEttinghausenGrabarJenkins-Madina200124-25) The renovated mosque was richly decorated with marble paneling and mosaics covering its walls. Later written accounts, such as that of [Ibn Jubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Jubayr "Ibn Jubayr") (1184), described the mosaics as containing inscriptions and depicting landscapes with trees, suggesting that they resembled the style of contemporary Umayyad mosaics in the [Dome of the Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome_of_the_Rock "Dome of the Rock") in Jerusalem and the [Great Mosque of Damascus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Mosque_of_Damascus "Great Mosque of Damascus").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:24-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-27)

The mosque's redevelopment entailed the demolition of the living quarters of [Muhammad's wives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wives_of_Muhammad "Wives of Muhammad") and the expansion of the structure to incorporate the graves of Muhammad, Abu Bakr and Umar.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKennedy2002127-28)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBacharach199635-22)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMunt2014106%E2%80%93108-29) The vocal opposition to the demolition of Muhammad's home from local religious circles was dismissed by al-Walid.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHillenbrand199473-19) A wall was built to segregate the mosque and the houses of the wives of Muhammad. The mosque was reconstructed in a trapezoid shape with the length of the longer side being 101.76 metres (333.9 ft).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200562-23)

According to the 10th-century writer [Ibn Rusta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Rusta "Ibn Rusta"), [minarets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minaret "Minaret") were also built for the first time during al-Walid's expansion as four towers were added to the mosque's corners.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom201349-30) They may be the first minarets in Islamic architecture,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEttinghausenGrabarJenkins-Madina200121-31) though it is not clear exactly what purpose these towers served in this early period.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom201349_(see_also_the_rest_of_this_chapter_for_context)-32) At the time of Ibn Rusta's writing, only one of the original four towers remained standing. The southwest minaret was demolished in 716 on the orders of [Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulayman_ibn_Abd_al-Malik "Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom201349-30)

### Abbasid era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Abbasid era")]

The [Abbasid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") caliph [al-Mahdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mahdi "Al-Mahdi") (r.775–785) extended the mosque to the north by 2,450 square metres (26,400 sq ft), the fifth expansion of the mosque which took four years to complete.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:3-18)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33) His name was also inscribed on the walls of the mosque. He also planned to remove six steps to the _minbar_, but abandoned this idea, fearing damage to the wooden platforms on which they were built.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMunt2014116-34) The project required the demolition of the two northern minarets of al-Walid's time but they were replaced by two new towers at the northern corners of the new expansion.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBloom201349%E2%80%9350-35) According to an inscription of [Ibn Qutaybah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Qutaybah "Ibn Qutaybah"), the caliph [al-Ma'mun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ma'mun "Al-Ma'mun") (r.813–833) did "unspecified work" on the mosque. [Al-Mutawakkil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mutawakkil "Al-Mutawakkil") (r.847–861) lined the enclosure of Muhammad's tomb with marble.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMunt2014118-36) In 1257–58 [Al-Musta'sim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Musta'sim "Al-Musta'sim") wanted to carry out a renovations program of the mosque but the renovation was interrupted by the [Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad "Siege of Baghdad").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33)

### Mamluk era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mamluk era")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Medina_Altes_Minaret_der_heiligen_Moschee%2C_erbaut_1483%3B_die_gr%C3%BCne_Kuppel_%C3%BCber_dem_Grabe_des_Propheten_erbaut_1840._1910._LCCN2002715728.jpg/250px-Medina_Altes_Minaret_der_heiligen_Moschee%2C_erbaut_1483%3B_die_gr%C3%BCne_Kuppel_%C3%BCber_dem_Grabe_des_Propheten_erbaut_1840._1910._LCCN2002715728.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Medina_Altes_Minaret_der_heiligen_Moschee,_erbaut_1483;_die_gr%C3%BCne_Kuppel_%C3%BCber_dem_Grabe_des_Propheten_erbaut_1840._1910._LCCN2002715728.jpg)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/The_Green_Dome%2C_Masjid_Nabawi%2C_Madina.jpg/250px-The_Green_Dome%2C_Masjid_Nabawi%2C_Madina.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Green_Dome,_Masjid_Nabawi,_Madina.jpg)

The Raisiyyah Minaret was built by Qaitbay in 1481 (886 AH). The [Green Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Dome "Green Dome") was originally built by Qalawun but was later rebuilt and painted green in 1837. Images in 1910 (left), and 2018 (right). The Green Dome is a defining symbol of the mosque.

In 1269, the [Mamluk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamluk_Sultanate "Mamluk Sultanate") sultan [Baybars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baybars "Baybars") sent dozens of artisans led by the eunuch Emir Jamal al-Din Muhsin al-Salihi to rebuild the sanctuary, including enclosures around the tombs of Muhammad and of Fatima.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-37) in 1279 sultan [Qalawun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qalawun "Qalawun") added a wooden dome over the tomb of the prophet,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:1-38) and rebuilt the south-western minaret (Bab Al-Salam minaret) in 1307, which still retains its lower structure but with the upper section being built during the [Ottoman era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33)

In 1474 the Mamluk sultan [Qaitbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qaitbay "Qaitbay") ordered major renovation to be conducted on the mosque's roofs, columns, walls and minarets, the work also included the rebuilding of the wooden dome to a stone dome over the prophet's tomb in 1476.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:1-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-39) and in 1481–1483 he carried out the sixth expansion of the mosque,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:3-18) and ordered the reconstruction of the Nabawi mihrab, Uthmani Mirhab and the Tahajjud Mihrab. In addition, he rebuilt the south-eastern Raisiyyah Minaret (main minaret) in 1481. It was subsequently renovated in 1483 and again in 1486. He also commissioned the construction of the Western Minaret, which was later demolished during the Saudi expansions.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33)

### Ottoman era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Ottoman era")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Medina_raja_ravi_varma-1910.jpg/250px-Medina_raja_ravi_varma-1910.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Medina_raja_ravi_varma-1910.jpg)

An illustration of the mosque in 1910

Sultan [Suleiman I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suleiman_the_Magnificent "Suleiman the Magnificent") (r.1520–1566) rebuilt the east and west walls of the mosque, and rebuilt the northeastern minaret known as _Sulaymaniyya_. He added a new altar called Ahnaf next to Muhammad's altar, Shafi'iyya, and placed a new steel-covered dome on the tomb of Muhammad. Sultan Suleiman I wrote the names of the [Ottoman sultans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_sultans "Ottoman sultans") from [Osman I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osman_I "Osman I") (r.1299–1324) to himself ([Kanuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suleiman_the_Magnificent "Suleiman the Magnificent")) and revived the "Gate of Mercy" (_Bab al-Rahma_) or the west gate. The pulpit that is used today was built under Sultan [Murad III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murad_III "Murad III") (r.1574–1595).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-40)

[Saud bin Abdul-Aziz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saud_bin_Abdul-Aziz_bin_Muhammad_bin_Saud "Saud bin Abdul-Aziz bin Muhammad bin Saud") took Medina from [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Arabia "Ottoman Arabia") control between 1805 and 1813 and his followers, the [Wahhabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wahhabis "Wahhabis"), [demolished nearly every tomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia") and dome in Medina to prevent their veneration,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Weston2008-41) except for the dome over Muhammad's tomb.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Behrens-AbouseifVernoit2006-42) According to their interpretation of Islam, they considered the veneration of tombs and places, which were thought to possess supernatural powers, as an offence against _[tawhid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawhid "Tawhid")_, and an act of _[shirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirk\_(Islam) "Shirk (Islam)")_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-43) Muhammad's tomb was stripped of its gold and jewel ornaments, but the dome was preserved either because of an unsuccessful attempt to demolish its complex and hardened structure, or because some time ago, [Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_ibn_Abd_al-Wahhab "Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab"), founder of the Wahhabi movement, wrote that he did not wish to see the dome destroyed.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Weston2008-41)

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/T_E_Lawrence_and_the_Arab_Revolt_1916_-_1918_Q58758.jpg/250px-T_E_Lawrence_and_the_Arab_Revolt_1916_-_1918_Q58758.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:T_E_Lawrence_and_the_Arab_Revolt_1916_-_1918_Q58758.jpg)

The interior of the mosque in 1916–1918

In 1817, Sultan [Mahmud II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmud_II "Mahmud II") (r.1808–1839) completed the reconstruction of _Al-Rawḍah Al-Sharīfah_ ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): ٱلرَّوْضَة ٱلشَّرِيْفَة, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'The Noble Garden') on the southeast side of the mosque, and reconsturcted its dome. The dome was painted green in 1837, and has been known as the "[Green Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Dome "Green Dome")" ever since.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Syed-4) Sultan Mahmud II's successor, Sultan [Abdulmejid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd%C3%BClmecid_I "Abdülmecid I") (r.1839–1861), carried out the seventh expansion of the mosque, and it took thirteen years to rebuild the mosque, beginning in 1849.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200564-44) Red stone bricks were used as the main material in reconstruction of the mosque. The floor area of the mosque was increased by 1,293 square metres (13,920 ft 2).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-46)

On the walls, verses from the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") were inscribed in [Islamic calligraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calligraphy "Islamic calligraphy"). On the northern side of the mosque, a _[madrasah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrasah "Madrasah")_ was built for teaching the Qur'an.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200565-47) An [ablution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wudu "Wudu") site was added to the north side. The prayer place on the south side was doubled in width, and covered with small domes. The interiors of the domes were decorated with verses from the Qur'an and couplets from the poem [Qasīdat al-Burda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Burda "Al-Burda"). The _[qibli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla")_ wall was covered with polished tiles with lines inscribed from the Qur'an. The places of prayer and courtyard were paved with marble and red stone. Following [Fakhri Pasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fakhri_Pasha "Fakhri Pasha")'s arrest by his own officers having resisted for 72 days after the end of the [Siege of Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Medina "Siege of Medina") on 10 January 1919, 400 years of Ottoman rule in the region came to an end.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-49)

### Saudi rule and modern history (1925–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Saudi rule and modern history (1925–present)")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/Masjid_e_Nabawi_Interior_2.jpg/250px-Masjid_e_Nabawi_Interior_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Masjid_e_Nabawi_Interior_2.jpg)

Interior of the Saudi expansion

After the foundation of the Kingdom of [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") in 1932, the mosque underwent several major modifications. The eighth expansion of the mosque started in 1951, [King Abdulaziz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Saud_of_Saudi_Arabia "Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia") (1932–1953) ordered demolitions around the mosque to make way for new wings to the east and west of the prayer hall, which consisted of concrete columns with pointed arches. Older columns were reinforced with concrete and braced with copper rings at the top. The western, north-western and north-eastern minarets were replaced with two minarets in [Mamluk revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Mamluk_architecture "Neo-Mamluk architecture") style. The two minarets were erected to the northeast and northwest of the mosque. A library and a museum were also built along the western wall to house historic Qurans and other religious texts.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200565-47)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-50) In 1974, [King Faisal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faisal_of_Saudi_Arabia "Faisal of Saudi Arabia") added 40,440 m 2 (435,300 sq ft) to the mosque.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Arabnews2012-51)

The largest and most monumental expansion of the Prophet's Mosque took place during the reign of [King Fahd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fahd_of_Saudi_Arabia "Fahd of Saudi Arabia"), beginning in 1985. This major project required the demolition of numerous buildings surrounding the mosque to accommodate its growth. As part of the expansion, six new minarets were constructed, each reaching a height of 103.89 meters. An additional 27 inner courtyards were also added, each covering an area of 324 m 2 (3,490 sq ft). Every courtyard was equipped with a movable dome that can be opened or closed depending on weather conditions, enhancing both comfort and functionality. The distinctive [Ablaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ablaq "Ablaq") pattern of the arches was preserved, maintaining continuity with the design established during the first Saudi expansion. The main Nabawi _mihrab_ was also renovated as part of the project. Beneath the mosque, a lower level covering approximately 28,000 m 2 (300,000 sq ft) was constructed to house essential infrastructure, including air-conditioning, water supply, warning and security systems, surveillance cameras, and remote-control equipment. In addition, an underground parking facility was built adjacent to the mosque. The expansion also included the construction of 15 service buildings around the outer courtyards, providing ablution facilities, restrooms, and drinking fountains to better accommodate the growing number of worshippers.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33) In 1992, when it was completed, the mosque took over 160,000 m 2 (1,700,000 sq ft) of space. Escalators were among the additions to the mosque.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:4-52)

In 2010, a major project was undertaken to install giant electrically operated retractable umbrellas across the outer courtyards of the Prophet's Mosque. A total of 250 umbrellas were erected, providing shade over approximately 143,000 square meters (1,540,000 square feet) of the mosque's surrounding courtyards. Designed to automatically open and close in response to weather conditions, the umbrellas significantly improved the comfort of worshippers by protecting them from the intense heat and direct sunlight while preserving the openness of the courtyards when not in use.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:4-52) A $6 billion project to increase the area of the mosque was announced in September 2012. After completion, the mosque should accommodate between 1.6 million to 2 million worshippers.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Arabnews2012-51) In March of the following year, the _[Saudi Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi\_Gazette "Saudi Gazette")_ reported that demolition work had been mostly complete, including the demolition of ten hotels on the eastern side, in addition to houses and other utilities.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-53)

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Architecture")]

The modern-day mosque is situated on a rectangular plot and is two stories tall. The [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") prayer hall, which is the oldest part of the mosque, lies towards the south. It has a [flat paved roof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flat_roof "Flat roof") topped with 27 sliding [domes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome "Dome") on square bases.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-54) Holes pierced into the base of each dome illuminate the interior when the domes are closed. The sliding roof is closed during the afternoon prayer (_[Dhuhr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuhr\_prayer "Zuhr prayer")_) to protect the visitors. When the domes slide out on metal tracks to shade areas of the roof, they create light wells for the prayer hall. At these times, the courtyard of the Ottoman mosque is also shaded with umbrellas affixed to freestanding [columns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Column "Column").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-55) The roof is accessed by stairs and [escalators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escalator "Escalator"). The paved area around the mosque is also used for prayer, equipped with umbrella tents.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-56) The sliding domes and [retractable umbrella-like canopies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina_Haram_Piazza "Medina Haram Piazza") were designed by the German Muslim architect [Mahmoud Bodo Rasch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmoud_Bodo_Rasch "Mahmoud Bodo Rasch"), his firm [SL Rasch GmbH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SL_Rasch_GmbH_Special_and_Lightweight_Structures "SL Rasch GmbH Special and Lightweight Structures"), and [Buro Happold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buro_Happold "Buro Happold").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-57)

### The Rawda

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: The Rawda")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Rawdah_by_Uleke.jpg/250px-Rawdah_by_Uleke.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rawdah_by_Uleke.jpg)

The area of _Al-Rawda al-Sharifah_ is distinguished by a series of uniquely colored columns. It lies between the minbar on the right and the wall of the burial chamber (Al-Hujrah - formerly the Prophet’s house) visible in the background. Entry to the Rawda is regulated through timed permits, with access granted during designated visitation slots.

_Al-Rawḍah Al-Sharīfah_ ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): ٱلرَّوْضَة ٱلشَّرِيْفَة, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'The Noble Garden') is an area between the _minbar_ and the burial-chamber of Muhammad (under the [Green Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Dome "Green Dome")). It is regarded as one of the _Riyāḍ al-[Jannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jannah "Jannah")_ (Arabic: رِيَاض ٱلْجَنَّة, lit.'Gardens of the Paradise').[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-58)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Syed-4) The area is distinguished by its marked columns and a green carpet, which historically contrasted with the red carpet used throughout the rest of the mosque. This distinction was eliminated when the carpeting throughout the mosque was later replaced with green. The Saudi [Ministry of Hajj and Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Hajj_and_Umrah "Ministry of Hajj and Umrah") lists the digital application [Nusuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nusuk "Nusuk") as the channel for booking appointments and issuing permits to visit Al-Rawda Al-Sharifah.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-59)

### The Green Dome

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: The Green Dome")]

Main article: [Green Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Dome "Green Dome")

The Sacred Prophetic Chamber adjacent to the Rawda holds the tombs of Muhammad and two of [his companions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Companions_of_the_Prophet "Companions of the Prophet") and [fathers-in-law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_tree_of_Muhammad "Family tree of Muhammad"), Abu Bakr and Umar. A fourth grave is reserved for [ʿĪsā](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus_in_Islam "Jesus in Islam") (Jesus), as Muslims believe that [he will return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Coming "Second Coming") and will be buried at the site. The site is covered by the [Green Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Dome "Green Dome"), which was originally built as a wooden dome by Mamluk sultan [Qalawun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qalawun "Qalawun") in 1279 and then replaced by a stone dome by Mamluk sultan [Qaitbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qaitbay "Qaitbay") in 1467.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:1-38) It was replaced by a new dome again in 1817, during the reign of the Ottoman sultan [Mahmud II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmud_II "Mahmud II"). This version was built in brick, covered in lead, and painted green in 1837.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-Syed-4)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIsm%C4%81%CA%BB%C4%ABl199856-60)

### Mihrabs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Mihrabs")]

In the early years of the mosque, there were two [mihrabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mihrab "Mihrab"), one was added by Muhammad (_Nabawi Mihrab_) and another was added after by Uthman (_Uthmani Mihrab_) after the expansion of the mosque in the [qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla") wall . The latter was larger than that of Muhammad's, and acted as the functional mihrab, whereas Muhammad's mihrab became a "commemorative" mihrab.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAriffin200557-61) The first concave mihrab niche was added to the qibla wall during the Umayyad renovation of the early 8th century.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:0523-24) The plate behind the current Nabawi mihrab indicates that the mihrab was built in 1484 by the Mamluk [sultan Qaitbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qaitbay "Qaitbay") (r.1468–1496).

The mosque also contains additional mihrabs that are no longer in use. The third mihrab, located to the west of the Nabawi Mihrab, is known as the Hanafi Mihrab. It was constructed by the Mamluk official Tughan Sheikh during the reign of Sultan [Sayf al-Din Inal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sayf_al-Din_Inal "Sayf al-Din Inal") (r.1453–1461) to accommodate prayers according to the [Hanafi school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanafi_school "Hanafi school") of thought, although the people of Medina initially rejected the installation of a separate mihrab for a different school of thought. The Hanafi mihrab was later renovated by Suleiman the Magnificent and subsequently named after him (Sulaimani Mihrab), an inscription behind the mihrab states that the renovation took place in 908 AH (1502–1503 CE); however, this date is considered incorrect. The inscription’s author likely intended to write either 928 AH (1522 CE) or 938 AH (1532 CE).[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-62) Other mihrabs that are not in use include the [Tahajjud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahajjud "Tahajjud") Mihrab which is currently covered, and the Fatima Mihrab in the burial chamber.

### Minbars

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Minbars")]

The mosque's previous minbar, commissioned by [Qaitbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qaitbay "Qaitbay"), was installed in 1483.

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Minbar_at_Masjid_Nabvi%2C_Medina.JPG/250px-Minbar_at_Masjid_Nabvi%2C_Medina.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Minbar_at_Masjid_Nabvi,_Medina.JPG)

The current minbar commissioned by Sultan [Murad III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murad_III "Murad III") installed in 1590

The original _minbar_ (مِنـۢبَر) used by Muhammad was a block of [date palm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Date_palm "Date palm") wood. This was replaced by him with a [tamarisk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamarisk "Tamarisk") one, which had dimensions of 50 cm ×125 cm (20 in ×49 in). In 629, a three staired ladder was added to it. Abu Bakr and Umar did not use the third step as a sign of respect to Muhammad, but Uthman placed a fabric dome over it, and the rest of the stairs were covered with [ebony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebony "Ebony").

According to [al-Saffarini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Saffarini "Al-Saffarini"), during the caliphate of [Muawiya I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu'awiya_I "Mu'awiya I") (r.661–680), he ordered his governor of Medina, [Marwan I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marwan_I "Marwan I"), to raise the Prophet's minbar, increasing it to nine steps. After the original minbar was destroyed in the fire of 1256 CE (654 AH), the Abbasid [Al-Musta'sim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Musta'sim "Al-Musta'sim") ordered that it be rebuilt. However, the [Mongol sack of Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad "Siege of Baghdad") interrupted the project before it could be completed. In response, the Sultan of Yemen [Al-Muzaffar Yusuf I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Muzaffar_Yusuf_I "Al-Muzaffar Yusuf I") commissioned a new sandalwood minbar and sent it to Medina. This was later replaced by one presented by the Mamluk sultan [Baybars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baybars "Baybars") in 1266 (664 AH), which remained in use until 1394 CE (797 AH), when [Barquq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barquq "Barquq") sent another minbar. It was subsequently replaced by one commissioned by [Al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mu'ayyad_Shaykh "Al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh") in 1417 CE (820 AH), which remained in the Prophet's Mosque until the fire of 1481 CE (886 AH). Following the fire, the people of Medina erected a temporary minbar until [Qaitbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qaitbay "Qaitbay") presented a white marble minbar in 1483 CE (888 AH). Finally, in 1590 CE (998 AH), the white marble minbar was replaced by another marble minbar commissioned by the Ottoman sultan [Murad III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murad_III "Murad III"), which became the mosque's permanent minbar.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:2-64) The minbar of Qaitbay was then moved to [Quba Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quba_Mosque "Quba Mosque"), and then to King Abdulaziz Library in Medina,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:2-64) in 2018 it was renovated and moved to the Prophet’s Mosque Architecture Exhibition, situated to the south of the Prophet's Mosque.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-65)

### Minarets

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Prophet%27s_Mosque&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Minarets")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Al-Masjid_An-Nabawi_%28Bird%27s_Eye_View%29.jpg/250px-Al-Masjid_An-Nabawi_%28Bird%27s_Eye_View%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Al-Masjid_An-Nabawi_(Bird's_Eye_View).jpg)

Bab al-Salam Minaret (foreground left), the Raisiyya Minaret next to the Green Dome (foreground right)

The earliest recorded [minarets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minaret "Minaret") were square stone towers,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-66) numbering four, that were built at the four corners of the mosque during the Umayyad period, they were constructed during the reign of [al-Walid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Walid_I "Al-Walid I") (r.705–715), under the supervision of the governor of Medina, [Umar ibn Abd al-aziz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar_ibn_Abd_al-Aziz "Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz"). The original minarets stood approximately 27.5 metres (90 ft) high with a base of 16 square metres (170 sq ft).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEttinghausenGrabarJenkins-Madina200121-31) The south-western minaret named Bab al-Salam minaret (مئذنة بَاب ٱلسَّلَام, _Miʾḏanat Bāb al-Salām_) was demolished by caliph [Sulayman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulayman_ibn_Abd_al-Malik "Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik") (r.715–717), only four years after it was built, because it overlooked the house of [Marwan ibn Al-Hakam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marwan_I "Marwan I"),[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-67) It was not rebuilt until 1307 by the Mamluk sultan [al-Nasir Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Nasir_Muhammad "Al-Nasir Muhammad"), restoring the number of minarets to four.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEttinghausenGrabarJenkins-Madina200121-31) The current Bab al-Salam minaret retains its Mamluk period lower structure, while its upper section was renovated during the Ottoman period.

The mosque's minarets underwent several phases of renovation and reconstruction. A fifth minaret, the western Bab al-Rahma Minaret (مئذنة بَاب الرحمة, _Miʾḏanat Bāb al-Raḥma_), was added in 1483–84 during the reign of the [Mamluk Sultan Qaitbay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qaitbay "Qaitbay") (r.1468–1496). During the same period, the south-eastern Raisiyyah ("Main") Minaret (المئذنة الرئيسية, _al-Miʾḏana al-Raʾīsiyya_), located beside the [Green Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Dome "Green Dome"), was rebuilt three times between 1481 and 1486, it has remained largely preserved in its original Mamluk architectural form to this day. By the time of the Ottoman expansion under [Sultan Abdulmejid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd%C3%BClmecid_I "Abdülmecid I") (r.1839–1861), the mosque had five minarets.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33) Of these, only the Raisiyyah Minaret has retained its original Mamluk architectural style, while the other four were rebuilt in the Ottoman architectural style.

Of the five minarets, only two remain today. The south-eastern Raisiyyah ("Main") Minaret (المئذنة الرئيسية), and the south-western Bab al-Salam minaret (مئذنة بَاب ٱلسَّلَام), The remaining three were demolished and replaced during the Saudi expansions of the mosque. During the first Saudi expansion (1952–1955), two new minarets were constructed at the northern end of the mosque, one on the eastern side and the other on the western side. During the second Saudi expansion (1985–1994), six additional minarets, each rising to 103.89 metres (340.8 ft), were added, bringing the mosque's total number of minarets to ten.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque#cite_note-:0-33)

# Masjid al-Haram

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

The Masjid al-Ḥarām (المسجد الحرام‎), literally meaning "the sacred mosque"), also called the Sacred Mosque, and the Grand Mosque or Great Mosque of Mecca, is the largest mosque in the world and surrounds Islam's holiest place, the Kaaba, in the historic city of Mecca, modern day Saudi Arabia. Being the primary site associated with the [Hajj](https://madainproject.com/hajj "Hajj") pilgrimage it is considered to be the most significant mosque in [Islam](https://madainproject.com/islamic_archaeology "Islam").

#### Overview

The Great Mosque of Mecca today is a large complex of buildings, ritual landmarks, pilgrimage facilities, includes other important significant sites, such as the _Hajar al-Aswad_, the Zamzam Well, Maqam Ibrahim, and the hills of Safa and Marwa.

The Great Mosque is the main setting for the Hajj and Umrah pilgrimages that occur in the month of _Dhu al-Hijja_ in the Islamic calendar and at any time of the year, respectively. It is one of the "Five Pillars of Islam" that requires every Muslim to undertake a pilgrimage journey, one of the largest annual gatherings of people in the world, at least once in their lifetime when able to do so (physically and financially), which includes a number of rituals including the central circumambulating the Kaaba.

#### Brief History

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 3](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mecca_timeline_370271.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/mecca_timeline_370271.jpg)

The [history of the Great Mosque of Mecca](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_al_haram "History of the Masjid al-Haram"), today known as the _Masjid al-Haram_, or simply the _Haram_, consists of two types in nature, first is the oral or religious tradition and the second is the material tradition.

**Early History and the Foundation of Masjid al-Haram**  
 The foundation of Masjid al-Haram, as a religious center, traces back to the time of Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), who, along with his son Isma'il, is believed to have built the Kaaba as a place of worship dedicated to the one true God. Islamic tradition holds that the original structure of the mosque was simple and modest, with the Kaaba at its center. The early mosque was open and unroofed, designed primarily for the worship of Allah by the small community of Ibrahim’s followers. The establishment of the mosque symbolized a place of worship that would eventually become the qibla for Muslims worldwide.

**The Quraysh Era and the Reconstruction of the Kaaba**  
 By the time of the Prophet Muhammad, the Quraysh tribe, who controlled Makkah, undertook significant renovations to the Kaaba and its surrounding area. The Quraysh rebuilt the Kaaba, reinforcing it with stronger materials and establishing a more structured space for prayer. During this period, the mosque around the Kaaba also began to take shape, albeit still without a roof. The mosque was primarily a space for prayer and the hosting of pilgrims who arrived to perform religious rites. It was also during this time that the Prophet Muhammad was born and the religious significance of the mosque began to grow, as it served as the focal point for many of the events in his early prophethood.

**The Umayyad Caliphate and the First Major Expansion**  
 Following the conquest of Makkah in 630 CE, under the leadership of Prophet Muhammad, the Masjid al-Haram began to receive substantial attention in terms of expansion and enhancement. The Prophet expanded the mosque's area slightly, with a focus on accommodating the growing number of Muslims who had come to perform pilgrimage and prayer. However, the most significant development occurred during the reign of the Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan in the late 7th century. He expanded the mosque to include additional space around the Kaaba and constructed a roofed area for prayer. The mosque began to take the form of a large and organized worship space, setting the foundation for later expansions.

**The Abbasid Caliphate and Further Expansions**  
 The Abbasid Caliphate, which succeeded the Umayyads in the 8th century, also made significant contributions to the development of Masjid al-Haram. Under the Abbasids, the mosque was expanded further, and more renovations were carried out to address the increasing number of pilgrims. They also made improvements to the surrounding infrastructure, including the addition of new gates and the development of paved pathways to facilitate access for pilgrims. The Abbasid period marked an era of institutionalizing the mosque as the primary site for Islamic worship and pilgrimage, consolidating its place as the epicenter of the Muslim world.

**The Ottoman Period and the Heightened Focus on Preservation**  
 During the Ottoman period, beginning in the early 16th century, Masjid al-Haram underwent extensive renovations, with the Ottomans dedicating significant resources to preserving and enhancing the mosque. The Ottomans constructed new domes and expanded the mosque’s boundaries to accommodate the growing number of pilgrims, particularly during the Hajj season. The iconic Ottoman-inspired elements, including the intricate calligraphy and design motifs, were added to the mosque’s architecture. This era also saw the introduction of new minarets and the establishment of a formalized system of maintenance for the mosque. Ottoman efforts focused on the preservation of the Kaaba and its surroundings, ensuring that the mosque remained a stable and welcoming place for worshippers.

**Modern Saudi Expansions and Technological Integration**  
 With the establishment of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the 20th century, Masjid al-Haram underwent its most extensive expansions, driven by the vision of King Abdulaziz and subsequent monarchs. The mosque's area was dramatically increased to accommodate the ever-growing number of Muslim pilgrims, and state-of-the-art technologies were introduced to manage crowd control, improve security, and ensure comfort for worshippers. New prayer halls, multi-level galleries, and additional minarets were added to accommodate millions of pilgrims. The area surrounding the Kaaba was restructured to improve access, and sophisticated cooling systems were introduced to provide relief during the hot summer months. The expansion of the mosque continued into the 21st century under King Fahd, who oversaw the addition of vast prayer spaces and the expansion of the Mataf (circumambulation area) to meet the needs of a larger number of pilgrims. This modern era represents the blending of historical reverence with contemporary engineering, ensuring that the Masjid al-Haram remains at the center of Islamic worship and pilgrimage, providing a sacred space for millions of Muslims each year.

#### Notable Structures

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 4: Bait ul-Allah, the Kaaba](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/kaaba_9328473.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/kaaba_9328473.jpg "Bait ul-Allah, the Kaaba")

**_Kaaba_**  
 The [Kaaba](https://madainproject.com/kaaba "Kabah"), (Bait ul-Allah) is the focal point of Muslim prayer i.e. Qibla, it is also the focal point of Hajj and Umrah pilgrimages. It is considered by Muslims to be the _Bayṫ Allāh_ (بَـيْـت ٱلله‎, literally meaning the "House of God"), and has a somewhat similar role to the Tabernacle and Holy of Holies in Judaic tradition. Being the _qiblah_ (قِـبْـلَـة‎, direction of prayer), Muslims would face it when praying. The Quran contains several verses regarding the origin of the Kaaba. It states that the Kaaba was the first House of Worship, and that it was built by prophets _Ibrahim_ and _Ishmael_ on Allah's instructions.

According to Islamic tradition, it was first built by Prophet Adam, but its current known structure traces its origins back to Prophet _Ibrahim_ (Abraham) and his son _Isma'il_ (Ishmael), who are believed to have rebuilt it upon divine command. The Kaaba is a cuboid-shaped building, with each side measuring approximately 12 meters in height and 10-12 meters in length. It is constructed from granite stones, with the exterior clad in a black silk and gold-embroidered cloth, known as the Kiswa, which is replaced annually during the Hajj season.

The Kaaba's location and its role in Islamic worship are grounded in both historical events and religious commandments. It is the qibla, the direction towards which Muslims around the world face during their daily prayers. This directionality was instituted after the Prophet Muhammad was instructed by Allah to turn from Jerusalem to Makkah, making the Kaaba the central point for all Islamic rituals. The black stone embedded in the eastern corner of the Kaaba, known as the Hajar al-Aswad, is believed to have been sent from Paradise as a sign of divine mercy and forgiveness. Pilgrims performing the Tawaf, the act of circumambulating the Kaaba during Hajj and Umrah, seek to kiss or touch the stone as a symbol of spiritual connection and submission to Allah.

Architecturally, the Kaaba has undergone several modifications and reconstructions throughout its history. It was initially a simple structure, with a roofless design and open interior. During the reign of the Quraish, it was rebuilt, and the structure was reinforced with more durable materials. Subsequent repairs and renovations were carried out under the Caliphate of various Islamic dynasties, including the Umayyads, Abbasids, and Ottomans, each contributing to the architectural enhancements that solidified its status as the center of Islamic worship. The most recent renovations, carried out under the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, have involved the installation of modern security measures, enhanced structural reinforcements, and the addition of an extensive framework to maintain the sanctity of the site during the continuous flow of millions of pilgrims.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 5](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_83274832.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_83274832.jpg)

**_Mataaf_**  
 The [Mataaf](https://madainproject.com/mataf "Mataf") is the open area around the Kaaba, where pilgrims and Muslims circumbulate around Ka'bah. Total area of current Mataf's ground floor is about 14,000 square meters. The Kaba is located in the center of Mataf area, along with Hateem (Hajr Ismaeel) and Maqam Ibrahim.

Integral to the performance of Hajj and Umrah, the Mataf has undergone significant changes throughout history to accommodate the increasing number of pilgrims. The Mataf area was originally a relatively small sandy area, with a natural, unpaved surface and was first plastered by _'Abdullah ibn Zubayr_, since then Mataaf has seen countless, building and rebuilding developments. Successive expansions—most notably during the Ottoman, Saudi, and modern eras—have transformed it into a vast, multi-level space capable of hosting millions.

The Mataf reflects meticulous planning to balance the preservation of its sacred atmosphere with modern functionality. The introduction of additional levels, smooth pathways, and barriers for crowd management ensures both accessibility and safety. Special lanes are designated for pilgrims with mobility needs, while advanced cooling systems keep the marble surface comfortable even in extreme heat.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 6](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/zamzam_2342288.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/zamzam_2342288.jpg)

**_ZamZam_ Well**  
 The [Zam Zam](https://madainproject.com/zam_zam "Zam Zam Well") is a water well near, approximately 20 meters east, of the [Kaaba](https://madainproject.com/kaaba "Kabah"), which according to Islamic Tradition sprang to quench the thirst of prophet [Ishmael](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram "Ishmael") (Ismail). Islamic tradition states that the Zamzam Well was revealed to Hajar, the second wife of Ibrahim's and mother of _Ismaʿil_.

According to Islamic tradition, Hajar ran seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah in search of water, until the Angel Jibreel (Gabriel) struck the ground, causing water to gush forth at her son's feet. This spring, known as Zamzam, has flowed continuously for millennia, sustaining pilgrims and locals alike, and is viewed as a sign of divine providence and mercy.

The well originally had two cisterns in the first era, one for drinking and one for ablution. In the era of the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur, circa 771 CE (154/155 Hijri), a dome was built above the well, and it was tiled with marble.

Hydrogeological studies have revealed that Zamzam draws from an underground aquifer fed by rainwater, yet its uninterrupted flow and purity are considered miraculous by believers. The well is approximately 30 meters deep, and its water, rich in minerals, is known for its distinct taste and remarkable properties. Traditionally, pilgrims partake in Zamzam water during Hajj and Umrah, fulfilling the Sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad, who described it as "a blessed water, and it is a cure for illness" (Sahih Muslim).

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 7](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/maqam_ibrahim_23847288.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/maqam_ibrahim_23847288.jpg)

**_Maqam Ibrahim_**  
 The so-called Maqam Ibrahim ([Station of Abraham](https://madainproject.com/station_of_abraham "Maqam Ibrahim")) (مقام ابراهیم) houses the stone or small rock on which Prophet _Ibrahim_ (Abraham) is believed to have stood while constructing the Kaaba. The rock that is believed to have an imprint of Abraham's foot and is kept in an ornate crystal dome next to the Kaaba. Maqam Ibrahim (also spelled as _Muqam Ibrahim_) is spoken of in Quran in Surah al-Baqarah verse 125:

وَاتَّخِذُوا مِن مَّقَامِ إِبْرَاهِیمَ مُصَلًّی
And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of salah (prayer).

The stone, encased in a gilded and glass structure for protection, remains visible to pilgrims and serves as a focal point of devotion. The Quran further references the collaborative effort of Ibrahim and his son Isma'il (Ishmael) in raising the Kaaba's foundations in Surah al-Baqarah 2:127.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 8: Mount Safa](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/safa_2384723.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/safa_2384723.jpg "Mount Safa, Jabl-i Safa or Koh-i Safa")

**Hills of _Safa_ and _Marwah_**  
 The [Safa and al-Marwah](https://madainproject.com/safa_and_marwah "Safa and Marwah") are twin hills of Sa'yee at Sacred Mosque. Safa and Marwah are two hills between which Abraham's wife Hagar ran, looking for water for her infant son Ishmael, an event which is commemorated in the saʿy ritual of the pilgrimage. Pilgrims make rounds at these hills from [Safa](https://madainproject.com/al_safa "al-Safa") towards [Marwah](https://madainproject.com/al_marwah "al-Marwah") seven times in commemoration of [Hajrah](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram "Hagar") doing the same in search of water almost 4000 years ago.

Historically, the hills were natural formations outside the original boundaries of the Kaaba's enclosure, but successive expansions of the mosque have incorporated them into the sacred complex. The modern-day Mas'a gallery preserves the geological features of Safa and Marwah, with their summits clearly marked for pilgrims performing the Sa'i. Safa lies approximately 130 meters from the Kaaba, while Marwah is about 300 meters away, with the path between them spanning a total of approx. 400 meters.

Despite their integration into the mosque's architecture, the hills themselves have retained some of their natural contours. They are no longer exposed to the open air but remain accessible through a multi-level gallery designed to accommodate the increasing number of pilgrims. Pilgrims begin their _Sa'i_ at mount Safa, ascending its slope to face the Kaaba in prayer before proceeding towards Marwah. The act of traversing the path seven times symbolizes not only Hajar’s historical journey but also a believer's continuous struggle and reliance on God.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 9](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masaa_8374289.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masaa_8374289.jpg)

**_Mas'a_ Gallery**  
 The [Mas'a](https://madainproject.com/al_masaa_(masjid_al_haram) "Masa'a (Masjid al-Haram)"), a corridor between the hills of Safa and Marwah within the _Masjid al-Haram_ complex, is an integral part of the sacred rituals or pilgrimages of Hajj and Umrah. During the Saudi period it was included in the Mosque, via roofing and enclosures. The length of Sayee gallery (distance between Safa and Marwa) is approximately 450 meters (1,480 feet). The two points and the path between them are now inside a long gallery that forms part of the mosque. The _Masa'a_ gallery connects two mounts preserving the memory of what Hajira and baby Ismail had endured after prophet Ibrahim left them.

This gallery marks the route for the _Sa'i_ ritual, where pilgrims reenact _Hajar_'s desperate search for water for her son, prophet _Isma'il_. Historically, the path was an open-air passage outside the mosque, but successive expansions have incorporated it within the mosque's structure, ensuring protection and accessibility for millions of pilgrims annually. The gallery is now a multi-level structure, with dedicated floors for walking and wheelchair access, designed to manage the enormous pilgrim flow while preserving the spiritual significance of this act of worship. Advanced cooling systems and markings indicating the exact locations of Safa and Marwah enhance the functionality of the _Mas'a_, blending modern engineering with profound historical and religious significance.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 10: Masjid al-Haram Gates](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bab_abdullah_324238.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bab_abdullah_324238.jpg)

**Gates of _Masjid al-Haram_**  
 Today there are about 210 [gates of the _Masjid al-Haram_ complex](https://madainproject.com/gates_of_masjid_al_haram "Gates of Masjid al-Haram (Great Mosque of Mecca)"), that grant access to different internal areas of the Grand Mosque. The gates of _Masjid al-Haram_ serve as both functional and symbolic thresholds to one of the most sacred spaces in Islam. Historically, the mosque's gates have evolved alongside its expansions, reflecting the architectural styles of different Islamic eras while adapting to the increasing number of pilgrims. Early references to the gates can be traced to the Abbasid and Mamluk periods, during which names like _Bab al-Salam_ and Bab Ibrahim emerged, often derived from their geographical location or associated historical events. Today, the mosque features over 210 gates, including iconic ones such as _Bab al-Malik Abdulaziz_ and _Bab al-Fath_, designed to facilitate smooth entry and exit for millions of worshippers. Constructed using high-quality marble, intricate calligraphy, and durable materials, these gates are equipped with advanced technology for crowd management, security, and accessibility, including escalators and signage to aid visitors. Each gate is meticulously maintained, embodying a blend of tradition and modernity, and serving as a testament to the enduring legacy of Islamic architecture and devotion.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 11](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_library_738162.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_library_738162.jpg)

**Library of _Masjid al-Haram_**  
 The Grand Mosque Library is situated on the second floor (accessible from the gate no. 79/80) of the King Fahd Expansion and occupies an area exceeding 800 square meters. The library is designed to accommodate individuals with special needs and provides a range of services, including information services, self-photography, digital book browsing, audio resources (such as sermons (_Khutub_ الخطب), lessons (الدروس), and recitations), and digital copying of books and sermons. Its establishment aims to reinforce the scientific and advocacy mission of the Two Holy Mosques by offering a comprehensive system of guidance, advisory, and educational services to their visitors.

The establishment of the Grand Mosque Library was initiated by His Excellency, the President General of the Affairs of the Grand Mosque, Sheikh Professor Dr. _Abdulrahman bin Abdulaziz al-Sudais_. Its inauguration took place on Saturday, June 1, 2013 (22 Rajab 1434 Hijri), under the patronage of His Royal Highness Prince Khalid al-Faisal, Governor of Makkah al-Mukarramah, within the King Fahd Expansion. Initially, the library operated under the direct supervision of the President General of the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and is currently affiliated with the Presidency Agency for the Affairs of the Grand Mosque and the Prophet's Mosque. The library features a reading hall, an audio library, a digital library, and computer facilities, providing visitors with access to a wide range of sciences and knowledge. Open to the public 24 hours a day, the Grand Mosque Library remains a pivotal resource for intellectual and educational engagement.

#### Historic Structures

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

circa 1930 CE

[![Image 12](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_23842231.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_23842231.jpg)

**Bab Bani Shaybah**  
 The [Bab Bani Shaybah](https://madainproject.com/bab_bani_shaiba "Bab Bani Shaiba") (left); until 1950s this single single free standing arch was a part of Mataaf area. al-Maqdisi accounts nineteen gates of Masjid al-Haram while naming these. According to al-Maqdisi's account it is preferable and desirable for pilgrims to enter the mosque through this gate. This gate has since 1960s been removed. The other two significant structures are Muqam Ibrahim (center) and Ka'bah (right).

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

circa

[![Image 13](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/maqamat_34827.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/maqamat_34827.jpg)

**Maqamat of the Four Imams**  
 The [stations (_maqamat_) of the four imams](https://madainproject.com/maqamat_of_the_four_imams "Maqamat of the Four Imams") were a series of four free-standing canopied structures which used to mark the _musalla_ (prayer leading spot for _imams_) in the _mataf_ area of the Great Mosque. These were of varying sizes, and were located around the Kaaba in four separate directions. These were demolished during the 1925/1926 CE demolition campaign.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

[![Image 14](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ottoman_porticos_938491839.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ottoman_porticos_938491839.jpg)

**Ottoman Porticoes**  
 The [Ottoman Porticoes](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram "Ottoman Porticoes"), are the arched porches built around the courtyard (mataaf) built during the Ottoman era. During the [King Abdullah Expansion](https://madainproject.com/king_abdullah_expansion "King Abdullah Expansion") these porticoes were designated to be preserved, and now stand re-built on three sides of the Mataaf area, except the _al-Masa'a_. Some of these porticoes were rebuilt some 15 years ago due to the damage suffered in earlier expansions. All the original porticoes will be preserved except these newly reconstructed ones.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

#### Expansions

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

circa 1500-1940 CE

[![Image 15](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ottoman_haram_77927.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ottoman_haram_77927.jpg)

**Ottoman and Early Saudi Era**  
 In 1570 CE, Sultan Selim II commissioned the chief architect [Mimar Sinan](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram "Mimar Sinan") to renovate the mosque. This renovation resulted in the replacement of the flat roof with domes decorated with calligraphy internally, and the placement of new support columns which are acknowledged as the earliest architectural features of the present mosque. These features are the oldest surviving parts of the building.

During heavy rains and flash floods in 1621 and 1629 CE, the walls of the Kaaba and the mosque suffered extensive damage. In 1629, during the reign of Sultan Murad IV, the mosque was renovated. In the renovation of the mosque, a new stone arcade was added, three more minarets (bringing the total to seven) were built, and the marble flooring was retiled. This was the unaltered state of the mosque for nearly three centuries until the Saudi Era.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

circa 1950-1975 CE

[![Image 16](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/saud_expansion_11389.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/saud_expansion_11389.jpg)

**King Saud Expansion**  
 The first major renovation under the Saudi kings was undertaken during the reign of Malik al-Saud between 1955 and 1973. In this renovation, four more minarets were added, the ceiling was refurnished, and the floor was replaced with artificial stone and marble. The Mas'a gallery (As-Safa and Al-Marwah) is included in the Mosque, via roofing and enclosures.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

circa 1975-1990 CE

[![Image 17](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/fahad_expansion_77298.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/fahad_expansion_77298.jpg)

**King Fahad Expansion**  
 The second Saudi renovations under King Fahd, added a new wing and an outdoor prayer area to the mosque. The new wing, which is also for prayers, is reached through the King Fahd Gate. This extension was performed between 1982 and 1988 CE.

[](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_haram)

circa 2008 CE

[![Image 18](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_82373848.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/masjid_haram_82373848.jpg)

**King _'Abdullah_ Expansion**  
[Malik 'Abdullah ibn Abdulaziz expansion](https://madainproject.com/king_abdullah_expansion "King Abdullah Expansion") of Masjid al-Haram, 2008- till date CE. The modern expansion included 300,000 square metres of space towards the north-west of existing structures. It can accommodate 1.2 million worshippers, including a multi-level extension on the north side of the complex, new stairways and tunnels, a gate named after King Abdullah (lower left). The Great Mosque of Mecca is a very dynamic structure, it has been ever expanding since the sixth century until very recently.

# Expansion Chronology of Masjid al-Nabawi

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

The expansion chronology of [Masjid al-Nabawi](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi") refers to the longitudinal architectural and spatial evolution of the Prophet’s Mosque in [Medina](https://madainproject.com/medina "Medina tu-Nabi"), encompassing its continuous physical development from its [inception in 621 CE](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi_at_the_time_of_prophet_muhammad "Masjid an-Nabawi at the Time of Prophet Muhammad") to the modern era. This chronology serves as a primary record of Islamic structural history, reflecting the transition of the site from a modest mud-brick enclosure to a globally significant complex. The expansion chronology of Masjid Nabawi is distinct from the overarching [history of the Prophet's Mosque](https://madainproject.com/history_of_masjid_nabawi "History of Masjid Nabawi").

#### Overview

The History (chronology) of Masjid an-Nabawi's expansions, or the construction history of Masjid Nabawi, refers to the evolution of the Islam's second holiest mosque over the centuries, since its inception in 622 CE. Soon after arriving in Medina, prophet Muhammad and his companions embarked on building the masjid. Originally a very modest structure, today it is one of the largest mosques in the world.

One of the world’s largest mosques, covering an area of approx. 160,000 square meters or 39.5 acres, today it is one of the few largest mosque in the world. The Prophet's Mosque underwent several expansions throughout its history, starting with the days of the caliphs, followed by the Umayyads, the Abbasids, the Ottomans, and, finally, the Saudi era, during which it underwent the largest expansion in its history and was the first place in the Arabian Peninsula to be lit by electric light bulbs in 1908/1909 (1327 Hijri).
