#### Overview

Situated south-west of [Masjid an-Nabawi](https://madainproject.com/masjid_al_nabawi "Masjid al-Nabawi"), it lead directly to the neighbourhood of Wadi al-Aqiq. It was used as entrance to the city of Medina by the people arriving from the seaport of Jeddah (جدة) and Yanbu (ينبع البحر).

[![Image 2: Bab Anbariya](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bab_anbariya_32.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bab_anbariya_32.jpg)

circa 1800 CE

[![Image 3: Bab Anbariya](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bab_anbariya_92.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/bab_anbariya_92.jpg)

The gate was named after the al-Anbariya neighbourhood of Madinah al-Munawarah, which in turn was named after the orchard of a cheiftan in the Ottoman Empire, who donated the part of the land close to the gate for a military academy.

[](https://madainproject.com/bab_anbariya)

#### _Masjid al-Anbariya_

circa 1800 CE

[![Image 4: Masjid Anbariya](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/amberiya_masjid_238728.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/amberiya_masjid_238728.jpg)

The Anbariya Mosque (مسجد العنبرية) also known as the Hamidiye Mosque, is also named after the Anbariya Gate, next to which the mosque was located. It was built by the Ottoman Turks in Medina, which is nowadays part of Saudi Arabia. The Masjid al-Anbariya was built as part of the Hejaz Railway project next to al-Muazzim Railway Station, which houses the Hejaz Railway Museum.

[](https://madainproject.com/bab_anbariya)

The Madain Project is an online archive of Abrahamic History and Archaeology.

Abrahamic History & Archaeology is the study of history and archaeology with respect to the three Abrahamic Faiths without considering the religious and theological aspects. The goal of Abrahamic History is to understand how and why the religious doctrines and behaviours have evolved and changed over time. Searching for patterns in the evolution of significant cultural events such as the development of farming, the emergence of cities, or the collapse of major civilizations for clues of why and how these have influenced the three major Abrahamic religions.

# About Makkah al-Mukarramah

### Geography and Significance

Makkah Mukarramah is situated on the northern part of the Arabian Peninsula, at an elevation of 280 meters above sea level, in a valley known as Batn Makkah (also called Beke). At the center of this valley lies the Kaaba. It is surrounded by the Hira and Sebir mountains to the northeast, the Abu Qubays hill to the east with Safa and Marwah, the Kuaykian hill to the west, and the Sevr hill to the southwest.

#### Makkah Mukarramah is:

*   The location of the Kaaba, the qibla of Muslims.
*   The site of the Masjid al-Haram, where every act of worship is rewarded manifold.
*   The birthplace of our Prophet Muhammad (SAW).
*   The place where Prophethood and Messengership were bestowed upon him.
*   The city where many verses of the Holy Quran were revealed.
*   The sacred city where the obligatory duty of Hajj is performed.

### Names in the Quran and Symbolism

Makkah has been mentioned with various names in the Holy Quran, highlighting its esteemed status:

1.   Makkah
2.   Bakkah
3.   Umm al-Qura (Mother of Cities)
4.   Al-Balad
5.   Al-Balad al-Amin (The Secure City)
6.   Al-Balad al-Haram
7.   Haramain Amin
8.   In the Valley of Zer
9.   Ma’ad (Place of Return)
10.   Qaryah
11.   Al-Masjid al-Haram

The world is shaped like a circle with the Kaaba at its center. Each country in the world faces one side of the Kaaba. Therefore, the act of Tawaf (circumambulation) around the Kaaba symbolizes the rotation of the world around its own axis. The Kaaba is the noblest point on earth and the center of the universe.

### The Sacred Sanctuary: Haram and Hill

#### Haram:

On the day Allah created the heavens and the earth, He declared Makkah as a sacred sanctuary (Haram). The reason for the name “Haram” is that within its boundaries, it is forbidden (haram) to kill any living creatures (except those that are harmful) or to harm vegetation. All forms of aggression are prohibited, making the area safe and inviolable. The boundaries of the Haram are marked by stones called “alem,” covering an area of 550 km².

**Important:** In the Haram area, both the rewards for good deeds and the consequences of sins are multiplied.

#### Hill:

The region between the Haram and the miqat points is known as Hill. In this area, the specific restrictions of the Haram are lifted.

> Prophet Muhammad (SAW) stated that the land closest and dearest to Allah on Earth is the vicinity of the Kaaba. During his migration, he turned to Makkah and said, “I swear by Allah! You are the best of Allah’s lands, and the most beloved to Him. If I were not driven away from you, I would never have left.”

The **Mosque of the Prophet** (or **Prophet's Mosque**) ( Arabic: [Шаблон:Unicode](javascript:; "Шаблон:Unicode (страница не существует)") ) [IPA /mæsʤıd ænːæbæwiː], in [Medina](link_20), is the second holiest mosque in [Islam](link_21) and the second largest mosque in the world after the [Masjid al-Haram](link_22) in [Mecca](link_23). It is the final resting place of Prophet [Muhammad](link_24). Masjid al-Haram in Mecca is the holiest and the largest mosque and the [Al-Aqsa Mosque](link_25) in [Jerusalem](link_26) is the third holiest in Islam.

...

###### See also

*   [Green Dome](link_27)
*   [Mosque of Al-Ghamama](link_28)
*   [Al-Baqi'](link_29)
*   [Al-Ijabah Mosque](link_30)

The original mosque was built by Prophet Muhammad. Subsequent Islamic rulers greatly expanded and decorated it. Early Muslim leaders Abu Bakr and [Umar](link_31) are buried in an adjacent area in the mosque.

[![Image 9: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286274 [link_32])

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](link_33)

The edifice was originally Prophet Muhammad's house; he settled there after his Hijra (emigration) to Medina, later building a mosque on the grounds. He himself shared in the heavy work of construction. The original mosque was an open-air building. The basic plan of the building has been adopted in the building of other mosques throughout the world.

[![Image 10: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2296463 [link_34])

[The Rawdah al-Sharifah in the Prophet's Mosque, Madinah, Saudi Arabia (5) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](link_35)

The mosque also served as a community center, a court, and a religious school. There was a raised platform for the people who taught the Qur'an.

## History

[Шаблон:Refimprovesect](javascript:; "Шаблон:Refimprovesect (страница не существует)") The original Mosque was built by Muhammad, next to the house where he settled after his journey to Medina in 622 AD. The original mosque was an open-air building with a raised platform for the reading of the Qur'an. It was a rectangular enclosure of 30x35 meters, built with palm trunks and mud walls, and accessed through three doors: Bab Rahmah to the south, Bab Jibril to the west and Bab al-Nisa' to the east. The basic plan of the building has since been adopted in the building of other mosques throughout the world.

[![Image 11: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286284 [link_36])

[Decoration of the interior of a dome in the Prophet's Mosque, Madinah, Saudi Arabia — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](link_35)

Inside, Muhammad created a shaded area to the south called the suffrah and aligned the [prayer](link_37) space facing north towards Jerusalem. When the qibla (prayer direction) was changed to Mecca, the mosque was re-oriented to the south. The mosque also served as a community center, a court, and a religious school. Seven years later (629 AD/7 AH), the mosque was doubled in size to accommodate the increasing number of [Muslim](link_38)s.

[![Image 12: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286273 [link_39])

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](link_40)

Subsequent Islamic rulers continued to enlarge and embellish the Prophet's Mosque over the centuries. In 707, Umayyad [Caliph](link_41) Al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik (705-715) replaced the old structure and built a larger one in its place, incorporating the tomb of Muhammad. This mosque was 84 by 100 meters in size, with stone foundations and a teak roof supported on stone columns. The mosque walls were decorated with mosaics by Coptic and Greek craftsmen, similar to those seen in the [Umayyad Mosque](link_42) in [Damascus](link_43) and the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (built by the same caliph). The courtyard was surrounded by a gallery on four sides, with four [minaret](link_44)s on its corners. A mihrab topped by a small dome was built on the qibla wall.

Abbasid Caliph al-Mahdi (775-785) replaced the northern section of Al-Walid's mosque between 778 and 781 to enlarge it further. He also added 20 doors to the mosque: eight on each of the east and west walls, and four on the north wall.

[![Image 13: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286286 [link_45])

[Interior of the Prophet's Mosque, Madinah, Saudi Arabia (2) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](link_35)

[![Image 14: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286279 [link_46])

[Masjid Nabawi — neo saed @ Flickr](link_47)

During the reign of the Mamluk [Sultan](link_48) Qalawun, a dome was erected above tomb of the Prophet and an ablution fountain was built outside of Bab al-Salam. Sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad rebuilt the fourth minaret that had been destroyed earlier. After a lightning strike destroyed much of the mosque in 1481, Sultan Qaitbay rebuilt the east, west and qibla walls.

The Ottoman sultans who controlled Medina from 1517 until World War I also made their mark. Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566) rebuilt the western and eastern walls of the mosque and built the northeastern minaret known as al-Suleymaniyya. He added a new mihrab (al-Ahnaf) next to prophet Muhammad's mihrab (al-Shafi'iyyah) and placed a new dome covered in lead sheets and painted green above the Prophet's house and tomb.

[![Image 15: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286288 [link_49])

[Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](link_35)

During the reign of Ottoman Sultan Abdülmecid (1839-1861), the mosque was entirely remodeled with the exception of Muhammad's Tomb, the three mihrabs, the minbar and the Suleymaniyya minaret. The precinct was enlarged to include an ablution area to the north. The prayer hall to the south was doubled in width and covered with small domes equal in size except for domes covering the mihrab area, Bab al-Salam and Muhammad's Tomb. The domes were decorated with Qur'anic verses and lines from Qaṣīda al-Burda (Poem of the Mantle), the famous poem by 13th century Arabic poet [Busiri](link_50). The qibla wall was covered with glazed tiles featuring Qur'anic calligraphy. The floors of the prayer hall and the courtyard were paved with marble and red stones and a fifth minaret (al-Majidiyya), was built to the west of the enclosure.

[![Image 16: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2296462 [link_51])

[Al-Masjid an-Nabawi — Fadhlur Rahman @ Flickr](link_52)

After the foundation of the [Kingdom of Saudi Arabia](link_53) in 1932, the Mosque of prophet Muhammad underwent several major modifications. In 1951 King Ibn Saud (1932-1953) ordered demolitions around the mosque to make way for new wings to the east and west of the prayer hall, which consisted of [concrete](link_54) columns with pointed arches. Older columns were reinforced with concrete and braced with [copper](link_55) rings at the top. The Suleymaniyya and Majidiyya minarets were replaced by two minarets in Mamluk revival style. Two additional minarets were erected to the northeast and northwest of the mosque. A library was built along the western wall to house historic Qur'ans and other religious texts.

In 1973 Saudi King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz ordered the construction of temporary shelters to the west of the mosque to accommodate the growing number of worshippers in 1981, the old mosque was surrounded by new prayer areas on these sides, enlarging five times its size.

[![Image 17: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286276 [link_56])

[بلال الدويك @ WikiCommons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User_talk:%D8%A8%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%84%20%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%8A%D9%83)

The latest renovations took place under King Fahd and have greatly increased the size of the mosque, allowing it to hold a large number of worshippers and pilgrims and adding modern comforts like air conditioning. He also installed twenty seven moving domes at the roof of Masjid Nabawi.

[![Image 18: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286283 [link_57])

[The Prophet's Mosque, Madinah, Saudi Arabia (5) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](link_35)

## Description

[Шаблон:Refimprovesect](javascript:; "Шаблон:Refimprovesect (страница не существует)") ]] As it stands today, the Prophet's Mosque has a rectangular plan on two [floors](link_58) with the Ottoman prayer hall projecting to the south. The main prayer hall occupies the entire first floor. The mosque enclosure is 100 times bigger than the first mosque built by the Prophet and can accommodate more than half a million worshippers.

The Prophet's Mosque has a flat paved roof topped with 24 [dome](link_59)s on square bases. Holes pierced into the base of each dome illuminate the interior. The roof is also used for prayer during peak times, when the 24 domes slide out on metal tracks to shade areas of the roof, creating light wells for the prayer hall. At these times, the courtyard of the Ottoman mosque is also shaded with umbrellas affixed to freestanding columns. The roof is accessed by stairs and escalators. The paved area around the mosque is also used for prayer, equipped with umbrella tents.

[![Image 19: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286287 [link_60])

[Interior of the Prophet's Mosque, Madinah, Saudi Arabia (1) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](link_35)

The north facade has three evenly spaced [portico](link_61)s, while the east, west and south facades have two. The walls are composed of a series of windows topped by pointed [arch](link_62)es with black and white voussoirs. There are six peripheral minarets attached to the new extension, and four others frame the Ottoman structure. The mosque is lavishly decorated with polychrome

# Islamic Archaeology

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

The Islamic archaeology is concerned with the investigation of the material culture and historical record of Muslim peoples and societies. As an area of academic inquiry and as a practical part of heritage management, Islamic archaeology is growing as the role of Islam in the world increases both as a political force and in terms of its financial resources.

#### Overview

Because the _Islamic Archaeology_ as a field of study is relatively young, there are a number of conceptual difficulties with the term “Islamic archaeology” which will be discussed further, but for the present it is used in broad inclusive fashion to encompass any archaeology where Islam is a significant factor in the history or heritage of the region or theme under consideration.

The emergence of the Islamic Civilization, which is no clearer than the emergence of the Sumerians or the Old Kingdom of Egypt, demands the attention of archaeological research. And the Islamic Archaeology presents a prime opportunity to address historical questions from complementary textual and archaeological evidence.

[![Image 2](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/dome_of_rock_283726.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/dome_of_rock_283726.jpg)

[](https://madainproject.com/islamic_archaeology)

#### Brief History of Islamic Archaeology

circa

[![Image 3](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jameh_isfahan_4791.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jameh_isfahan_4791.jpg)

**Emergence and Definition**  
 Islamic archaeology emerged as an independent field about 100 years ago, initially focused on artifact recovery for funding. Born from the fields of Islamic art and architectural history, the archaeological study of the Islamic societies is a relatively young discipline. Over time, it evolved into a more rigorous examination of material remains, influenced by the historical significance of art and Orientalist studies. Early studies lacked critical interest due to Hegel's portrayal of art history, which relegated Islamic contributions to a lesser status. This perception began to change in the mid-nineteenth century with a more secular understanding of Islamic civilization's historical role. With its roots in the colonial periods of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, its rapid development since the 1980s warrants a reevaluation of where the field stands today.

Marcus Milwright defines the field of Islamic archaeology as a specialism within the discipline of archaeology. The term Islamic archaeology may be broadly defined as the examination of the physical remains of human activity and of the wider environment in regions of the world where the ruling elite professed the faith of Islam [[UR2](https://madainproject.com/islamic_archaeology#ur2)].

**Historical Context**  
 The historical context of Islamic archaeology was shaped by the political motives of colonial powers. For instance, the excavation of _Madinat al-Zahra_ in Spain / _al-Andalus_ was linked to Spain's political ambitions in Morocco. The German involvement in the Ottoman Empire prior to World War I also played a significant role, as German archaeologists conducted numerous excavations in Palestine and Mesopotamia, supported by the state.

There was a significant methodological shift in Islamic archaeology from mere artifact recovery to a comprehensive examination of Islamic art and architecture. This change was driven by an increased interest in the historical role of Islamic civilization, leading to a more interdisciplinary approach that linked archaeology with history and anthropology.

**Methodological Evolution**  
 There was a significant methodological shift in Islamic archaeology from mere artifact recovery to a comprehensive examination of Islamic art and architecture. This change was driven by an increased interest in the historical role of Islamic civilization, leading to a more interdisciplinary approach that linked archaeology with history and anthropology.

**Political and Colonial Influences**  
 Political and colonial influences were deeply intertwined with the development of Islamic archaeology. The discipline was often used to bolster national identities, particularly during the colonial expansions of European powers. The excavation practices were influenced by the political context, with significant archaeological efforts aimed at asserting control over regions like North Africa.

**Excavation Processes and Practices**  
 Excavation practices in the early days of Islamic archaeology often overlooked Islamic levels at pre-Islamic sites. However, as nationalist sentiments grew, there was a push for the establishment of antiquities policies and museums, which aimed to protect and promote the archaeological heritage of Islamic regions. Key scholars such as Max van Berchem and Friedrich Sarre made significant contributions the field of Islamic archaeology. Their work, along with advancements from Russian scholars, opened new areas for exploration and excavation, enhancing the understanding of Islamic history and culture.

**Changes in Sponsorship and Regulation**  
 Post-World War I, there were notable changes in the sponsorship and regulation of archaeological expeditions. The establishment of national departments of antiquities and the shift from museum sponsorship to national schools and institutes marked a new era in the conduct of archaeological research in Islamic lands.

**Modern Developments**  
 Modern developments in Islamic archaeology have seen an increase in inquiry, particularly in Iran and the Middle East, following World War II. The geographical scope of the field has expanded to include sub-Saharan Africa and East Africa, reflecting a broader understanding of Islamic influence and trade networks.

**Challenges and Critiques**  
 Islamic archaeology has faced various challenges and critiques, including a lack of scientific methods and poorly trained archaeologists. There have been concerns regarding publication records and the use of archaeology to construct national identities, prompting calls for more rigorous standards in the field.

**Interdisciplinary Approaches**  
 The emergence of interdisciplinary approaches has been a significant development in Islamic archaeology, linking it with history and anthropology. This shift has allowed for a more nuanced understanding of local communities and economies, moving beyond the constraints of political history.

### Egypt

Egypt was one of the earliest regions to be influenced by the Islamic civilization after the Arab conquest in the mid seventh century CE. The study of Islamic archaeology in Egypt allows scholars to explore the transition from Byzantine and Coptic periods to the Islamic era, understanding the continuity and change in material culture, architecture, and societal structures. [![Image 6: History and Archaeology of Iraq](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ziggurat_ur_497525.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/iraq "Iraq")
### Iraq

Iraq has played a central role as the cradle of various civilizations, including the earliest Islamic civilizations, particularly in cities like Baghdad, Samarra, and Najaf, and has witnessed the rise and fall of empires, making it a treasure trove for archaeological exploration. The archaeological sites in these areas offer insights into the early years of the Islamic Caliphate, including the Umayyad and Abbasid periods. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/iraq "Iraq")

[![Image 7: History and Archaeology of Jordan](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/obelisk_tomb_2374632766.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/jordan "Jordan")
### Jordan

Jordan holds significant importance in the context of Islamic archaeology due to its historical role in the development of Islamic civilization. It is known for its Umayyad Desert Castles, a series of early Islamic structures built during the Umayyad Caliphate (7th-8th centuries). These castles, such as Qasr Amra and Qasr Kharana, provide insights into Umayyad architecture, art, and the economic and administrative functions of these structures. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/jordan "Jordan")

[![Image 8: History and Archaeology of Ancient Syria](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/aleppo_jami_umavi_3748.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/syria "Syria")
### Syria

Syria holds immense significance in the context of Islamic archaeology due to its rich history and its role as a cultural crossroads. The country is home to numerous archaeological sites that span various periods, including the Islamic era. The Umayyad Mosque in Damascus, medieval castles from the Crusader and Muslim periods and Aleppo Citadel are few of the notable archaeological sites in Syria. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/syria "Syria")

### Saudi Arabia

More recently, Saudi Arabia has been increasingly recognized for its significant role in the field of archaeology in general and Islamic archaeology in specific, for which the country has undertaken various initiatives to explore and preserve its cultural heritage. Recent archaeological efforts have been directed towards the restoration and preservation of a large number of historical and archaeological structures and sites. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/saudi_arabia "Saudi Arabia")

[![Image 10: History and Archaeology of Israel/Palestine](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/hisham_palace_11726.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/palestine "Palestine")
### Israel/Palestine

The region of Israel and Palestine is of immense significance in the context of Islamic archaeology due to its rich history, diverse cultures, and the presence of major historical and religious sites. The study of Islamic archaeology in Israel and Palestine is complex and often intersects with broader historical and cultural narratives. The geopolitical situation adds unique challenges but also underscores the importance of cultural heritage in fostering understanding and dialogue. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/palestine "Palestine")

## Featured Article[Amulet of _Kareem_](https://madainproject.com/list_of_seals_found_in_israel#kareem-amulet "Arabic talisman dating back to Abbasid Era")

The amulet was dated by Dr. _Nitzan Amitai-Preiss_ of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem based on its calligraphy, which is typical of the early third caliphate period (circa 750–1258 CE); the dating of the archaeological structure in which it was found; and pottery fragments found at the site, including a complete lamp, which are typical of the Abbasid period.

Beautifully inscribed in Arabic, the rare thumbnail-sized talisman has been dated to the ninth or tenth century CE, the time of the Abbasid Caliphate. The devotional writing appears on two lines and has been translated as reading: “Kareem trusts in Allah – Lord of the Worlds is Allah.”

[The _Kareem_ Amulet](https://madainproject.com/list_of_seals_found_in_israel#kareem-amulet) | [Explore Seals/Bullae Found in Israel/Palestine](https://madainproject.com/list_of_seals_found_in_israel "List of Seals found in Palestine")

## Featured Article[The Islamic Coinage](https://madainproject.com/islamic_coinage "Islamic Coinage")

The first dated coins that can be assigned to the Muslims are copies of silver Dirhams of the Sassanian ruler Yazdegerd III, struck during the Caliphate of Uthman. These coins differ from the original ones in that an Arabic inscription is found in the obverse margins, normally reading "in the Name of Allah". The subsequent series was issued using types based on drachmas of Khosrau II, whose coins probably represented a significant proportion of the currency in circulation.

Dated coins exist from 680 CE (74 Hijri) and are named as '_Dinars_'. These experimental issues were replaced in 683 CE (77 Hijri), except in North Africa and Spain, by completely epigraphical designs very similar to the designs adopted for the silver pieces but with a shorter reverse legend and no annulets or inner circles.

# Middle East

By _[the Editors of the Madain Project](https://madainproject.com/help#editors-of-the-madain-project)_

Ancient Middle East, history of the region from prehistoric times to the rise of civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and other areas. The high antiquity of civilization in the Middle East is largely due to the existence of convenient land bridges and easy sea lanes passable in summer or winter, in dry or wet seasons. Movement of large numbers of people north of the Caspian Sea was virtually impossible in winter, because of the severity of the climate, and central Eurasia was often too dry in summer. Land passage between Asia and Africa was in early times limited to narrow strips of land in the Isthmus of Suez. Large-scale desert travel was limited to special routes in Iran and in North Africa, both east and west of the Nile valley.

[Fertile Crescent](https://madainproject.com/middle_east "Fertile Crescent") / [Mesopotamia](https://madainproject.com/middle_east "Mesopotamia") / [Levant](https://madainproject.com/levant "Levant")

[![Image 2: Middle East](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ur_ziggurat_117289.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ur_ziggurat_117289.jpg)

[](https://madainproject.com/middle_east)

### Brief History

The history of the ancient Middle East, often referred to as the "Cradle of Civilization", unfolds as a captivating tapestry of human achievement, innovation, and cultural evolution. Encompassing a vast and diverse region that stretches from the Nile River in Egypt to the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in Mesopotamia, the ancient Middle East served as the crucible where some of humanity's most remarkable achievements took root.

In the millennia before the Common Era, the ancient Middle East bore witness to the birth of the world's earliest civilizations. Along the fertile banks of the Nile, the mighty Egyptian civilization emerged, boasting awe-inspiring pyramids, complex hieroglyphic writing, and an enduring reverence for the afterlife. Meanwhile, in the land of Mesopotamia, the Sumerians, Akkadians, and Babylonians laid the foundations for urban life, legal codes, and intricate cuneiform script. These early societies set the stage for an unprecedented era of innovation and cultural exchange.

The history of the ancient Middle East is punctuated by the rise and fall of powerful empires and kingdoms. The Assyrians and Persians expanded their dominions through military conquests, while the Phoenicians and Minoans became influential maritime traders, disseminating goods and ideas across the Mediterranean. The Persian Empire, under the leadership of Cyrus the Great, famously embraced religious tolerance and human rights, leaving a lasting legacy of administrative excellence.

This region was also a vibrant cultural melting pot where art, literature, and philosophy thrived. The epic of Gilgamesh, the poetry of Sappho, and the wisdom of Confucius found their roots here, influencing generations of thinkers and writers. Cities like Babylon, Nineveh, and Persepolis were renowned for their architectural splendor and artistic achievements.

The ancient Middle East gave birth to several major world religions. Zoroastrianism emerged in Persia, while the monotheistic faiths of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam trace their roots to this region. The story of Abraham's journey, the teachings of the Hebrew prophets, and the life of Muhammad are deeply intertwined with the sacred landscapes of the Middle East.

[History of the Middle East](https://madainproject.com/middle_east "Fertile Crescent")

### Levant

The Levant is a historical and geographical term referring to the easternmost region of the Mediterranean, encompassing lands where Europe, Asia, and Africa converge. In its broadest sense, it signifies the coastal and hinterland zones.

### Babylon (Mesopotamia)

The history and archaeology of ancient Babylon, located in the region of Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq), represent a significant chapter in the story of human civilization. Babylon was one of the most influential and well-known cities of the ancient world, renowned for its architecture, culture, and role in shaping the history of Mesopotamia. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/babylon "Babylon")

[![Image 5: Gate of All Nations (Persepolis, Persia)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/all_nations_gate_82372.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/persia "Persia")
### Persia

This remarkable chapter in human history, shaped by the rise and reign of the Achaemenid Empire, showcases the birth of a powerful and influential empire that left an indelible mark on the ancient world. The Persian civilization emerged from the annals of prehistory and evolved into a vast empire that stretched from the Mediterranean to the Indus River. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/persia "Persia")

[![Image 6: Ancient Arabia](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/roads_of_arabia_341947.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/arabia "Arabia")
### Arabia

Ancient Arabian civilization refers to the complex and diverse cultures that thrived on the Arabian Peninsula long before the emergence of Islam. This rich history spans thousands of years and encompasses various tribes, kingdoms, and empires. Archaeological evidence indicates that early humans inhabited the region around 1.2 million years ago. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/arabia "Arabia")

[![Image 7: Ancient Egypt](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/abu_simbel_878392.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/egypt "Egypt")
### Egypt

Spanning over three millennia along the banks of the Nile River, Egypt's rich past is marked by incredible achievements in culture, science, architecture, and governance. Egypt's history is traditionally divided into dynastic periods. Archaeological findings include the tombs of the early pharaohs at Abydos, Hierakonpolis, and Saqqara, displaying the first examples of monumental architecture and hieroglyphic writing. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/egypt "Egypt")

[![Image 8: Ancient Palestine](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ghawanim_minaret_22178.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/palestine "Palestine")
### Israel/Palestine

The history and archaeology of ancient Israel and Palestine are deeply intertwined, spanning thousands of years, this history is marked by significant events, religious developments, and cultural transformations. The history and archaeology of ancient Israel and Palestine offer a rich tapestry of cultures, religions, and historical events. Archaeological excavations continue to unearth new evidence that enhances our understanding. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/palestine "Palestine")

[![Image 9: Ancient Persepolis, Persia](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/tachara_66729.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/persepolis "Persepolis")
### Ancient Persepolis

Persepolis, located in modern-day Iran, was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, one of the most influential and powerful empires of the ancient world, built to celebrate the empire's glory. Its history and archaeology offer profound insights into the culture, art, and achievements of ancient Persia. Persepolis, characterized by grand palaces and monumental staircases, was founded by Darius the Great, who ruled the Achaemenid Empire from 522 to 486 BCE. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/persepolis "Persepolis")

[![Image 10: Works of the Old Men](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/pendants_33971.jpg) ### Works of the Old Men](https://madainproject.com/works_of_the_old_men "Works of the Old Men")

## Featured[Works of the Old Men](https://madainproject.com/works_of_the_old_men "Works of the Old Men")

The "works" demonstrate specific geometric patterns and extend from a few tens of meters up to several kilometers, evoking parallels to the well-known system of geometric lines of Nazca, Peru. In comparison the Nazca Lines in Peru are dated between 200 BCE and CE 500). These occur throughout the entire Arabia region, from Syria across Jordan and Saudi Arabia to Yemen. Archaeological studies indicate that some of the wheels date back to circa 8,500 years, a prehistoric time when the climate was wetter in parts of the Middle East.

### Oman

Located on the southeastern tip of the Arabian Peninsula, Oman has been a crossroads of cultures and a center of trade for thousands of years. The history and archaeology of ancient Oman unfold as a captivating tale of a land deeply connected to maritime trade, cross-cultural interactions, and the enduring legacies of several great civilizations. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/oman "Oman")

[![Image 12: Saudi Arabia](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/madain_saleh_87238.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/saudi_arabia "Saudi Arabia")
### Saudi Arabia

The history and archaeology of ancient Saudi Arabia unveil a complex and diverse narrative that spans millennia, revealing a land of great historical and cultural significance. As the cradle of Islam and home to several ancient civilizations, including the Nabateans and the kingdoms of Arabia, Saudi Arabia's past is rich and multifaceted. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/saudi_arabia "Saudi Arabia")

[![Image 13: Ancient Syria](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/aleppo_citadel_34782.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/syria "Syria")
### Syria

Ancient Syria, which includes present-day Syria and parts of modern-day Lebanon, Jordan, and Turkey, has been home to some of the world's oldest and most influential civilizations. Modern archaeological excavations in Syria have uncovered a wealth of historical sites and artifacts, providing insights into its ancient history. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/syria "Syria")

## Featured[Gate of Xerxes](https://madainproject.com/gate_of_all_nations "Gate of All Nations")

The "Gate of All Nations," also known as the "Gate of Xerxes" or "Gate of Darius," was a prominent architectural feature of the ancient Persian city of Persepolis. Persepolis, located in modern-day Iran, served as the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire during its zenith in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE. The Gate of All Nations was one of the main entrances to the city and was situated in the eastern wall of the terrace upon which Persepolis was built.

[Explore](https://madainproject.com/gate_of_all_nations "Gate of All Nations")

[![Image 14: Gate of All Nations (Persepolis, Persia)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/all_nations_gate_82372.jpg) ### Gate of Xerxes](https://madainproject.com/gate_of_all_nations "Gate of All Nations")

[![Image 15: Turkey](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ephesus_11626.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/turkey "Turkey / Türkiye")
### Turkey (_Türkiye_)

The history and archaeology of ancient Anatolia, which is modern-day Turkey, is a story of remarkable civilizations, diverse cultures, and significant historical events that have shaped this region for thousands of years. Anatolia is often considered one of the world's earliest centers of human civilization. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/turkey "Turkey / Türkiye")

[![Image 16: Jordan](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/al_deir_petra_28212.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/jordan "Jordan")
### Jordan

This region, strategically located at the crossroads of the Middle East, has been home to numerous civilizations and has witnessed significant historical developments. Jordan's archaeological record reveals evidence of human habitation dating back to the Paleolithic period, with findings such as flint tools and rock shelters. Jordan's archaeological sites, including Petra, Jerash, Amman, and others, offer a glimpse into the region's storied past. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/jordan "Jordan")

[![Image 17: Ancient Assur](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/tabira_gate_assur_117793.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/assur "Assur")
### Assur

The ancient city of Assur, also known as Ashur, holds a pivotal place in the annals of Mesopotamian history. Situated on the western bank of the Tigris River in present-day Iraq, Assur was the political, religious, and cultural epicenter of the Assyrian civilization. With roots stretching back to the third millennium BCE, Assur emerged as a significant urban center during the early Bronze Age. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/assur "Assur")

[![Image 18: Tomb of Cyrus the Great](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/%C3%A2r%C3%A2mg%C3%A2h_kuro%C5%A1_217462.jpg) ### Tomb of Cyrus the Great](https://madainproject.com/tomb_of_cyrus "Tomb of Cyrus the Great")

## Featured[Tomb of Cyrus the Great](https://madainproject.com/tomb_of_cyrus "Tomb of Cyrus the Great")

The Tomb of Cyrus the Great (who ruled from 559 to 530 BCE) is an ancient funerary monument located near the ancient city of Pasargadae in modern-day Iran. It is one of the most significant archaeological sites in Iran and holds historical and cultural importance as the resting place of Cyrus II, commonly known as Cyrus the Great. The tomb's construction is attributed to Cyrus, and its location signifies his connection to Pasargadae and his desire for a simple burial.

[![Image 19: Ancient Kalhu (Nimrud)](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/kalhu_lamassu_palace_557281.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/nimrud "Nimrud")
### Nimrud (Kalhu)

Nimrud was founded by Shalmaneser I, an Assyrian king, in the thirteenth century BCE. It became the capital of the Assyrian Empire under the reign of Ashurnasirpal II. The city reached its peak during the ninth and eighth centuries BCE and was known for its impressive architecture, including palaces, temples, and fortifications. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/nimrud "Nimrud")

[![Image 20: Ancient Hatra](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/hatra_iwan_117729.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/hatra "Hatra")
### Hatra

Ancient Hatra, located in present-day Iraq, was a prominent city of the Parthian Empire and later the capital of the first Arab kingdom. The city, established around the 3rd or 2nd century BCE, thrived as a major trading hub on the Silk Road, connecting the Roman and Persian worlds. Hatra's unique position allowed it to extensively prosper economically and culturally. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/hatra "Hatra")

### Niver River

Historically, Nile water was excellent for irrigation because the annual flood deposited nutrient-rich silt that renewed soil fertility. This is what allowed Egypt and Nubia to sustain intensive agriculture in otherwise desert zones. In the modern period, after the Aswan High Dam ended the natural flood cycle. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/nile "Nile")

## Featured Article[Roads of Arabia Exhibition](https://madainproject.com/roads_of_arabia_exhibition "Roads of Arabia Exhibition")

The Roads of Arabia exhibition delves into the historical and cultural evolution of Arabia, starting from early human history. It explores ancient incense trade routes and early-Islamic pilgrimage roads that linked Arabia with regions like Iraq, Syria, Egypt, and the Mediterranean. The exhibition provides valuable insights into the cultural exchanges between Arabia and its varied neighbors. Among the intriguing findings is the al-Hamra cube, showcasing the blend of Egyptian and Mesopotamian motifs in local religious practices. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article lists [mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") from around the world by available capacity, that belong to any [Islamic school or branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_schools_and_branches "Islamic schools and branches"), that can accommodate at least 15,000 worshippers in all available places of [prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salah "Salah") such as prayer halls (_[muṣala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musalla "Musalla")_), courtyards (_[ṣaḥn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahn "Sahn")_) and porticoes (_[riwāq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riwaq\_(arcade) "Riwaq (arcade)")_). All the mosques in this list are [congregational mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_mosque "Congregational mosque") – a type of mosque that hosts the [Friday prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friday_prayer "Friday prayer") (_ṣalāt al-jumuʿa_) in [congregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_prayer_(Islam) "Congregational prayer (Islam)") (_jamāʿa_).

# Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina

![Image 4: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina hac 2](blob:http://localhost/353ad08187169bdf2b11ae2019ee8822)

PLACES OF VISIT AND SACRED SITES IN MEDINA

## Jannat al-Baqi

The cemetery of Medina known as “Baqi’ al-Gharqad” or “Baqi'” is located to the southeast of Masjid al-Nabawi in Medina.

[![Image 5: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina cennetul baki](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=724)

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=724)

[![Image 6: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina hz ebubekir mescidi](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=730)

## Masjid Abu Bakr al-Siddiq

One of the mosques located in the Medina prayer ground. It is situated at the beginning of Amidyya Street to the northwest of the Musalla Mosque.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=730)

[![Image 7: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina medine demiryolu](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=734)

## Medina Railway Station

Construction began in 1900, and in 1908, the Hejaz Railway reached Medina, establishing a connection between Medina and Istanbul.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=734)

[![Image 8: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina kibleteyn mescidi](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=738)

## Masjid al-Qiblatain

Located in the northwest of Medina, in the Wabara area, and 5 km away from Masjid al-Nabawi, this mosque’s first name was “Masjid Bani Salim” due to the tribe it was situated in.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=738)

[![Image 9: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina cuma mescidi](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=740)

## Masjid al-Jumu'ah

During the migration, the Prophet (SAW) arrived at Quba and stayed there for 14 days, waiting for Hazrat Ali (RA) and the other migrants from Mecca.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=740)

[![Image 10: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina gamame mescidi](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=727)

## Masjid al-Ghamama

The Prophet of Islam performed Eid prayers in this mosque located 500 meters southwest of Masjid al-Nabawi, not in the Prophet’s Mosque itself.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=727)

[![Image 11: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina hz ali mescidi](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=732)

## Masjid Ali ibn Abi Talib

In 1662, Abu Salim al-Ayyashi, who visited Medina, records that the Prophet Muhammad (SAW) performed Eid prayers in various places, three of which are famous.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=732)

[![Image 12: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina uhud 768](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=736)

## Mount Uhud

Mount Uhud surrounds the plain upon which Medina was founded, from the north. It is 8 kilometers long and 110 meters high. Its distance from Masjid al-Nabawi is 5 kilometers.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=736)

[![Image 13: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina kuba mescidi](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=752)

## Masjid al-Quba

Situated on a fertile oasis known for its wells and date gardens, Quba takes its name from a well located there. Quba was a village located on the road to Mecca.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=752)

[![Image 14: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Medina zulhuleyfe mescidi](blob:http://localhost/84402906ab26ae6906447c56cfa0a7ba)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=742)

## Masjid al-Zulhulaifah (Miqat Mosque)

Zulhulaifah is designated by the Prophet (SAW) as the miqat (ritual boundary) for those going from Medina to Mecca. Today, it is referred to as “Abar-i Ali” or “Ebyar-i Ali,” named after Hazrat Ali.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=742)

# Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah

![Image 4: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah hac 2](blob:http://localhost/353ad08187169bdf2b11ae2019ee8822)

PLACES OF VISIT AND SACRED SITES IN MAKKAH

[![Image 5: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah dogdugu ev](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=428)

## The House Where Our Prophet (saw) Was Born

The beloved Prophet, who was sent as a mercy to all worlds, was born on the 12th of Rabi’ al-Awwal, which coincided with the 20th of April in the year 571 AD. This blessed event occurred in the early hours of Monday, as dawn was breaking, in Makkah. The place where he was born is now a library.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=428)

[![Image 6: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah cennetul mualla](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=481)

## Jannat al-Mu'alla

Cemetery in Makkah, has existed since the pre-Islamic era and continues to the present day. Located approximately 2 kilometers north of the Haram al-Sharif, it serves as the burial ground for Makkah. This area, situated near Masjid al-Jinn, holds historical and religious significance both before and during the early years of Islam.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=481)

[![Image 7: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah mescid i secere](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=493)

## Masjid al-Shajarah

Masjid al-Shajarah is a mosque located in line with the Masjid of the Jinn . It is said that Prophet Muhammad (SAW) had an encounter with a group of jinn at the location of the Masjid of the Jinn. He also conveyed revelations to the jinn at different times and places for the spread of Islam.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=493)

[![Image 8: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah mescidi nemire](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=502)

## Masjid al-Namirah

Masjid al-Namirah is the large mosque where our Prophet led the combined Dhuhr and Asr prayers in Arafat. During the Farewell Pilgrimage, on a small hill west of Arafat known as Nemire,

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=502)

![Image 9: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah 1](blob:http://localhost/5798896d311b3410bc9cb88a5837442b)

## ARAFAT

Arafat is our mountain. There, our prayers are accepted (Yunus Emre). Arafat, a flat area located 25 km southeast of the sacred city of Mecca, on the road to Taif, is the most crucial pillar of the Hajj pilgrimage.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=345)

[![Image 10: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah mina cadirlari](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=530)

## mına

Mina: It signifies both ‘counting’ and ‘beneficence’ in meaning, and at the same time, in Arabic, the term ‘mina’ is used to refer to the place where people gather or where blood is shed. Mina, located between the Sacred Mosque (Masjid al-Haram) in Mecca and Muzdalifah, is the location where the symbolic ritual of stoning during Hajj pilgrimage takes place.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=530)

[![Image 11: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah cemerat](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=554)

## Jamarat

During the days of Eid al-Adha, the small stones that pilgrims throw in Mina are called ‘cemre’ (plural: ‘cemerât’). These stones are thrown at three separate designated spots. Starting from Mina, the sequence is as follows: The First Jamarat…

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=554)

[![Image 12: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah daral erkam](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=566)

## Dar al-Arqam

It is the house of Ibn Harkam (RA), one of the honorable companions. The Prophet (SAW) stayed there until the number of Muslims reached 40, that is, until the conversion of Umar ibn Khattab (RA).

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=566)

[![Image 13: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah cirane mescidi](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=576)

## Masjid al- Ji'rranah

This Noble Mosque is located between Mecca and Taif. The Prophet (SAW) returned from the conquest of Taif during the eighth year of Hijrah, and on the twelfth Wednesday of the month of Zul-Qadah, he

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=576)

[![Image 14: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah ebukubeys](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=447)

## Jabal al-Abu Qubays

A noble mountain located approximately 100 meters to the east of the Kaaba, and it stands at an elevation of 420 meters on top of the Safa hill. Today, it is the site of a hotel. The mountain of Abu Qubays was considered a sacred place even before the advent of Islam. In Makkah, it holds significant historical and spiritual significance.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=447)

[![Image 15: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah mescid i cin](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=510)

## MASJID JINN

The Sacred Mosque (Masjid al-Haram) in Makkah is located on a hill overlooking the city, near Cennet al-Mu’alla Cemetery and approximately 2 kilometers north of the Haram al-Sharif. This revered mosque has a history dating back to early times and holds great significance for Muslims.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=510)

[![Image 16: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah sevr dagi](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=515)

## Mount Thawr and Cave

In the southern facade of the Masjid al-Haram, approximately 4 km away, on the road to Arafat, is located. The foothill to the summit of the mountain is 458 meters, a distance that can be covered on foot in about 1.5 hours. Our Prophet (SAW) and Hazrat Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA)

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=515)

[![Image 17: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah muzdelife](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=520)

## Muzdalifah

Muzdalifah: It is the sacred place located between Arafat and Mina within the boundaries of the Haram, where the second major ritual is performed after the Arafat sermon. Covering a total area of 963 hectares, it is marked by specific boundaries in present times.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=520)

[![Image 18: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah cebel i rahme](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=525)

## JABAL AL-RAHMAH AND MASJID AL-SAKHRAH

Jabal al-Rahmah: Located on the northern side of the Arafat Plain, commonly known as the ‘Mountain of Arafah,’ this hill is composed of granite stones. It is believed to be the place where Prophet Adam (AS) and Hawwa descended to Earth.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=525)

[![Image 19: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah hayf mescidi](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=535)

## Masjid al-Khayf

Masjid al-Khayf, located to the south of Mount Arafat, near the first Jamarat site, is where the Prophet Muhammad (SAW) set up his tent and performed congregational prayers during his Farewell Pilgrimage.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=535)

[![Image 20: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah cebel i nur](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=598)

## Jabal al-Nour and Cave Hira

Jabal al-Nour: Located approximately 5 km northeast of the Sacred Mosque (Masjid al-Haram) in Mecca, it is the mountain that includes the cave where the Prophet received his first revelation. Jabal al-Nur (Mountain of Light).

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=598)

[![Image 21: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah hz aise mescidi](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=571)

## Masjid al-Aisha

It is located 6 km from the Noble Sanctuary, within the boundaries of the sanctuary from the side of Medina, in a place called Tan’im. Hz. Aisha performed Hajj together with the Prophet during the Farewell Pilgrimage. Due to her excuse, she had not been able to perform Umrah.

[READ MORE](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=571)

[![Image 22: Places of Visit and Sacred Sites in Makkah hudeybiye](blob:http://localhost/924c2a85de7681caacb0fab7f1a80b29)](https://hisartravel.sg/?page_id=582)

## How to search Madain Project database?

 The Search is very dynamic, it starts looking in to its database as soon as you've entered a single letter, and will start to narrow down the results with every next letter entered. Simply click on the result you were looking for and search will give you a preview snippet with article title, overview and related topics.

Help: [How to search database](javascript:;) | [Video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QnFTijYu4wE)

*   **Tip 1: Searching the Madain Project**  
 You do not have to type the entire keyword, as soon as you start typing the dynamic search starts looking in to its database and keeps narrowing down with each letter typed. Do not hit enter, simply click on the result from the list and search will give you a preview snippet with article title, overview and related topics. 
*   **Tip 2: Using Breadcrumbs**  
 Each article has breadcrumb trail that helps you determine your location for any given webpage. In most cases, on the Madain Project website, these are located right below the 'contents menu'. These breadcrumbs are preceded by button called 'Location', when you click on this button, it will show you the 'Subject' of the page you're on. 
*   **Tip 3: History of an Article**  
 The articles on the Madain Project keep on evolving with depth of content, visual aids such as photgraphs and videos. All the content related changes are archived on the Archive.org, in order to maintain transparency and track the changes made by the editors. You can click on the clock icon  in the tools section on any page to see the history of the article. 
*   **Tip 4: Citing an Article**  
 The icon  in the tools section on any page shows the available formats (APA, MLA & Chicago) for the citing the article. This tool provides the ability to copy the citations by clicking them. The citations snippet provides inline and detailed citations as well.

Theban Mapping Project

# Egyptian Timeline

There is evidence of human activity in northeastern Africa since the Middle Pleistocene Period. By the Middle and Upper Paleolithic, between 90,000 to 10,000 years ago, there was a gradual movement of hunter-gatherer populations into the prehistoric Nile Valley and the drying lake and savannah regions of the Eastern Sahara precipitated by climatic changes. Traces of these early peoples survive in the forms of stone tools and rock carvings on the higher terraces along the Nile (including the western Theban plateau) and in the oases. As the nomadic hunter-gatherers came to settle along the edges of the Nile Valley, a transition to a settled lifestyle dependent on agriculture took place.

# Featured Readings

[![Image 4: Ara Pacis Augustae](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ara_pacis_augustae_117291.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/altar_of_augustan_peace "Altar of Augustan Peace (Ara Pacis)")
### Ara Pacis Augustae

Altar of the Augustan Peace, an iconic ancient Roman monument, stands as a testament to Augustus' vision of peace and prosperity for the Roman Empire, showcasing intricate reliefs and symbolizing an era of cultural and political transformation. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/altar_of_augustan_peace "Altar of Augustan Peace (Ara Pacis)")

[![Image 5: Hattusa](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/sphinx_gate_hattusa_28378.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/hattusa "Hattusa")
### Hattusa

The archaeological site of Hattusa, Anatolia's most significant archaeological sites, in Turkey unveils the captivating remnants of an ancient Hittite capital, offering a window into the sophisticated civilization that thrived in Anatolia over three millennia ago. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/hattusa "Hattusa")

[![Image 6](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/buhen_fortress_348599.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/buhen_fortress "Buhen Fortress")
### Buhen Fortress

The Buhen Fortress, strategically positioned along the Nile River in ancient Nubia, served as a significant Egyptian military installation, safeguarding trade routes and asserting control over the southern territories during the era of the New Kingdom. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/buhen_fortress "Buhen Fortress")

[![Image 7](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ur_ziggurat_117289.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/great_ziggurat_(ur) "Great Ziggurat of Ur")
### Great Ziggurat of Ur

The Ziggurat of Ur, originally built during the Early Bronze Age, is a Neo-Sumerian ziggurat in what was the city of Ur near Nasiriyah, in present-day Dhi Qar Province, Iraq. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/great_ziggurat_(ur) "Great Ziggurat of Ur")

[![Image 8](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/tomb_bh3_83747.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/procession_of_the_aamu "The Procession of the Aamu")
### Procession of the Āāmu

The well known scene of the Asiatic nomadic traders who are sometimes considered Hyksos or at least their forerunners; from an ancient Egyptian Tomb. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/procession_of_the_aamu "The Procession of the Aamu")

[![Image 9](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/pantheon_14928.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/pantheon_(rome) "Pantheon (Rome)")
### Pantheon (Rome)

The Pantheon of Rome is one of the best-preserved of all Ancient Roman buildings, in large part because it has been in continuous use throughout its history. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/pantheon_(rome) "Pantheon (Rome)")

[![Image 10](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/parthenon_7753621.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/parthenon "Parthenon")
### Parthenon

Parthenon, temple that dominates the hill of the Acropolis at Athens. It was built in the mid-5th century BCE and dedicated to the Greek goddess Athena Parthenos. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/parthenon "Parthenon")

[![Image 11](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qasr_alfarid_481.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/madain_saleh "Madain Saleh")
### Madain Saleh (Hegra)

Dating from the Nabataean Kingdom, first century CE, the site constitutes the Nabataean kingdom's southernmost and second largest city after Petra. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/madain_saleh "Madain Saleh")

[![Image 12](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/qarawiyyin_mosque_247189.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/mosque_university_of_al_qarawiyyin "Mosque-University of al-Qarawiyyin")
### al-Qarawiyyin University

Originally founded as a mosque by _Fatima al-Fihri_ in 857–859 CE it subsequently became one of the leading spiritual and educational centers of the Islamic Golden Age. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/mosque_university_of_al_qarawiyyin "Mosque-University of al-Qarawiyyin")

[![Image 13](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/pergamum_altar_22778.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/pergamon_altar "Pergamon Altar")
### Pergamon Altar of Zeus

Once a thriving and sophisticated Roman city, Pompeii was buried under meters of ash and pumice after the catastrophic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/pergamon_altar "Pergamon Altar")

[![Image 14](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ishtar_gate_5812769.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/ishtar_gate "Ishtar Gate")
### Ishtar Gate

Built in 224 CE by King Ardashir I in the ancient city "_Peroz_" (lit. victorious) when he established the Sassanian Empire by overthrowing Ardavan. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/ishtar_gate "Ishtar Gate")

[![Image 15](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/jericho_tower_77314.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/tower_of_jericho "Tower of Jericho")
### Neolithic Tower of Jericho

The round stone tower of Pre-pottery Neolithic A era Jericho was probably the world’s first stone building, its first public building, and its first work of monumental architecture. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/tower_of_jericho "Tower of Jericho")

[![Image 16](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/faun_house_11378.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/pompeii "Pompeii")
### Archaeological Site of Pompeii

Once a thriving and sophisticated Roman city, Pompeii was buried under meters of ash and pumice after the catastrophic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/pompeii "Pompeii")

[![Image 17](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ardashir_palace_00972.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/palace_of_ardashir "Palace of Ardashir Papakan")
### Palace of Ardashir I

Built in 224 CE by King Ardashir I in the ancient city "_Peroz_" (lit. victorious) when he established the Sassanian Empire by overthrowing Ardavan. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/palace_of_ardashir "Palace of Ardashir Papakan")

[![Image 18](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/khazneh_82615.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/al_khazneh "al-Khazneh")
### al-Khazneh

Believed to have been the mausoleum of the Nabatean King Aretas IV, it is one of the most elaborate temples in Petra, city of the Nabatean Kingdom. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/al_khazneh "al-Khazneh")

[![Image 19](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/giza_sphinx_459202.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/great_sphinx_of_giza "Great Sphinx of Giza")
### Great Sphinx of Giza

Facing directly from west to east the Great Sphinx of Giza, a limestone statue of a reclining sphinx, a mythical creature, stands on the Giza Plateau in Egypt. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/great_sphinx_of_giza "Great Sphinx of Giza")

[![Image 20](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/beersheba_2392899.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/tel_beersheva "Beersheba")
### Tel es-Seba

Mentioned 33 times in the Hebrew Bible, the ancient Beersheva is a significant center in the patriarchal narratives of the three major Abrahamic Faiths. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/tel_beersheva "Beersheba")

[![Image 21](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/tower_of_babel_012.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/tower_of_babel_stele "Tower of Babel Stele")
### Tower of Babel Stele

The Tower of Babel Stele, of which two of the original three parts are preserved, presents an image of the Etemenaki ziggurat contemporary with Nebachadnezzar. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/tower_of_babel_stele "Tower of Babel Stele")

[![Image 22](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ubar_828281.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/ubar "Ubar")
### Ubar: Atlantis of Sands

Archaeological site of Ubar, identified with the "_Iram_" an ancient city mentioned in the Quran, the city of the people of _Ad_ to whom the prophet _Hud_ was sent. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/ubar "Ubar")

[![Image 23](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/ur_ekhursag_118.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/temenos_of_ur "Temenos of Ur")
### Temenos of Ur

To the north-west of the city center, the Temenos of Ur (_E-gish-shir-gal_), was an enclosed area which consisted of the religious and royal building structures. [Read more](https://madainproject.com/temenos_of_ur "Temenos of Ur")

[![Image 24](https://madainproject.com/content/media/collect/kv01_47387.jpg)](https://madainproject.com/tombs_in_valley_of_the_kings "Tombs in the valley of the Kings")
### Tombs in Valley of the Kings

The valley contains at least 63 tombs, beginning with Thutmose I (or earlier, during the reign of Amenhotep I circa 1539 BCE) and ending with Ramesses X or XI (1075 BCE). [Read more](https://madainproject.com/tombs_in_valley_of_the_kings "Tombs in the valley of the Kings")

The Madain Project is an online archive of Abrahamic History and Archaeology.

Abrahamic History & Archaeology is the study of history and archaeology with respect to the three Abrahamic Faiths without considering the religious and theological aspects. The goal of Abrahamic History is to understand how and why the religious doctrines and behaviours have evolved and changed over time. Searching for patterns in the evolution of significant cultural events such as the development of farming, the emergence of cities, or the collapse of major civilizations for clues of why and how these have influenced the three major Abrahamic religions.

**Mosque of Al-Ghamamah** (Arabic: مسجد الغمامة‎) is one of the oldest mosques in Medina, Saudi Arabia, located in the place believed to be where the Islamic prophet Muhammad performed an Eid prayer in the year 631. It is also narrated that Prophet Muhammad offered Salat ul-Istasqa when the city of Madina faced a shortage of rain. For a while, this mosque was closed for daily prayers because of its proximity to the Al-Masjid an-Nabawi. However quite recently it has been reopened for the worshipers for praying. Five times prayers are held in this mosque now with an internal sound system to avoid the clash of sounds from the Prophet's Mosque. The mosque is one of the historical relics of Medina.

...

###### See also

*   [Al-Masjid al-Nabawi](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Al-Masjid-al-Nabawi-1985)

*   [Anbariya Mosque](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Anbariya-Mosque-29302)
*   [Hejaz Railway Museum](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Hejaz-Railway-Museum-29319)

## Location

It is located at 500 meters west of As-Salam door of Al-Masjid an-Nabawi.

[![Image 9: Mosque of Abu Bakr, Madinah, Saudi Arabia, renovated 1789 by the Ottomans (5)](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2263278)

[Mosque of Abu Bakr, Madinah, Saudi Arabia, renovated 1789 by the Ottomans (1) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/43714545@N06/)

## Etymology

"Ghamamah" means cloud, and it is named as such as it is narrated that rain clouds covered the city when Muhammad had performed Salat ul-Istasqa here.

[![Image 10: Mosque of Abu Bakr, Madinah, Saudi Arabia, renovated 1789 by the Ottomans (5)](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2263279)

[Mosque of Abu Bakr, Madinah, Saudi Arabia, renovated 1789 by the Ottomans (2) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/43714545@N06/)

## History

The mosque was built during the reign of the Caliph Umar bin Abdul Aziz between the hijri calendar of 86 to 93, and renovated by the Sultan Hasan bin Muhammad bin Qalawan Ash-Shalihi in 1340 during the Sharifate of Mecca era. It was renovated again by the Sharif Saifuddin Inal Al-Ala'i in 1622, and the time of the Sultan Abd-ul-Mejid I in 1859 during the Ottoman era, using new tools and the look resembled more or less the shape of today. After that it was renovated again during the time of the Sultan Sultan Abdul Hamid II and by the Saudi government.

## Description

The mosque is rectangular shaped, and made of two parts, which are entrance door and prayer room. The entrance door is also rectangular shaped and has a length of 26 meters and width of 4 meters, and has five dome-shaped circles drawn on facade. Prayer room has a length of 30 meters and width of 15 meters, and has six domes in the shape of a circle. The largest dome is at the top of the mihrab.
