# King Khalid Grand Mosque Riyadh: Transit Prayer Tips

# King Khalid Grand Mosque Riyadh: Transit Prayer Tips

Planning a Singapore to Saudi journey with a layover in Riyadh? The **King Khalid Grand Mosque Riyadh** is a convenient, serene place to pause for Salah near the Diplomatic Quarter. This Singapore-focused guide covers how to reach the mosque from King Khalid International Airport (RUH), prayer timings, wudhu facilities, family and women’s areas, etiquette, and practical transit tips—so you can pray comfortably and continue your trip with confidence.

## Why Pray Here During a Riyadh Transit

The King Khalid Grand Mosque is one of Riyadh’s most prominent modern mosques, situated near the Diplomatic Quarter (DQ). For Singapore travellers in transit, it offers:

*   Reliable access to congregational prayers in a peaceful setting
*   Clean wudhu facilities and dedicated women’s halls
*   Accessible location by airport taxi or ride-hailing (Uber/Careem)
*   Room for families and travellers with carry-on bags

Category note: This article sits under Ziyarah & sacred sites. While the mosque itself is not a historical ziyarah site like Makkah or Madinah, it is a significant contemporary masjid that supports your spiritual journey en route to Umrah.

## King Khalid Grand Mosque Riyadh: Quick Facts For Transit

*   **Location:** Near the Diplomatic Quarter (DQ), Riyadh. Search _“King Khalid Grand Mosque Riyadh”_ on Google Maps or use [this map query](https://maps.google.com/?q=King+Khalid+Grand+Mosque+Riyadh).
*   **Distance from RUH:** Approximately 40 km by road; 30–50 minutes by car depending on traffic.
*   **Access:** Airport taxis or ride-hailing (Uber/Careem). Public transport options are limited for short layovers.
*   **Prayer times:** Check a reliable app (e.g., Muslim Pro, Athan) for _prayer timings in Riyadh_. Jumu’ah is busiest; arrive early.
*   **Facilities:** Separate men’s and women’s prayer halls, wudhu/ablution areas, shoe racks, and basic washrooms.
*   **Language:** Arabic signage is common; some bilingual signs. Staff and worshippers are often helpful to travellers.

## Location, Access, And Timings

### Getting From RUH To The Mosque

From King Khalid International Airport (RUH), the simplest option is a taxi or ride-hailing service:

*   **Ride-hailing:** Uber/Careem are widely used. Connect to airport Wi‑Fi, set your destination to _King Khalid Grand Mosque_, and confirm the pickup terminal.
*   **Airport taxi:** Official taxis queue outside arrivals. Agree to a metered ride or a quoted fare before boarding.
*   **Travel time:** Off‑peak 30–35 minutes; peak 45–60 minutes, especially around office hours and Friday midday.
*   **Estimated cost:** Typically SAR 100–160 one way (about SGD 36–58), depending on traffic and surge pricing.

Tip for Singapore travellers: Save the Arabic name of the mosque and your return terminal in your notes app. Show these to the driver if language becomes a barrier.

### Parking Near Mosque

If you are on a longer stopover with a rental car, you’ll find surface parking near the mosque and along adjacent streets. Arrive earlier for Jumu’ah and Maghrib/Isha when demand is highest.

### Prayer Timings And Best Windows

*   Use a reputable app set to **Riyadh** for accurate daily Salah times.
*   **Best transit windows:** Dhuhr/Asr for daytime layovers; Maghrib/Isha for evening connections.
*   **Jumu’ah (Friday):** Expect heavy attendance. Plan to arrive 30–45 minutes early to find parking and a place inside.
*   **Ramadan:** Taraweeh draws large crowds; allocate extra time if transiting in the evening.

## Facilities: Wudhu, Women’s Prayer Hall, And Family Areas

The mosque’s facilities are traveller‑friendly and generally well maintained:

*   **Wudhu facilities in Riyadh:** Dedicated ablution areas for men and women. Floors may be wet—wear slip‑resistant footwear and bring a small towel.
*   **Women’s prayer hall:** Separate entrance and prayer area; look for signs reading _“Women”_ or ask a volunteer/guard.
*   **Family areas:** Families with young children are common outside peak khutbah times. Keep children nearby and quiet to maintain the sanctuary.
*   **Accessibility:** Main entrances usually have ramps; if you need assistance, request it from staff or fellow worshippers.

Ablution area map: On site, follow signage or ask the security/volunteer team for directions to the nearest wudhu area and washrooms.

## Etiquette And Dress Code For Saudi Mosques

*   **Dress code:** Men should wear long trousers and covered shoulders. Women should wear an abaya and a headscarf. Singapore travellers may pack a lightweight abaya in carry‑on for quick access.
*   **Conduct:** Silence mobile phones, keep voices low, and avoid filming worshippers.
*   **Shoe storage:** Use the racks. Consider a shoe bag to keep your pair together during busy times.
*   **Modesty items:** Bring a spare hijab cap, socks, and a compact prayer mat if you prefer your own.

## Step-By-Step Transit Prayer Plan From Singapore Flights

*   **Before You Fly:** Download a prayer time app for Riyadh; save the mosque’s map link; prepare a small wudhu kit (travel towel, slippers, plastic bag).
*   **Upon Landing:** Clear immigration (transit/stopover visa may be required), collect any checked luggage if applicable, and connect to Wi‑Fi.
*   **Book Transport:** Order an Uber/Careem or take an official taxi to _King Khalid Grand Mosque Riyadh_.
*   **At The Mosque:** Store shoes, refresh wudhu, and join the congregational prayer or pray individually if between jama’ah times.
*   **Return Buffer:** Plan to leave 2–2.5 hours before your next international departure to clear security and reach your gate comfortably.

Connections caution: Saudi entry rules, processing times, and traffic can change. Always keep generous buffers. Confirm visa/stopover eligibility with your airline and official Saudi sources before travel.

## Ziyarah && Sacred Sites Context In Riyadh

While most ziyarah itineraries focus on the Holy Cities of Makkah and Madinah, Riyadh’s King Khalid Grand Mosque is a meaningful stop to maintain your daily prayers during travel. Nearby, the Diplomatic Quarter features landscaped walking paths and contemporary architecture that reflect the city’s cultural life. For Singapore pilgrims heading to Umrah, this mosque serves as a spiritual waypoint—recenter your intention, recite Qur’an briefly, then continue your journey refreshed.

## Time And Budget Planning For a Singapore To Riyadh Layover

*   **Minimum time needed:** For a smooth round trip (airport ⇄ mosque ⇄ airport) with one prayer, allow 4–5 hours including buffers.
*   **Transport budget:** Return ride typically SAR 200–320 total (about SGD 72–116), varying by time of day and surge.
*   **Connectivity:** Pre‑purchase a travel eSIM for Saudi Arabia or use airport Wi‑Fi to manage rides and maps.
*   **Payments:** Cards are widely accepted in Riyadh. Keep small cash for tips and incidentals.

## Practical Pointers For a Stress-Free Visit

*   **Google Maps pin:** Save the listing in advance and download the area offline in case mobile data is patchy.
*   **Language:** Simple English is widely understood in service settings. Learn a few Arabic phrases: _As‑salaamu ‘alaykum_ (greeting), _Shukran_ (thank you).
*   **Luggage:** No public lockers on site. Keep carry‑ons with you and avoid blocking walkways.
*   **Security checkpoints:** Approaches to the Diplomatic Quarter may include routine checks; carry your passport and visa/entry proof.
*   **Heat management:** Riyadh is dry and hot most months. Hydrate before you arrive and avoid lingering outdoors around midday.
*   **Family considerations:** For toddlers, bring quiet activities and snacks; dispose of rubbish responsibly.

## Sample Itineraries Based On Prayer Windows

### Daytime Layover (6–8 Hours)

*   Land before late morning → clear formalities → ride to mosque.
*   Perform wudhu → pray Dhuhr → short Qur’an recitation.
*   Rest 15–20 minutes → pray Asr (if time allows).
*   Return to RUH with a 2+ hour buffer pre‑departure.

### Evening Layover (4–6 Hours)

*   Arrive late afternoon → ride to mosque before sunset.
*   Pray Maghrib → short break → pray Isha if schedule permits.
*   Head back to RUH promptly after Isha to avoid queues.

## What Makes This Mosque a Good Transit Choice

*   **Proximity to DQ:** Safe, organised precinct with clear roads, making airport transfers straightforward.
*   **Spacious prayer halls:** Comfortable even during busy times outside Jumu’ah.
*   **Traveller‑friendly amenities:** Clean ablution areas and clear signage.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Can non-Arabic speaking Singapore travellers navigate the mosque easily?

Yes. While most signage is in Arabic, the mosque layout is straightforward. Save the Arabic name in your phone, and don’t hesitate to ask guards or worshippers—many are happy to assist.

How much time should I budget from RUH for one prayer at the mosque?

A comfortable plan is 4–5 hours door‑to‑door: 30–60 minutes each way for transport, 30–60 minutes for entry/security/wudhu, and a 2‑hour pre‑flight buffer back at RUH. Add more time on Fridays or during Ramadan evenings.

Is there a women’s prayer hall and are abayas available on site?

There is a dedicated women’s prayer hall. Abayas are not typically provided, so bring your own lightweight abaya and headscarf in your carry‑on.

Do I need a Saudi stopover or transit visa to leave the airport?

Visa requirements depend on your passport and ticket. Saudi Arabia offers a stopover visa for eligible itineraries. Always verify with your airline and official Saudi sources before travel; Hisar Travel can advise on current practices for Umrah-bound passengers.

# About Medina al-Munawwarah

## About Medina al-Munawwarah

Medina al-Munawwarah, located in the northwest of Arabia, 130 km away from the Red Sea, stands at an elevation of 619 meters above sea level. Today, transportation between Medina and Mecca is facilitated by a 418 km-long highway known as the Hijra Road. The city is surrounded by Uhud Mountain to the north, Ayr Mountain to the south, and volcanic lava fields known as Vebere on the east (Waqim) and west sides. Its current population is approximately 900,000. (November 2006) Formerly known as Yathrib, this city is referred to as Dār al-Hijra, Madīnat al-Nabī, and Medina al-Munawwarah due to the enlightenment brought to the city by the Prophet Muhammad.

**MEDINA AL-MUNAWWARAH**

Medina al-Munawwarah is the sanctuary of the Prophet’s migration.  
It is the city that extends its helping hand while others withdraw theirs.  
It is the first capital of the Islamic state.  
It is the city from which messengers were sent to foreign lands to convey the pure faith of Islam.  
It is the most blessed city after Mecca al-Mukarramah.  
It is the place where over half of the Qur’an was revealed.

**That luminous city where:**

The Seal of Prophets resides, with no distance between him and those who approach him.  
The Companions, companions of both this world and the Hereafter, two martyrs, Abu Bakr and Umar, reside there.  
The window to the Hereafter, the garden of paradise (Raudah al-Mutahhara), is there. (Besides Raudah al-Mutahhara, there is no other place on earth declared to be as if it were a part of paradise.)  
Jannat al-Baqi where 10,000 Companions, including foremost among them Hz. Uthman (RA), are buried, is there.  
The Uhud Mountain, blessed by the presence of 70 martyrs, including Hz. Hamza, whose sight would illuminate eyes, is there.  
Masjid al-Qiblatayn, where the qibla direction changed, is there.  
Masjid al-Quba and the “Seven Mosques” are there.

How can one refrain from shedding tears and being heedless in this place? There is a consensus that Mecca al-Mukarramah and Medina al-Munawwarah surpass all other cities.

The Prophet(SAW) said:

“Medina is the dome of Islam, the abode of faith, the land of migration, and the place where what is permissible and forbidden is explained.” (Targhib, 2/228)

“Whoever is able to die in Medina should die there. Certainly, I will intercede for those who die there.” (Targhib, 2/223)

Respect and reverence are required for Medina al-Munawwarah. The acts of worship performed here hold superiority and abundance in both virtues and rewards, both in blessings and in outcomes. For those who cannot adhere to the rights and etiquettes of Mecca al-Mukarramah and Medina al-Munawwarah, it is reprehensible to reside there. (Lubab Sharh, p. 351)

When Imam Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, entered Medina al-Munawwarah and a donkey was brought for him to ride, he refused to ride it due to a valid excuse, saying, “It is not appropriate for me to step on the ground that the blessed feet of the Prophet have touched with the hooves of a donkey.”

The poet Nabi, upon accompanying a delegation for pilgrimage, noticed a pasha in the group who stretched out his legs and reclined as they approached Medina al-Munawwarah. He recited the following verse aloud:

Beware! Leaving etiquette aside, this is the beloved of God.  
This is the holy place of God, the station of the Chosen One.  
The gathering place of the Exalted Prophet’s greatness,  
It transcends even the Throne of the Majestic Lord in virtue.  
Enter this sanctuary with respect and observance of etiquette, O Nabi,  
It is the sacred threshold of the Prophets, the sanctuary of the chosen ones.

**Meaning**:

When morning comes, the minarets’ muezzins recite these verses. They ask, “Where did you learn these verses?” They reply, “Last night, the Prophet himself taught us these verses and ordered us to recite them from the minarets.”

Our ancestors showed immense respect for this blessed city. Abdul Hamid II, may Allah have mercy on him, gave this order during the construction of the Hejaz Railway to the team building the railway: “When you approach Medina al-Munawwarah, cover the possible equipment with felt so that there is not much noise. Let the souls of the Prophet, Ahl al-Bayt, and the residents here not be disturbed.”

O morning breeze, if you reach the direction of the Two Holy Mosques,  
Present my respect, O breeze, to the chosen one among men.

The **Mosque of the Prophet** (or **Prophet's Mosque**) ( Arabic: [Шаблон:Unicode](javascript:; "Шаблон:Unicode (страница не существует)") ) [IPA /mæsʤıd ænːæbæwiː], in [Medina](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Medina), is the second holiest mosque in [Islam](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Islam) and the second largest mosque in the world after the [Masjid al-Haram](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Masjid+al-Haram) in [Mecca](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Mecca). It is the final resting place of Prophet [Muhammad](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Muhammad). Masjid al-Haram in Mecca is the holiest and the largest mosque and the [Al-Aqsa Mosque](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Al-Aqsa+Mosque) in [Jerusalem](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Jerusalem) is the third holiest in Islam.

# KAFD Grand Mosque Riyadh: Transit Prayer and Tips Guide

# KAFD Grand Mosque Riyadh: Transit Prayer and Tips Guide

If you have a short stop in Riyadh, the KAFD Grand Mosque Riyadh in the King Abdullah Financial District is a serene, modern space to perform Salah during a layover. This Singapore-focused guide explains how to plan a smooth Riyadh transit prayer, reach the mosque from the airport, and make the most of a brief ziyarah while staying on schedule.

## Why Visit KAFD Grand Mosque Riyadh During Transit

For travellers from Singapore, Riyadh often appears as a convenient hub when routing to Europe, North Africa, or other parts of the Middle East. The KAFD Grand Mosque offers a peaceful environment, excellent facilities, and quick access from major roads—ideal when your time is limited. As part of your ziyarah to sacred sites, even a short visit to a mosque can recalibrate your journey with intention and remembrance.

*   Modern, well-maintained prayer halls for men and women
*   Efficient wudu facilities and clear signage
*   Located within the prestigious King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD)
*   Good road access from King Khalid International Airport (RUH)
*   Safe, business-district environment with security presence

Note: This guide focuses on practical, on-the-ground details for a short spiritual stop—perfect for the Ziyarah & sacred sites theme—without replacing official travel or visa information.

## Where Is KAFD Grand Mosque Riyadh And How To Reach It

The mosque sits within the **King Abdullah Financial District**, a landmark business precinct in northern Riyadh known for its striking architecture and pedestrian skywalks. It’s near major arteries such as King Fahd Road and the Northern Ring Road.

### Distance And Travel Time From The Airport

From _King Khalid International Airport (RUH)_ to KAFD is roughly 30–35 km. Off-peak, the drive can take 25–35 minutes; during peak office hours, budget 40–60 minutes. Always allow extra time for airport security and traffic variability.

*   Ride-hailing/taxi: Approx. SAR 80–120 (about S$30–S$45), depending on time and demand
*   Self-drive: Use well-marked expressways; set your navigation to “KAFD Grand Mosque”
*   Return buffer: Add 15–20 minutes beyond the map estimate when heading back to RUH

Tip: Keep an eye on live traffic via your preferred maps app. In Riyadh, traffic can change quickly, especially around office-hour peaks.

### Parking And Access Inside KAFD

**Mosque parking (KAFD)** is typically available in designated visitor areas and underground car parks, with signage and security staff to assist. During Friday prayer and peak timings, arrive early to avoid circling.

*   Use visitor parking where signposted; follow security instructions
*   Keep your passport/ID with you when moving between parking and the mosque
*   Allow time to walk across pedestrian-friendly plazas to the mosque entrance

### Riyadh Metro Access

The **Riyadh Metro** is being introduced in phases. KAFD has a high-profile station on Line 1 (Blue) and a local monorail interface within the district. For the most current public operating status and timings, check the official metro app or city announcements before you travel. For short layovers, ride-hailing remains the faster, more predictable option.

## Planning a Riyadh Transit Prayer: Time Windows

When planning an **airport layover Riyadh** stop for Salah, two variables matter most: total connection time and prayer times. As a rule of thumb for Singapore travellers, consider the following planning blocks.

*   **Arrival to curbside (RUH):** 30–60 minutes if arriving internationally and clearing immigration
*   **RUH to KAFD drive:** 25–60 minutes depending on traffic
*   **At the mosque:** 30–60 minutes (wudu + Salah + brief reflection)
*   **Return drive to RUH:** 25–60 minutes
*   **Security + boarding buffer:** 60–90 minutes for international departures

For a same-airline, single-ticket transit where you do not clear immigration, visiting the mosque may not be feasible unless you have a confirmed **Saudi stopover visa** and sufficient time. If you do plan to exit the airport, ensure your visa and time buffers are in order.

### Checking Prayer Times In Riyadh

Use reliable prayer-time apps and set location to **Riyadh**. Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha timings differ from Singapore; verify daily. If your flight spans Maghrib/Isha or Dhuhr/Asr, you may have more flexibility.

*   Confirm the day’s schedule before take-off from Singapore (SGT → AST time shift)
*   Re-check on landing; some apps refresh times once GPS locks
*   Coordinate transport arrival to align with a prayer window, not the tail end

Warning: Always prioritise flight timings. If delays occur, be prepared to pray at the airport prayer rooms instead of leaving for the city.

## Facilities At The KAFD Grand Mosque

KAFD’s mosque pairs contemporary design with practical amenities—ideal for a quick, purposeful ziyarah.

### Prayer Halls

Separate halls for men and women are standard in Riyadh’s mosques, and KAFD is no exception. Expect clear signage, carpeted floors, and orderly rows. Arrive a little early for Jumu’ah; space fills quickly.

### Wudu Facilities

Look for modern, well-maintained **wudu facilities** with adequate drainage and seating. Keep the area tidy, minimise water use, and follow the posted etiquette guidelines.

*   Bring a small towel to speed up your exit
*   Use slip-on footwear for quick ablution transitions
*   Keep belongings secure; use a slim daypack or waist pouch

### Accessibility And Family Considerations

Entrances and walkways around KAFD are designed with accessibility in mind. Lifts and ramps are common across the district. For families, consider having one adult complete wudu while the other waits with children, then swap to keep timings tight.

### Etiquette For Ziyarah In a Business District Mosque

*   Dress modestly; long sleeves and full-length trousers/skirts recommended
*   Lower your voice; be mindful of people praying or reciting
*   Avoid blocking entrances and prayer lines when taking brief photos
*   Refrain from extended phone calls inside the mosque

Tip: If your schedule becomes tight, RUH has prayer rooms in-terminal. Ask airport staff for the nearest musalla rather than rushing to exit.

## Sample Stopover Plans For Singapore Travellers

Below are sample outlines to help you judge feasibility. Conditions and traffic vary—treat these as planning references.

### 5–6 Hour Layover (Aggressive, Only If Everything Aligns)

*   0:00–0:45 Land + immigration (best case)
*   0:45–1:25 Ride to KAFD (off-peak traffic)
*   1:25–2:10 Wudu + Salah (Dhuhr/Asr or Maghrib/Isha)
*   2:10–2:50 Return ride to RUH
*   2:50–4:00 Security + boarding buffer

Only attempt with a _confirmed_ visa, off-peak traffic, and a prayer time that neatly fits your window.

### 8–12 Hour Daytime Stopover (Comfortable)

*   Land, clear immigration, freshen up
*   Head to KAFD; perform Salah and short reflection
*   Quick walk around KAFD’s pedestrian areas; stay close to the mosque
*   Plan lunch/coffee nearby; avoid heavy detours
*   Return to RUH 3 hours before departure to allow for traffic

### Overnight Stop (Most Flexible)

*   Check in to a nearby hotel in northern Riyadh
*   Visit KAFD Grand Mosque for Maghrib and/or Isha
*   Return at Fajr if your schedule permits
*   Head back to RUH well ahead of morning traffic

## Saudi Stopover Visa: Practical Notes

**Saudi stopover visa** options have made short visits more accessible in recent years. Typically linked to specific airlines and itineraries, these allow a limited stay (for example, up to 96 hours) so travellers can exit the airport and, where permitted, perform Umrah. Policies can change; always refer to official Ministry of Foreign Affairs (KSA) sources and your airline for current eligibility, fees, and inclusions.

*   Book your itinerary (often with participating carriers)
*   Apply for the stopover visa online via official channels
*   Receive confirmation before travel; carry copies (digital and printed)
*   Ensure travel insurance requirements are met as stipulated

Note: This is general guidance only and not legal advice. Requirements may change without notice. Verify details with official KSA sources and your airline.

## Safety, Timing, And Cost Pointers For Singaporeans

*   **Costs:** Budget SAR 80–120 each way for rides (about S$30–S$45). Food and coffee in KAFD are similar to Singapore CBD prices.
*   **Payments:** Cards are widely accepted; keep a small amount of SAR cash for tips or minor purchases.
*   **Connectivity:** Consider a roaming plan or local eSIM to manage ride-hailing and prayer-time apps reliably.
*   **Dress:** Pack a light, modest outfit in your carry-on; Riyadh can be hot but indoors are air-conditioned.

## Nearby Touchpoints For a Short, Mindful Ziyarah

Within KAFD, you’ll find landscaped plazas and striking architecture. For a transit-focused ziyarah, keep it simple: pray, spend a few minutes in quiet remembrance, then return calmly to the airport. Avoid venturing far beyond the mosque if your layover is tight.

Is The KAFD Grand Mosque Open For All Five Daily Prayers?

Daily prayers are standard in Riyadh mosques, though specific opening times may vary with local management and events. Arrive a little early, especially around Jumu’ah, and follow on-site guidance from mosque staff.

Are There Adequate Wudu Facilities For Transit Travellers?

Yes—KAFD’s wudu facilities are modern and efficient, with clear signage. To save time, carry a small towel and keep your items consolidated in a compact bag while performing ablution.

How Long Is The Drive From RUH To KAFD Grand Mosque Riyadh?

Plan for 25–35 minutes off-peak and up to 60 minutes during busy office hours. Always build a buffer for the return to the airport, especially before international departures.

Can I Visit During A Short Airport Layover Riyadh Without A Visa?

Exiting the airport typically requires an appropriate visa (such as a stopover visa). Policies change; check official KSA sources and your airline before planning to leave the terminal.

The **Masjid al-Qiblatayn** (Arabic: مسجد القبلتين‎, lit. 'Mosque of the Two Qiblas'), also spelt **Masjid al-Qiblatain**, is a mosque in Medina believed by Muslims to be the place where the final Islamic prophet, Muhammad, received the command to change the _Qibla_ (direction of prayer) from Jerusalem to Mecca. The mosque was built by Sawad ibn Ghanam ibn Ka'ab during the year 2 AH (623 CE) and is one of the few mosques in the world to have contained two _mihrabs_ (niches indicating the _qibla_) in different directions.

...

###### See also

*   [Hejaz Railway Museum](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Hejaz-Railway-Museum-29319)
*   [Anbariya Mosque](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Anbariya-Mosque-29302)
*   [Mosque of Al-Ghamama](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Mosque-of-Al-Ghamama-29304)
*   [Al-Masjid al-Nabawi](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Al-Masjid-al-Nabawi-1985)

In 1987, during the reign of King Fahd, the mosque was completely torn down and rebuilt. In the course of the reconstruction, the old prayer niche facing Jerusalem was removed, and the one facing Mecca was left. The Qiblatayn Mosque is among the earliest mosques that date to the time of Muhammad, along with the Quba'a Mosque and Masjid an-Nabawi, considering that the Great Mosques of Mecca and Jerusalem are associated with earlier Prophets in Islamic thought.

## History

See also::Muhammad in Medina

 The mosque is among the earliest mosques in Medina and was built by Sawad ibn Ghanam ibn Ka'ab al-Ansari in the Islamic year 2 AH, and the name of the mosque goes back to the lifetime of Muhammad, when his companions named it after an event that took place on the 15th of Sha'baan the same year, when Muhammad received revelation from Allah instructing him to take the Kaaba as the _qibla_ during the Dhuhr prayer, instead of the _qibla_ of the Jews, which was the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. He later announced this to his companions in his own mosque, after which the news began to spread. Many pilgrims who go to Mecca for Hajj often visit Medina, where some visit this mosque because of its historical significance. 
> Indeed, We see you ˺O Prophet˺ turning your face towards heaven. Now We will make you turn towards a ˺direction of prayer˺ that will please you. So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque ˺in Mecca˺—wherever you are, turn your faces towards it. Those who were given the Scripture certainly know this to be the truth from their Lord. And Allah is never unaware of what they do. – (translated by Mustafa Khattab)

 A hadith from Sahih Bukhari says: 
> Narrated Ibn Umar: While some people were offering Fajr prayer at Quba' (mosque), some-one came to them and said, "Tonight some Qur'anic Verses have been revealed to the Prophet and he has been ordered to face the Kaaba (during prayers), so you too should turn your faces towards it." At that time their faces were towards Shaam (Jerusalem) so they turned towards the Kaaba (at Mecca).

The main prayer hall adopts rigid orthogonal geometry and symmetry which is accentuated by the use of twin minarets and twin domes. Living accommodations for the Imam, the Muezzin and the caretaker are discretely grouped in one block to the west of the main structure. The difference in level at the southeast corner of the site has been exploited to incorporate a sub-basement level which serves as the ablutions area for worshippers. To the north, where the ground level is lower, the prayer hall is raised one-storey above ground level. Entry to the prayer hall is from the raised courtyard, also to the north, which can be reached by stairs and ramps from the main directions of approach. The prayer hall consists of a series of arches which support barrel-vaults running parallel to the qibla wall. These vaults are interrupted by two domes which establish an axis in the direction of Mecca.

[![Image 10: Site of the Battle of the Trench](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2301257)

[Qiblatayn Mosque Madinah, Saudi Arabia (9) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/43714545@N06/)

The main dome to the south is raised on a drum of clerestory windows which allow light to filter into the interior directly above the mihrab. The second, false dome is linked to the first by a small cross-vault to symbolise the transition from one qibla to another. Below it, a replica of the mihrab found in the lower chamber of the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem reminds onlookers of the oldest extant mihrab of Islam. Externally, the architectural vocabulary is inspired by traditional elements and motifs in a deliberate effort to offer an authentic image for the historic site. The mosque is located on the north-west of the city of Medina, on Khalid ibn al-Walid Road. The mosque was initially maintained by Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattāb. The last pre-modern renovation was by Suleiman the Magnificent who reconstructed the mosque.

# King Saud Mosque Jeddah: Architecture and Prayer Tips

# King Saud Mosque Jeddah: Architecture and Prayer Tips

Planning a meaningful ziyarah in Jeddah? King Saud Mosque Jeddah is a standout stop for Singapore pilgrims and families transiting for Umrah. This guide explains its acclaimed architecture, how to get there smoothly, what to expect for prayer, and practical tips around parking, Wudhu, dress code, and Friday Prayer.

## Why Visit King Saud Mosque Jeddah During Ziyarah

King Saud Mosque is one of Jeddah’s most recognisable mosques, designed by the renowned Egyptian architect **Abdel-Wahed El-Wakil**, a leading voice in contemporary Islamic architecture rooted in tradition. Beyond its striking geometry and serene courtyards, the mosque offers a calm, contemplative environment to perform Salah, recite Qur’an, and begin or conclude your Umrah journey with gratitude.

For Singapore travellers, it is an accessible ziyarah stop—close enough to the airport and to **Al-Balad** (Jeddah’s Historic District) to combine heritage exploration with prayer in a landmark mosque. Whether you have a short _umrah layover_ or a full day in the city, the mosque’s scale, acoustic warmth, and thoughtful climate-friendly design make it a memorable spiritual pause.

## Quick Facts And Orientation

### Location And Distance

The mosque is located in central Jeddah, a short drive east of Al-Balad. Typical travel times:

*   From King Abdulaziz International Airport (JED): about 20–35 km depending on terminal and route; roughly 30–45 minutes in normal traffic.
*   From Al-Balad (Historic Jeddah): approximately 10–15 minutes by car in off-peak hours.

### Architecture Highlights

El-Wakil’s approach emphasises traditional forms, passive cooling, and human-scale details. Expect geometric massing, a prominent minaret, shaded exterior walkways, and a tranquil interior that invites khushu’. The layout intuitively guides flow to the main prayer hall, with ancillary areas for Wudhu and women’s sections. The result is a space that feels both monumental and welcoming—ideal for reflection during ziyarah.

### Prayer Times In Jeddah

Local **prayer times Jeddah** are widely available via masjid display boards and popular apps. Use a reliable app (e.g., Muslim Pro, Athan, or your Hisar Travel itinerary reminders) and verify with the mosque’s posted times, especially for Jumu’ah.

Prayer schedules can shift slightly by mosque. Always follow timings displayed onsite if they differ from your app.

## Getting There From The Airport Or Al-Balad

Travellers from Singapore typically enter Jeddah via one-stop flights through Riyadh, Doha, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, or Muscat. On arrival, the simplest way to reach King Saud Mosque is by taxi or e-hailing.

*   **E-hailing (Uber/Careem):** Convenient for language and fare transparency. Usual airport–central Jeddah fares range with traffic. As a broad guide, plan for a mid-range fare and confirm the estimate in-app.
*   **Airport Taxi:** Official taxis are available at the terminal. Expect higher rates at peak times; agree on an approximate fare before departing if the meter isn’t used.
*   **From Al-Balad:** A short hop by taxi or ride-hailing (often 10–20 minutes depending on traffic). Walking is possible only for nearby segments—summer heat and wide roads make a short ride safer and more comfortable.

Have the mosque name in Arabic ready: مسجد الملك سعود (Masjid Al-Malik Saud). Showing the pin on your map app helps drivers unfamiliar with English names.

### Parking Near The Mosque

There is generally surface parking around the mosque. On Fridays and during peak Salah times, lots can fill quickly. Arrive early, follow local attendants if present, and park only in marked areas to avoid fines or towing.

### Step-By-Step: A Smooth Arrival

*   Pin the mosque location in Google Maps/Apple Maps before you depart.
*   Check Salah time windows and buffer your journey by at least 20–30 minutes for traffic.
*   Carry a small pouch with wudhu essentials (face towel, slippers) and a lightweight prayer mat if preferred.
*   If driving, identify overflow parking streets on your map in advance.
*   For rideshare pick-up after prayer, move a block away from the main entrance to avoid congestion.

## What To Expect At The Mosque

### Wudhu Facilities

Dedicated Wudhu areas serve both men and women. They are straightforward to use, but can be busy just before the Adhan. Consider performing Wudhu earlier if you are on a tight schedule.

*   Bring a small towel for drying hands and feet.
*   Footwear racks are usually provided—keep your pair together to avoid mix-ups.

### Women’s Sections

Women’s prayer areas are typically sited with clear signage. As with many Saudi mosques, entrances may be separate for privacy and ease of access. If unsure, ask a staff member or a regular worshipper for guidance.

### Dress Code Saudi: Practical Notes

*   **Men:** Long trousers and modest shirts are standard. For Jumu’ah, many wear a thobe, but it’s not compulsory.
*   **Women:** An abaya with a headscarf is the norm for entering mosques. Choose breathable fabrics for Jeddah’s warm climate.
*   **Footwear:** Easy-on sandals help during Wudhu and entry/exit.

### Friday Prayer (Jumu’ah) Tips

Jumu’ah is a beautiful time to experience the mosque’s community atmosphere, but do plan ahead:

*   Arrive 30–45 minutes before the Khutbah to secure parking and a comfortable spot.
*   Carry your own prayer mat if you prefer extra cushioning on marble floors.
*   Keep valuables close and silenced devices off to maintain focus.
*   If you’re with elderly family, ask an attendant to direct you to seating with back support near pillars.

Expect heavy congestion around the mosque right after Jumu’ah. If using ride-hailing, set your pick-up point a few minutes’ walk away along a quieter side street.

### Etiquette And Photography

Always prioritise worshippers’ privacy and the sanctity of Salah. Avoid photography during prayer times and never photograph people without permission. Keep conversations soft and phones muted.

## Suggested Ziyarah Route In Jeddah

Blend spiritual reflection at King Saud Mosque with history and local flavours in Al-Balad—perfect for the _Ziyarah & Sacred Sites_ theme:

*   **Start:** Arrive at King Saud Mosque outside peak traffic; perform Sunnah prayers and spend time in dhikr.
*   **Move to Al-Balad:** A short taxi ride to explore coral-stone houses, spice lanes, and restored heritage squares.
*   **Historic Mosques Jeddah:** If time allows, visit Al-Shafi’i Mosque in Al-Balad for its centuries-old heritage and courtyard serenity.
*   **Breaks:** Hydrate often; summer temperatures can be high. Choose shaded routes and rest between sites.
*   **Return:** Head back to your hotel or the airport with a 60–90 minute buffer, especially during peak hours.

Travelling with parents or young children? Plan two focused stops instead of many quick hops. Depth over distance keeps the ziyarah meaningful and unrushed.

## For Singapore Travellers On An Umrah Layover

Many Singaporeans pass through Jeddah en route to Makkah and Madinah. If you have a long layover or a free day before/after Umrah, a short ziyarah is possible with careful planning.

*   **Entry And Transit:** Saudi Arabia offers various entry options, including a stopover scheme for short visits. Requirements may change—check official sources and your airline before you fly.
*   **Time Budget:** For a relaxed visit to King Saud Mosque plus Al-Balad, aim for at least 5–6 hours landside, excluding immigration and airport transfers.
*   **Luggage:** Use airport storage if available, or check with your airline about through-checked bags to reduce hassle.
*   **Connectivity:** Airport and city eSIMs are widely available; maps and ride-hailing work smoothly with mobile data.
*   **Payments:** International cards are widely accepted in Jeddah. Carry a small amount of SAR cash for taxis, water, and small purchases.

### Short-On-Time: Do This

*   Pre-check prayer times and select one Salah to anchor your visit (e.g., Dhuhr or Maghrib).
*   Go directly airport → King Saud Mosque for Wudhu and Salah.
*   Optional quick hop to Al-Balad for a brief heritage walk and refreshments.
*   Return to the airport with ample buffer for security and boarding.

## Safety, Comfort, And Seasonal Notes

*   **Weather:** Jeddah is warm year-round. Lightweight, breathable clothing helps, alongside a foldable umbrella for shade.
*   **Hydration:** Keep bottled water handy. Many convenience stores dot central Jeddah.
*   **Footwear:** Expect polished stone surfaces around the mosque; non-slip sandals are practical after Wudhu.
*   **Respect:** Follow mosque signage and any instructions from attendants or authorities.

## Planning With Hisar Travel (Singapore)

Yes. Dedicated Wudhu areas for men and women are signposted and close to prayer halls. They can be busy just before the Adhan, so allow a few extra minutes, especially if you’re on a tight layover schedule.

Plan to arrive 30–45 minutes before the Khutbah for a comfortable space and easier parking. If you’re with seniors or young children, arrive even earlier and request a spot near a pillar or wall for back support.

**Al-Masjid al-Ḥarām** (**[Шаблон:Lang](javascript:; "Шаблон:Lang (страница не существует)")**[Шаблон:IPA2](javascript:; "Шаблон:IPA2 (страница не существует)") "The Sacred Mosque"), is the largest mosque in the world. Located in the city of [Mecca](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Mecca), it surrounds the Kaaba, the place which Muslims turn towards while offering daily [prayer](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Salat)s and is considered the holiest place on Earth by Muslims. The mosque is also known as the **Grand Mosque**.

The current structure covers an area of [Шаблон:Convert](javascript:; "Шаблон:Convert (страница не существует)") including the outdoor and indoor praying spaces and can accommodate up to 4 million worshippers during the Hajj period, one of the largest annual gatherings of people in the world.

[![Image 9: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2145567)

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](https://vk.com/photo-110953195_456240138)

## History

[Шаблон:Weasel](javascript:; "Шаблон:Weasel (страница не существует)")[Islam](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Islam)ic tradition holds that the Mosque was first built by the angels before the creation of mankind, when [God](https://en.advisor.travel/city/God) ordained a place of worship on Earth to reflect the house in heaven called _al-Baytu l-Maˤmur_ (Arabic: البيت المعمور, "The Worship Place of Angels"). _Al-Baytu l-Maˤmur_ is believed to be located in heaven directly above the Kaaba. The first Kaaba was built by angels and Adam was the first human to rebuild it. From time to time the Mosque was destroyed and rebuilt anew. According to Islamic belief it was built by [Ibrahim](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Ibrahim) (Abraham), with the help of his son [Ishmael](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Ishmael). They were ordered by [Allah](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Allah) to build the mosque, and the Kaaba. The [Black Stone](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Black+Stone) is situated near the eastern corner of the Kaaba. Some believe it is to start the circumambulation around the Kaaba, while some believe it to be the only remnant of the original structure made by Abraham.[Шаблон:Who](javascript:; "Шаблон:Who (страница не существует)") The Kaaba is the direction for all the Muslims to pray across the globe thus signifying unity among all. The Islamic teaching specifically mentions that nothing is magical about the Grand Mosque except for the oasis [Zamzam](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Zamzam+Well) which has never dried ever since it was revealed.

[![Image 10: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2302260)

[Panoramio upload bot @ WikiCommons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User_talk:Panoramio%20upload%20bot)

[Шаблон:Cquote](javascript:; "Шаблон:Cquote (страница не существует)")

[Шаблон:Cquote](javascript:; "Шаблон:Cquote (страница не существует)")

[![Image 11: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2302265)

[BotMultichillT @ WikiCommons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User_talk:BotMultichillT)

[Шаблон:Cquote](javascript:; "Шаблон:Cquote (страница не существует)")

[![Image 12: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2145561)

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](https://vk.com/photo11523240_456240885)

Muslim belief places the story of Ishmael and his mother's search for water in the general vicinity of the mosque. In the story, Hagar runs between the hills of [Safa and Marwah](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Al-Safa+and+Al-Marwah) looking for water for her son, until God eventually reveals to her the [Zamzam Well](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Zamzam+Well), from where water continues to flow non-stop to this day.

After the Hijra, upon Muhammed's victorious return to Mecca, the people of Mecca themselves removed all the idols in and around the Kaaba and cleansed it. This began the Islamic rule over the Kaaba, and the building of a mosque around it.

[![Image 13: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2302261)

[Courtyard of the Great Mosque of Mecca, Saudi Arabia (1) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/43714545@N06/)

The first major renovation to the Mosque took place in 692. Before this renovation – which included the mosque’s outer walls been risen and decoration to the ceiling – the Mosque was a small open area with the Kaaba at the centre. By the end of the 700s the Mosque’s old wooden columns had been replaced with marble columns and the wings of the prayer hall had been extended on both sides along with the addition of a [minaret](https://en.advisor.travel/city/minaret). The spread of Islam in the Middle East and the influx of pilgrims required an almost complete rebuilding of the site which came to include more marble and three further minarets.

[![Image 14: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2145559)

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](https://vk.com/photo-174275406_457240079)

In 1399, the Mosque caught fire and what was not destroyed in the fire (very little) was damaged by unseasonable heavy rain. Again the mosque was rebuilt over six years using marble and wood sourced from nearby mountains in the Hejaz region of current day Saudi Arabia. When the mosque was renovated again in 1570 by Sultan Selim II’s private architect it resulted in the replacement of the flat roof with domes decorated with calligraphy internally and the placement of new support columns. These features – still present at the Mosque – are the oldest surviving parts of the building and in fact older than the Kaaba itself (discounting the [black stone](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/black+stone) itself) which is currently in its fourth incarnation made in 1629. The Saudi government acknowledges 1570 as the earliest date for architectural features of the present Mosque.

Following further damaging rain in the 1620s, the Mosque was renovated yet again: a new stone arcade was added, three more minarets were built and the marble flooring was retiled. This was the unaltered state of the Mosque for nearly three centuries.

[![Image 15: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2302262)

[Nightflyer @ WikiCommons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User_talk:Nightflyer)

### Saudi Development

The most significant architectural and structural changes came, and continue to come, from the Saudi status of ‘Guardian of the Holy Places’ and the honorific title of Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques (the other being the Mosque of the Prophet in [Medina](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Medina)) been afforded to King Abdul Aziz. Many of the previously mentioned features – particularly the support columns – were destroyed in spite of their historical value. In their place came artificial stone and marble, the ceiling was refurnished and the floor was replaced. The [Al-Safa and Al-Marwah](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Al-Safa+and+Al-Marwah), an important part of both Hajj and Umrah, came to be included in the Mosque itself during this time via roofing and enclosement. Also during this first Saudi renovation four minarets were added.

[![Image 16: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2145560)

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](https://vk.com/photo-174275406_457240077)

The second Saudi renovations, this time under King Fahd, added a new wing and an outdoor prayer area to the Mosque. The new wing which is also for prayers is accessed through the King Fahd Gate. This extension is considered to have been from 1982-1988.

The third Saudi extension (1988-2005) saw the building of further minarets, the erecting of a King’s residence overlooking the Mosque and further prayer area in and around the mosque itself. These developments have taken place simaltenously with those in [Arafat](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Arafat), [Mina](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Mina) and [Muzdalifah](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Muzdalifah). This third extension has also resulted in 18 more gates been built, three domes corresponding in position to each gate and the installation of nearly 500 marble columns.

[![Image 17: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2302263)

[يافا @ WikiCommons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User_talk:%D9%8A%D8%A7%D9%81%D8%A7)

Modern but essentially non-architectural developments have been the addition of heated floors, air conditioning, escalators and a drainage system.

[![Image 18: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2302264)

[Today is Friday — M Reza Faisal @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/47122184@N05/)

The death of King Fahd means that the Mosque is now undergoing a fourth extension which began in 2007 and is projected to last until 2020. King Abdullah bin Abdul-Aziz plans to increase the capacity of the mosque by 35% from its current maximum capacity of 800,000 with 1,120,000 outside the Mosque itself.

## Religious significance

The importance of the mosque is twofold. It not only serves as the common direction towards which Muslims pray, but is also the main location for pilgrimages.

[![Image 19: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/93643)

[Al-Masjid Al-Haram — King | حسن أبوالريش @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/48036003@N04/)

### Qibla

[Шаблон:Unreferenced section](javascript:; "Шаблон:Unreferenced section (страница не существует)")[Шаблон:Main](javascript:; "Шаблон:Main (страница не существует)") The qibla—the direction that Muslims turn to in their prayers ([salah](https://en.advisor.travel/city/salah))—is toward the Kaaba and symbolizes unity in worshipping one God. At one point the direction of the qibla was toward Bayt al-Maqdis ([Jerusalem](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Jerusalem)) (and is therefore called the _First of the Two Qiblas_),[Шаблон:Fact](javascript:; "Шаблон:Fact (страница не существует)") however, this only lasted for seventeen months, after which the qibla became oriented towards the Kaaba in [Mecca](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Mecca). According to accounts from [Muhammad](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Muhammad)'s companions, the change happened very suddenly during the noon prayer at Medina in the Masjid al-Qiblatain.

[![Image 20: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2145568)

[Hassan II Mosque — Jorge Lascar @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/8721758@N06/)

### Pilgrimage

[Шаблон:Main](javascript:; "Шаблон:Main (страница не существует)")

The Haram is the focal point of the hajj and umrah pilgrimages that occur in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah in the Islamic calendar and at any time of the year, respectively. The Hajj pilgrimage is one of the Five Pillars of Islam, required of all able-bodied Muslims who can afford the trip. In recent times, about 3 million Muslims perform the hajj every year.

[![Image 21: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2145555)

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](https://vk.com/photo-174275406_457240074)

Some of the rituals performed by pilgrims are symbolic of historical incidents. For example, the episode of Hagar's search for water is emulated by Muslims as they run between the two hills of Safa and Marwah whenever they visit Mecca.

[![Image 22: Masjid al-Haram](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2145564)

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](https://vk.com/photo-171004463_456239520)

The **Hejaz Railway Museum** (Arabic: متحف سكة الحجاز) in Medina is a railway museum that was opened in 2006. It is on the grounds of the restored historic Ottoman railway station at Medina, locally called استسيون "Istasyōn" (Hejazi pronunciation:]), including a stretch of the historic track and a train shed with originally four tracks. There are several engines and pieces of rolling stock on display, some of which has been transported to the museum from other places along the historic Hejaz railway line. At least one engine has been restored enough to be driveable on the museum tracks. It is, along with the old train station at Mada'in Saleh, one of two museums in Saudi Arabia dedicated to the Hejaz railway.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article lists [mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") from around the world by available capacity, that belong to any [Islamic school or branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_schools_and_branches "Islamic schools and branches"), that can accommodate at least 15,000 worshippers in all available places of [prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salah "Salah") such as prayer halls (_[muṣala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musalla "Musalla")_), courtyards (_[ṣaḥn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahn "Sahn")_) and porticoes (_[riwāq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riwaq\_(arcade) "Riwaq (arcade)")_). All the mosques in this list are [congregational mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_mosque "Congregational mosque") – a type of mosque that hosts the [Friday prayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friday_prayer "Friday prayer") (_ṣalāt al-jumuʿa_) in [congregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_prayer_(Islam) "Congregational prayer (Islam)") (_jamāʿa_).

**Mecca**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-4) officially **Makkah al-Mukarramah**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-5) is a city in the [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz") region of western [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia") and is the capital of [Mecca Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca_Province "Mecca Province").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-6) Mecca is considered the birthplace of [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-7)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-8) and the [Islamic prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophets_and_messengers_in_Islam "Prophets and messengers in Islam")[Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad"), as well as being the [holiest city in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiest_sites_in_Islam "Holiest sites in Islam").

It is located 70 km (43 mi) inland from [Jeddah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeddah "Jeddah") on the [Red Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea "Red Sea") in a narrow valley 277 m (909 ft) above sea level. Its metropolitan population in 2022 was 2.4 million, making it the [third most populated city in Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Saudi_Arabia "List of cities and towns in Saudi Arabia") after [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh") and Jeddah. The [Cave of Hira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal_al-Nour#Cave_of_Hira "Jabal al-Nour") atop the _[Jabal al-Nour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal\_al-Nour "Jabal al-Nour")_ just outside the city is where Muslims believe the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") was first revealed to Muhammad.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-9) The [Great Mosque of Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram "Masjid al-Haram"), known as the _Masjid al-Haram_, is home to the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba"), believed by Muslims to have been built by [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam") and [Ishmael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael_in_Islam "Ishmael in Islam"). It is the direction of prayer (_[qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla")_) for all Muslims worldwide.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-10) Around 44.5% of the population are [Saudi citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudis "Saudis") and around 55.5% are [Muslim foreigners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_world "Islamic world") from other countries.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-11) Pilgrims more than triple the population number every year during the _[Ḥajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj")_[pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrimage#Islam "Pilgrimage"), observed in the twelfth [Hijri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calendar "Islamic calendar") month of _[Dhūl-Ḥijjah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu\_al-Hijjah "Dhu al-Hijjah")_ as an obligation for all Muslims at least once in their lives.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-12) With over 19.3 million international visitors in 2024, Mecca was one of the five [most visited cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_by_international_visitors "List of cities by international visitors") in the world.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-13)

Muslim rulers from in and around the region long tried to rule the city, and thus, much like most of the Hejazi region, has seen several [regime changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regime_change "Regime change"). The city was most recently conquered in the [Saudi conquest of Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_conquest_of_Hejaz "Saudi conquest of Hejaz") by [Ibn Saud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Saud "Ibn Saud") and his allies in [1925](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Mecca_(1924) "Capture of Mecca (1924)"). Since then, Mecca has seen a tremendous expansion in size and infrastructure, with newer, modern buildings such as [The Clock Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clock_Towers "The Clock Towers"), the world's fourth–tallest building and [fifth–largest by floor area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_buildings "List of largest buildings"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-14) towering over the Great Mosque. The [Saudi government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Saudi_Arabia "Politics of Saudi Arabia") has also carried out the [destruction of several historical structures and archaeological sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Britannica-15) such as the [Ajyad Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajyad_Fortress "Ajyad Fortress").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-independent-16)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-17)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-NYT-18) However, many of the demolitions have officially been part of the continued expansion of the [Masjid al-Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram "Masjid al-Haram") at Mecca and the [Prophet's Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet's_Mosque "Prophet's Mosque") in Medina and their auxiliary service facilities in order to accommodate the ever-increasing number of Muslims performing the pilgrimage.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-19) Non-Muslims are [prohibited from entering the city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_city "Closed city").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-peters_206-20)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-21)

Under the Saudi government, Mecca is governed by the Mecca Regional Municipality, a municipal council of 14 locally elected members headed by the mayor (called _Amin_ in Arabic) appointed by the [Saudi government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Saudi_Arabia "Politics of Saudi Arabia"). As of January 2022, the mayor of the city is Saleh Al-Turki.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-22) The City of Mecca _[amanah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdivisions\_of\_Saudi\_Arabia "Subdivisions of Saudi Arabia")_, which constitutes Mecca and the surrounding region, is the capital of the Mecca Province, which includes the neighbouring cities of Jeddah and [Taif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif "Taif"), even though Jeddah is considerably larger in population than Mecca. [Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Saud "House of Saud")[Khalid Al-Faisal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalid_Al-Faisal "Khalid Al-Faisal") has been the provincial governor since 16 May 2007.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-23)

## Etymology

Mecca has been referred to by many names. Its [etymology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etymology "Etymology") is obscure as with many Arabic words.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Versteeghp513-24) Widely believed to be a synonym for _Makkah_, it is said to be more specifically the early name for the valley located therein. At the same time, Muslim scholars generally use it to refer to the sacred area of the city that immediately surrounds and includes the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-autogenerated1-25)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Petersonp22-26)

_Makkah_ is the official transliteration used by the Saudi government and is closer to the Arabic pronunciation.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hamp76-27)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-28) The government adopted _Makkah_ as the official spelling in the 1980s, but it is not universally known or used worldwide.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hamp76-27) The full official name is _Makkah al-Mukarramah_ ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): مكة المكرمة, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'Makkah the Honored').[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hamp76-27)_Makkah_ is used to refer to the city in the Quran in [Surah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surah "Surah")[Al-Fath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Fath "Al-Fath") (48), verse 24.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Versteeghp513-24)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hittip6-29)

The word _Mecca_ in English has come to be used to refer to any place that draws large numbers of people, and because of this some English-speaking Muslims have come to regard the use of this spelling for the city as offensive.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hamp76-27) Nonetheless, _Mecca_ is the familiar form of the English transliteration for the Arabic name of the city.

_Macoraba_, another ancient city name [Claudius Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy "Ptolemy") says was within [Arabia Felix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabia_Felix "Arabia Felix"), was also claimed to be Mecca.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-30) Some studies have questioned this association.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Morris-31) Many etymologies have been proposed: the traditional one is that it is derived from the [Old South Arabian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_South_Arabian "Ancient South Arabian") root M-K-R-B which means "temple."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Morris-31)

### Other names

Another name used for Mecca in the Quran is at 6:92 where it is called _Umm al-Qurā_[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-32) (أُمّ ٱلْقُرَى, meaning "Mother of all Settlements").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hittip6-29) The city has been called several other names in both the Quran and _[ahadith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadith "Hadith")_. Another name used historically for Mecca is _[Tihāmah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tihamah "Tihamah")_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-33) According to an Islamic suggestion, another name for Mecca, _Fārān_, is synonymous with the [Desert of Paran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert_of_Paran "Desert of Paran") mentioned in the [Hebrew Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_Bible "Hebrew Bible") at [Genesis 21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vayeira "Vayeira"):21.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Khanp74-34)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Sefaria-Genesis-21-21-35) Arab and Islamic tradition holds that the wilderness of Paran, broadly speaking, is the [Tihamah coastal plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tihamah "Tihamah") and the site where Ishmael settled was Mecca.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Khanp74-34)[Yaqut al-Hamawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaqut_al-Hamawi "Yaqut al-Hamawi"), the 12th-century Syrian geographer, wrote that _Fārān_ was "an Arabized Hebrew word, one of the names of Mecca mentioned in the Torah."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Firestonep65-36)

#### _Bakkah_

Main article: [Bakkah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakkah "Bakkah")

The Quran refers to the city as [_Bakkah_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakkah "Bakkah") in [Surah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surah "Surah")[Al Imran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Imran "Al Imran") (3), verse 96: "Indeed the first [House [of worship]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_of_worship "Place of worship"), established for mankind was that at Bakkah." This is said to have been the name of the city at the time of [Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam") and it is also transliterated as _Baca, Baka, Bakah, Bakka, Becca_ and _Bekka_, among others.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Kipferp342-37)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Glassep302-38)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Phippsp85-39) It was a name for the city in the ancient world.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-:2-40)

## History

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Mecca "Timeline of Mecca").

### Prehistory

See also: [Prehistoric Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_Arabia "Prehistoric Arabia")

In 2010, Mecca and the surrounding area became an important site for [paleontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontology "Paleontology") with respect to [primate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primate "Primate") evolution, with the discovery of a _[Saadanius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saadanius "Saadanius")_ fossil. _Saadanius_ is considered to be a primate closely related to the common ancestor of the [Old World monkeys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_World_monkey "Old World monkey") and [apes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ape "Ape"). The fossil habitat, near what is now the Red Sea in western Saudi Arabia, was a damp forest area between 28 million and 29 million years ago.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-41) Paleontologists involved in the research hope to find further fossils in the area.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-42)

### Early history (up to 6th century CE)

See also: [Pre-Islamic Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Islamic_Arabia "Pre-Islamic Arabia")

The early history of Mecca is still largely shrouded by a lack of clear sources. The city lies in the hinterland of the middle part of western Arabia of which there are sparse textual or archaeological sources available.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Literary-43) This lack of knowledge is in contrast to both the northern and southern areas of western Arabia, specifically the Syro-Palestinian frontier and Yemen, where historians have various sources available such as physical remains of shrines, inscriptions, observations by Greco-Roman authors, and information collected by church historians. The area of the Hejaz that surrounds Mecca was characterized by its remote, rocky, and inhospitable nature, supporting only meagre settled populations in scattered oases and occasional stretches of fertile land. The Red Sea coast offered no easily accessible ports and the oasis dwellers and bedouins in the region were illiterate.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Literary-43)

One study by Majied Robinson, based on early Islamic genealogical records, estimates that at the time of Muhammad the population of Mecca was around 550.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-44) Muslim scholars using traditional sources may place the number as high as 10,000.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-45)

The first clear reference to Mecca in non-Islamic literature appears in 741, long after the death of Muhammad, in the Byzantine-Arab Chronicle or _[Chronicle of 741](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronicle\_of\_741 "Chronicle of 741")_. However, English writer [Tom Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Holland_(author) "Tom Holland (author)") claims that here the author places the region in [Mesopotamia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesopotamia "Mesopotamia") rather than the Hejaz.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-TH-46)[_[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable\_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_]

Possible earlier mentions are ambiguous. The Greek historian [Diodorus Siculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diodorus_Siculus "Diodorus Siculus") writes about Arabia in the 1st century BCE in his work _[Bibliotheca Historica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibliotheca\_Historica "Bibliotheca Historica")_, describing a holy shrine: "And a temple has been set up there, which is very holy and exceedingly revered by all Arabians."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-47) Claims have been made this could be a reference to the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") in Mecca.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-48) However, the geographic location Diodorus describes is located in northwest Arabia, around the area of [Leuke Kome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leuke_Kome "Leuke Kome"), within the former [Nabataean Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nabataean_Kingdom "Nabataean Kingdom") and the Roman province of [Arabia Petraea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabia_Petraea "Arabia Petraea").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-49)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-50)

Ptolemy lists the names of 50 cities in Arabia, one going by the name of Macoraba. There has been speculation since 1646 that this could be a reference to Mecca. Historically, there has been a general consensus in scholarship that Macoraba mentioned by [Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy "Ptolemy") in the 2nd century CE is indeed Mecca, but more recently, this has been questioned.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-52) Historian [Glen Bowersock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Bowersock "Glen Bowersock") favors the identity of the former, with his theory being that "Macoraba" is the word "_Makkah"_ followed by the aggrandizing [Aramaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aramaic "Aramaic") adjective _rabb_ (great). The Roman 4th-century historian [Ammianus Marcellinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammianus_Marcellinus "Ammianus Marcellinus") also enumerated many cities of Western Arabia, most of which can be identified. According to Bowersock, he did mention Mecca as "Geapolis" or "Hierapolis," the latter one meaning "holy city" potentially referring to the sanctuary of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-53) Danish writer [Patricia Crone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Crone "Patricia Crone"), from the [Revisionist school of Islamic studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revisionist_school_of_Islamic_studies "Revisionist school of Islamic studies") on the other hand, writes that "the plain truth is that the name Macoraba has nothing to do with that of Mecca [...] if Ptolemy mentions Mecca at all, he calls it Moka, a town in [Arabia Petraea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabia_Petraea "Arabia Petraea")."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-54)

[Procopius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Procopius "Procopius")' 6th century statement that the [Ma'add](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma'add "Ma'add") tribe possessed the coast of western Arabia between the [Ghassanids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghassanids "Ghassanids") and the [Himyarites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himyar "Himyar") of the south supports the Arabic sources tradition that associates [Quraysh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quraysh "Quraysh") as a branch of the Ma'add and Muhammad as a direct descendant of Ma'add ibn Adnan.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-55)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-56)

Patricia Crone and Tom Holland has cast doubt on the claim that Mecca was a major historical trading outpost.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-ReferenceB-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-58) However, other scholars such as Glen W. Bowersock disagree and assert that Mecca was a major trading outpost.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-59)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-60) Crone later on disregarded some of her theories. She argues that Meccan trade relied on skins, hides, manufactured leather goods, clarified butter, Hijazi woollens, and camels. She suggests that most of these goods were destined for the Roman army, which is known to have required colossal quantities of leather and hides for its equipment.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-61) The earliest Muslim inscriptions are from the Mecca–[Taif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif "Taif") area.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-62)

**Islamic narrative**

In the Islamic view, the beginnings of Mecca are attributed to the [Biblical figures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_people_in_Islam "Biblical people in Islam"), [Adam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam "Adam"), [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham "Abraham"), [Hagar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar "Hagar") and [Ishmael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael "Ishmael"). It was Adam himself who built the first God's house in Mecca according to a heavenly prototype but this building was destroyed in the [Noahic Flood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_flood_narrative "Genesis flood narrative").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Literary-43) The civilization of Mecca is believed to have started after [Ibrāhīm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam") (Abraham) left his son Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) and wife [Hājar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam") (Hagar) in the valley at [Allah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allah "Allah")'s command.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Some people from the Yemeni tribe of [Jurhum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurhum "Jurhum") settled with them, and Isma'il reportedly married two women, one after divorcing the first, on Ibrahim's advice. At least one man of the Jurhum helped Ismāʿīl and his father to construct or according to Islamic narratives, reconstruct, the _[Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")_ ('Cube'),[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-63)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-autogenerated1-25)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-64) which would have social, religious, political and historical implications for the site and region.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Glasse1991-65)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Lings1983-66)

Muslims see the mention of a pilgrimage at the [Valley of the Bakha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakkah#Valley_of_the_Bakha "Bakkah") in the [Old Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Testament "Old Testament") chapter [Psalm 84](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_84 "Psalm 84"):3–6 as a reference to Mecca, similar to the Quran at Surah [3:96](https://quran.com/3?startingVerse=96) In the _['āl ʿimrān](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al\_Imran "Al Imran")_, a commentary on the [Samaritan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samaritans "Samaritans")[midrashic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midrash "Midrash") chronology of the Patriarchs, of unknown date but probably composed in the 10th century CE, it is claimed that Mecca was built by the sons of [Nebaioth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebaioth "Nebaioth"), the eldest son of Ismāʿīl or [Ishmael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael "Ishmael").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-67)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-68)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-69)
