#### Under the Quraysh

Sometime in the 5th century, the Ka'bah was a place of worship for the deities of [Arabia's pagan tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_pre-Islamic_Arabia "Religion in pre-Islamic Arabia"). Mecca's most important [pagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paganism "Paganism")[deity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deity "Deity") was [Hubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubal "Hubal"), which had been placed there by the ruling [Quraysh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quraysh "Quraysh") tribe,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-70)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-71) and remained until the [Conquest of Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Mecca "Conquest of Mecca") by [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In the 5th century, the Quraish took control of Mecca, and became skilled merchants and traders. In the 6th century, they joined the lucrative [spice trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spice_trade "Spice trade"), since battles elsewhere were diverting [trade routes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_route "Trade route") from dangerous sea routes to more secure overland routes. The [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") had previously controlled the [Red Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea "Red Sea"), but [piracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piracy "Piracy") had been increasing.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Another previous route that ran through the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf") via the [Tigris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigris "Tigris") and [Euphrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphrates "Euphrates") rivers was also being threatened by exploitations from the [Sasanian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_Empire "Sasanian Empire"), and was being disrupted by the [Lakhmid kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakhmid_kingdom "Lakhmid kingdom"), the [Ghassanids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghassanids "Ghassanids"), and the [Roman–Persian wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman%E2%80%93Persian_wars "Roman–Persian wars"). Mecca's prominence as a trading center also surpassed the cities of [Petra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petra "Petra") and [Palmyra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmyra "Palmyra").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-EIE-72)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-14-73) The Sassanids however did not always pose a threat to Mecca, as in 575 they protected it from a Yemeni invasion, led by its Christian leader [Abraha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraha "Abraha"). The tribes of southern Arabia asked the Persian king [Khosrow I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khosrow_I "Khosrow I") for aid, in response to which he came south to Arabia with foot-soldiers and a fleet of ships near Mecca.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-74)

By the middle of the 6th century, there were three major settlements in northern [Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula "Arabian Peninsula"), all along the south-western coast that borders the Red Sea, in a habitable region between the sea and the Hejaz mountains to the east. Although the area around Mecca was completely barren, it was the wealthiest of the three settlements with abundant water from the renowned [Zamzam Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well") and a position at the crossroads of major [caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camel_train "Camel train") routes.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-world-13-75)

The harsh conditions and terrain of the Arabian peninsula meant a near-constant state of conflict between the [local tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribes_of_Arabia "Tribes of Arabia"), but once a year they would declare a truce and converge upon Mecca in an annual pilgrimage. Up to the 7th century, this journey was intended for religious reasons by the pagan Arabs to pay homage to their shrine, and to drink [Zamzam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well"). However, it was also the time each year that disputes would be arbitrated, debts would be resolved, and trading would occur at Meccan fairs. These annual events gave the tribes a sense of common identity and made Mecca an important focus for the peninsula.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-16-76)

#### Year of the Elephant (570)

The "[Year of the Elephant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_of_the_Elephant "Year of the Elephant")" is the name in [Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") history for the year approximately equating to 570–572, when, according to Islamic sources such as [Ibn Ishaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Ishaq "Ibn Ishaq"), [Abraha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraha "Abraha") descended upon Mecca, riding an elephant, with a large army after building a [cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_(building) "Church (building)") at [San'aa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanaa "Sanaa"), named _al-Qullays_ in honor of the [Negus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negus "Negus") of [Axum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axum "Axum"). It gained widespread fame, even gaining attention from the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire"). Abraha attempted to divert the pilgrimage of the Arabs from the Ka'bah to al-Qullays, effectively converting them to Christianity. According to Islamic tradition, this was the year of Muhammad's birth. Abraha allegedly sent a messenger named Muhammad ibn Khuza'i to Mecca and [Tihamah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tihamah "Tihamah") with a message that al-Qullays was both much better than other houses of worship and purer, having not been defiled by the housing of idols.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Hajjah-77) When Muhammad ibn Khuza'i got as far as the land of [Banu Kinana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinana "Kinana"), the people of the lowland, knowing what he had come for, sent a man of [Hudhayl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Hudhayl "Banu Hudhayl") called ʿUrwa bin Hayyad al-Milasi, who shot him with an arrow, killing him. His brother Qays who was with him, fled to Abraha and told him the news, which increased his rage and fury and he swore to raid the Kinana tribe and destroy the Ka'bah. Ibn Ishaq further states that one of the men of the [Quraysh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quraysh "Quraysh") tribe was angered by this, and going to Sana'a, entering the church at night and defiling it; widely assumed to have done so by [defecating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defecation "Defecation") in it.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-DACB-78)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Muller-79)

Abraha marched upon the Kaaba with a large army, which included one or more [war elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_elephant "War elephant"), intending to demolish it. When news of the advance of his army came, the Arab tribes of Quraysh, Kinanah, [Banu Khuza'ah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Khuza'ah "Banu Khuza'ah") and Hudhayl united in the defense of the Kaaba and the city. A man from the [Himyarite Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himyar "Himyar") was sent by Abraha to advise them that Abraha only wished to demolish the Ka'bah and if they resisted, they would be crushed. [Abd al-Muttalib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Muttalib "Abd al-Muttalib") told the Meccans to seek refuge in the hills while he and some members of the Quraysh remained within the precincts of the Kaaba. Abraha sent a dispatch inviting Abdul-Muttalib to meet with Abraha and discuss matters. When Abdul-Muttalib left the meeting he was heard saying: "The Owner of this House is its Defender, and I am sure he will save it from the attack of the adversaries and will not dishonor the servants of His House."[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-80)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-81)

Abraha eventually attacked Mecca. However, the lead elephant, known as Mahmud,[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-82) is said to have stopped at the boundary around Mecca and refused to enter. It has been theorized that an epidemic such as by [smallpox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox "Smallpox") could have caused such a failed invasion of Mecca.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-83) The reference to the story in [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran") is rather short. According to the 105th [Surah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surah "Surah") of the Quran, [Al-Fil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Fil "Al-Fil"), the next day, a dark cloud of small birds sent by Allah appeared. The birds carried small rocks in their beaks, and bombarded the Ethiopian forces, and smashed them to a state like that of eaten straw.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-84)

#### Economy

See also: [Economy and trade of pre-Islamic Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_and_trade_of_pre-Islamic_Arabia "Economy and trade of pre-Islamic Arabia")

Camel caravans, said to have first been used by Muhammad's great-grandfather, were a major part of Mecca's bustling economy. Alliances were struck between the merchants in Mecca and the local nomadic tribes, who would bring goods – leather, livestock, and metals mined in the local mountains – to Mecca to be loaded on the caravans and carried to cities in [Shaam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria_(region) "Syria (region)") and [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq "Iraq").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-world-85) Historical accounts also provide some indication that goods from other continents may also have flowed through Mecca. Goods from Africa and the Far East passed through en route to Syria including spices, leather, medicine, cloth, and slaves; in return Mecca received money, weapons, cereals, and wine, which in turn were distributed throughout Arabia.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The Meccans signed treaties with both the Byzantines and the [Bedouins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedouin "Bedouin"), and negotiated safe passages for caravans, giving them water and pasture rights. Mecca became the center of a loose confederation of client tribes, which included those of the [Banu Tamim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Tamim "Banu Tamim"). Other regional powers such as the [Abyssinians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habesha_peoples "Habesha peoples"), Ghassanids, and Lakhmids were in decline leaving Meccan trade to be the primary binding force in Arabia in the late 6th century.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-16-76)

### Muhammad and the conquest of Mecca

Main articles: [Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad "Muhammad"), [Conquest of Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Mecca "Conquest of Mecca"), [Muhammad in Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Mecca "Muhammad in Mecca"), and [List of expeditions of Muhammad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_expeditions_of_Muhammad "List of expeditions of Muhammad")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Site_of_the_birthplace_of_the_Prophet_Muhammad%2C_Mecca%2C_Saudi_Arabia.jpg/250px-Site_of_the_birthplace_of_the_Prophet_Muhammad%2C_Mecca%2C_Saudi_Arabia.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Site_of_the_birthplace_of_the_Prophet_Muhammad,_Mecca,_Saudi_Arabia.jpg)

[Makkah Al Mukarramah Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makkah_Al_Mukarramah_Library "Makkah Al Mukarramah Library") is believed to stand on the spot where Muhammad was born, so it is also known as the _Bayt al-Mawlid_ (House of the Birth)

Muhammad was [born](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mawlid "Mawlid") in Mecca in 570, and thus Islam has been inextricably linked with it ever since. He was born into the faction of [Banu Hashim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Hashim "Banu Hashim") in the ruling tribe of [Quraysh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quraysh "Quraysh"). It was in the nearby mountain cave of Hira on [Jabal al-Nour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal_al-Nour "Jabal al-Nour") that Muhammad began receiving divine [revelations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revelation "Revelation") from God through the [archangel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archangel "Archangel")[Jibreel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel "Gabriel") in 610, according to Islamic tradition. Advocating his form of [Abrahamic monotheism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abrahamic_religions "Abrahamic religions") against Meccan paganism, and after enduring persecution from the pagan tribes for 13 years, Muhammad emigrated ([Hijrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah "Hijrah")) in 622 with his companions, the _[Muhajirun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhajirun "Muhajirun")_, to Yathrib (later renamed [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina")). The conflict between the Quraysh and the Muslims is accepted to have begun at this point. Overall, Meccan efforts to annihilate Islam failed and proved to be costly and unsuccessful.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-86) During the [Battle of the Trench](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Trench "Battle of the Trench") in 627, the combined armies of Arabia were unable to defeat Muhammad's forces (as the trench surrounding Muhammad's forces protected them from harm and a storm was sent to breach the Quraysh tribe).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-32-87) In 628, Muhammad and his followers wanted to enter Mecca for pilgrimage, but were blocked by the Quraysh. Subsequently, Muslims and Meccans entered into the [Treaty of al-Hudaybiya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_al-Hudaybiya "Treaty of al-Hudaybiya"), whereby the Quraysh and their allies promised to cease fighting Muslims and their allies and pledged to permit Muslims into the city to perform the pilgrimage the following year. It was meant to be a ceasefire for 10 years; however, just two years later, the [Banu Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banu_Bakr "Banu Bakr"), allies of the Quraish, violated the truce by slaughtering a group of the Banu Khuza'ah, allies of the Muslims. Muhammad and his companions, now 10,000 strong, marched into Mecca and conquered the city. The pagan imagery was destroyed by Muhammad's followers and the location [Islamized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spread_of_Islam "Spread of Islam") and rededicated to the worship of [Allah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allah "Allah") alone. Mecca was declared the holiest site in Islam ordaining it as the center of Muslim pilgrimage (_[Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj")_), one of the Islamic faith's [Five Pillars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Pillars_of_Islam "Five Pillars of Islam").

Muhammad then returned to Medina, after assigning [Attab ibn Asid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attab_ibn_Asid "Attab ibn Asid") as governor of the city. His other activities in Arabia led to the unification of the Arabian Peninsula under the banner of Islam.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-EIE-72)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-lapidus-32-87) Muhammad died in 632. Within the next few hundred years, the area under the banner of Islam stretched from North Africa into Asia and parts of Europe. As the [Islamic realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate "Rashidun Caliphate") grew, Mecca continued to attract pilgrims from all across the [Muslim world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_world "Islamic world") and beyond, as Muslims came to perform the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Mecca attracted a year-round population of scholars, pious Muslims who wished to live close to the Kaaba, and local inhabitants who served the pilgrims. Due to the difficulty and expense of the Hajj, pilgrims arrived by boat at Jeddah, and came overland, or joined the annual caravans from Syria or Iraq.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-88)

### Medieval and pre-modern times

Mecca was never the capital of any of the [Islamic states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphate "Caliphate") except the [Zubayrid Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr"). Muslim rulers did contribute to its upkeep, such as during the reigns of '[Umar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar "Umar") (r. 634–644) and [Uthman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthman "Uthman") (r. 644–656) when concerns of flooding caused the caliphs to bring in Christian engineers to build barrages in the low-lying quarters and construct dykes and embankments to protect the area around the Kaaba.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-EIE-72)

Muhammad's return to Medina shifted the focus away from Mecca and later even further away when '[Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali "Ali"), the fourth caliph, took power and chose [Kufa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kufa "Kufa") as his capital. The [Umayyad Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate "Umayyad Caliphate") moved the capital to [Damascus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus "Damascus") in Syria and the [Abbasid Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") to [Baghdad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad"), in modern-day Iraq, which remained the center of the Islamic Empire for nearly 500 years. Mecca re-entered Islamic political history during the [Second Fitna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Fitna "Second Fitna"), when it was held by [Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr") and the Zubayrids.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The city was twice besieged by the Umayyads in [683](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mecca_(683) "Siege of Mecca (683)") and [692](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mecca_(692) "Siege of Mecca (692)"), and for some time thereafter, the city figured little in politics, remaining a city of devotion and scholarship governed by various other factions. In 930, Mecca was [attacked and sacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Mecca "Sack of Mecca") by [Qarmatians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qarmatians "Qarmatians"), a [millenarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millenarianism "Millenarianism")[Shi'a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shia_Islam "Shia Islam")[Isma'ili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismailism "Ismailism")[Muslim sect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_schools_and_branches "Islamic schools and branches") led by [Abu Tahir al-Jannabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Tahir_al-Jannabi "Abu Tahir al-Jannabi") and centered in eastern Arabia.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-89) The [Black Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death "Black Death")[pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandemic "Pandemic") hit Mecca in 1349.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-90)

#### Ibn Battuta's description of Mecca

One of the most famous travelers to Mecca in the 14th century was a Moroccan scholar and traveler, [Ibn Battuta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibn_Battuta "Ibn Battuta"). In his _rihla_ (account), he provides a vast description of the city. Around the year 1327 (729 AH), Ibn Battuta arrived at the holy city. Immediately, he says, it felt like a holy sanctuary, and thus he started the rites of the pilgrimage. He remained in Mecca for three years and left in 1330. During his second year in the holy city, he says his caravan arrived "with a great quantity of alms for the support of those who were staying in Mecca and Medina." While in Mecca, prayers were made for (not to) the King of Iraq and also for [Salaheddin al-Ayyubi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saladin "Saladin"), Sultan of Egypt and Syria at the Ka'bah. Battuta says the Ka'bah was large, but was destroyed and rebuilt smaller than the original. According to Ibn Battuta, the original Kaaba, prior to the conquest of Makkah by the Prophet, contained images of angels and prophets including Jesus (Isa in Islamic tradition), his mother Mary (Maryam in Islamic tradition), and many others - Ibn Battuta however states these were all destroyed by the Prophet in the year of victory. Battuta describes the Ka'bah in his time as an important part of Mecca due to the fact that many people make the pilgrimage to it. Battuta describes the people of the city as being humble and kind, and also willing to give a part of everything they had to someone who had nothing. The inhabitants of Mecca and the village itself, he says, were very clean. There was also a sense of elegance to the village.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-91)

#### Under the Ottomans

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Khalili_Collection_Hajj_Mecca_panorama.jpg/250px-Khalili_Collection_Hajj_Mecca_panorama.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Khalili_Collection_Hajj_Mecca_panorama.jpg)

Panorama of Mecca, 1845, from the [Khalili Collection of Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalili_Collection_of_Hajj_and_the_Arts_of_Pilgrimage "Khalili Collection of Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage")

In 1517, the Sharif of Mecca, Barakat bin Muhammad, acknowledged the supremacy of the [Ottoman Caliph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Caliphate "Ottoman Caliphate") but retained a great degree of local autonomy.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-92) In 1803 the city was captured by the [First Saudi state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Saudi_state "First Saudi state"),[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-93) which held Mecca until 1813, destroying some of the historic tombs and domes in and around the city. The Ottomans assigned the task of bringing Mecca back under Ottoman control to their powerful _[Khedive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khedive "Khedive")_ (viceroy) and _[Wali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wali\_(administrative\_title) "Wali (administrative title)")_ of Egypt, [Muhammad Ali Pasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_of_Egypt "Muhammad Ali of Egypt"). Muhammad Ali Pasha successfully returned Mecca to Ottoman control [in 1813](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Mecca_(1813) "Capture of Mecca (1813)"). In 1818, the Saud were defeated again but survived and founded the [Second Saudi state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Saudi_state "Second Saudi state") that lasted until 1891 and led on to the present country of Saudi Arabia. In 1853, Sir [Richard Francis Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Francis_Burton "Richard Francis Burton") undertook the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina disguised as a Muslim. Although Burton was certainly not the first non-Muslim European to make the _Hajj_ ([Ludovico di Varthema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovico_di_Varthema "Ludovico di Varthema") did this in 1503),[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-94)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-Webb_01-2023-95) his pilgrimage remains one of the most famous and documented of modern times. Mecca was regularly hit by [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera")[outbreaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_cholera "History of cholera"). Between 1830 and 1930, cholera broke out among pilgrims at Mecca 27 times.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-96)

### Modern history

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Makkah-1910.jpg/250px-Makkah-1910.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Makkah-1910.jpg)

Mecca in 1910

#### Hashemite revolt and subsequent control by the Sharifate of Mecca

In [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), the Ottoman Empire was at war with the [Allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_I "Allies of World War I"). It had successfully repulsed an attack on [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") in the [Gallipoli campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallipoli_campaign "Gallipoli campaign") and on Baghdad in the [Siege of Kut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Kut "Siege of Kut"). The British intelligence officer [T. E. Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._E._Lawrence "T. E. Lawrence") conspired with the Ottoman governor, [Hussain bin Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussein,_King_of_Hejaz "Hussein, King of Hejaz"), the Sharif of Mecca to revolt against the Ottoman Empire and it was the first city captured by his forces in the [Battle of Mecca (1916)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mecca_(1916) "Battle of Mecca (1916)"). Sharif's revolt proved a turning point of the war on the eastern front. Hussein declared a new state, the [Kingdom of Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hejaz "Kingdom of Hejaz"), declaring himself the Sharif of the state and Mecca his capital. News reports in November 1916 via contact in [Cairo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairo "Cairo") with returning Hajj pilgrims, stated that with the Ottoman Turkish authorities gone, the Hajj of 1916 was free of the previous massive extortion and monetary demands made by the Turks who were agents of the Ottoman government.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-97)

#### Saudi conquest

Following the [Capture of Mecca (1924)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Mecca_(1924) "Capture of Mecca (1924)"), the Sharif of Mecca was overthrown by the Saud family, and Mecca was incorporated into Saudi Arabia.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-encarta-98) Under Saudi rule, much of the historic city has been demolished as a result of the Saudi government fearing these sites might become sites of association in worship besides Allah (_[shirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirk\_(Islam) "Shirk (Islam)")_). The city has been expanded to include several towns previously considered to be separate from the holy city and now is just a few kilometers outside the main sites of the Hajj, Mina, Muzdalifah, and Arafat. Mecca is not served by any airport, due to concerns about the city's safety. It is instead served by the [King Abdulaziz International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdulaziz_International_Airport "King Abdulaziz International Airport") in [Jeddah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeddah "Jeddah") (approx. 70 km away) internationally and the [Taif International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif_International_Airport "Taif International Airport") (approx. 120 km away) for domestic flights.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The city today is at the junction of the two most important highways in all of the Saudi Arabian highway system, Highway 40, which connects the city to Jeddah in the west and the capital, [Riyadh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riyadh "Riyadh") and [Dammam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dammam "Dammam") in the east and Highway 15, which connects it to [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina"), [Tabuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabuk,_Saudi_Arabia "Tabuk, Saudi Arabia") and onward to [Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan") in the north and [Abha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abha "Abha") and [Jizan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jizan "Jizan") in the south. The Ottomans had planned to extend their railway network to the holy city, but were forced to abandon this plan due to their entry into [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). This plan was later carried out by the Saudi government, which connected the two holy cities of Medina and Mecca with the modern [Haramain High Speed Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haramain_High_Speed_Railway "Haramain High Speed Railway") system which runs at 300 km/h (190 mph) and connects the two cities via Jeddah, King Abdulaziz International Airport and [King Abdullah Economic City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Abdullah_Economic_City "King Abdullah Economic City") near Rabigh within two hours.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The [haram area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haram_(site) "Haram (site)") of Mecca, in which the entry of non-Muslims is forbidden, is much larger than that of Medina.

#### 1979 Grand Mosque seizure

See also: [Grand Mosque seizure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_seizure "Grand Mosque seizure")

On 20 November 1979, two hundred armed dissidents led by [Juhayman al-Otaybi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juhayman_al-Otaybi "Juhayman al-Otaybi"), [seized the Grand Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_seizure "Grand Mosque seizure"), claiming the Saudi royal family no longer represented pure Islam and that the [Masjid al-Haram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram "Masjid al-Haram") and the Ka'bah, must be held by those of true faith. The rebels seized tens of thousands of pilgrims as hostages and barricaded themselves in the mosque. The siege lasted two weeks, and resulted in several hundred deaths and significant damage to the shrine, especially the [Safa and Marwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safa_and_Marwa "Safa and Marwa") gallery. A multinational force was finally able to retake the mosque from the dissidents.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-99) Since then, the Grand Mosque has been expanded several times, with many other expansions being undertaken in the present day.

#### Destruction of Islamic heritage sites

Main article: [Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia")

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Makkah_Aerial_View.jpg/330px-Makkah_Aerial_View.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Makkah_Aerial_View.jpg)

Mecca, as seen from [Jabal al-Nour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabal_al-Nour "Jabal al-Nour"). [The Clock Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clock_Towers "The Clock Towers") is visible in the skyline.

Under Saudi rule, it has been estimated that since 1985, about 95% of Mecca's historic buildings, most over a thousand years old, have been demolished.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-independent-16)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-independent.co.uk-100) It has been reported that there are now fewer than 20 structures remaining in Mecca that date back to the time of Muhammad. Some important buildings that have been destroyed include the house of [Khadijah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khadija_bint_Khuwaylid "Khadija bint Khuwaylid"), the wife of Muhammad, the house of [Abu Bakr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Bakr "Abu Bakr"), Muhammad's birthplace, and the Ottoman–era [Ajyad Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajyad_Fortress "Ajyad Fortress").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-101) The reason for much of the destruction of historic buildings has been for the construction of hotels, apartments, parking lots, and other infrastructure facilities for Hajj pilgrims.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-independent.co.uk-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca#cite_note-102)

## History

[Шаблон:Refimprovesect](javascript:; "Шаблон:Refimprovesect (страница не существует)") The original Mosque was built by Muhammad, next to the house where he settled after his journey to Medina in 622 AD. The original mosque was an open-air building with a raised platform for the reading of the Qur'an. It was a rectangular enclosure of 30x35 meters, built with palm trunks and mud walls, and accessed through three doors: Bab Rahmah to the south, Bab Jibril to the west and Bab al-Nisa' to the east. The basic plan of the building has since been adopted in the building of other mosques throughout the world.

[![Image 11: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286284)

[Decoration of the interior of a dome in the Prophet's Mosque, Madinah, Saudi Arabia — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/43714545@N06/)

Inside, Muhammad created a shaded area to the south called the suffrah and aligned the [prayer](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Salah) space facing north towards Jerusalem. When the qibla (prayer direction) was changed to Mecca, the mosque was re-oriented to the south. The mosque also served as a community center, a court, and a religious school. Seven years later (629 AD/7 AH), the mosque was doubled in size to accommodate the increasing number of [Muslim](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Muslim)s.

[![Image 12: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286273)

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](https://vk.com/photo220981401_367570676)

Subsequent Islamic rulers continued to enlarge and embellish the Prophet's Mosque over the centuries. In 707, Umayyad [Caliph](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Caliph) Al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik (705-715) replaced the old structure and built a larger one in its place, incorporating the tomb of Muhammad. This mosque was 84 by 100 meters in size, with stone foundations and a teak roof supported on stone columns. The mosque walls were decorated with mosaics by Coptic and Greek craftsmen, similar to those seen in the [Umayyad Mosque](https://en.advisor.travel/poi/Umayyad+Mosque) in [Damascus](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Damascus) and the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (built by the same caliph). The courtyard was surrounded by a gallery on four sides, with four [minaret](https://en.advisor.travel/city/minaret)s on its corners. A mihrab topped by a small dome was built on the qibla wall.

Abbasid Caliph al-Mahdi (775-785) replaced the northern section of Al-Walid's mosque between 778 and 781 to enlarge it further. He also added 20 doors to the mosque: eight on each of the east and west walls, and four on the north wall.

[![Image 13: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286286)

[Interior of the Prophet's Mosque, Madinah, Saudi Arabia (2) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/43714545@N06/)

[![Image 14: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286279)

[Masjid Nabawi — neo saed @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/44656211@N02/)

During the reign of the Mamluk [Sultan](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Sultan) Qalawun, a dome was erected above tomb of the Prophet and an ablution fountain was built outside of Bab al-Salam. Sultan Al-Nasir Muhammad rebuilt the fourth minaret that had been destroyed earlier. After a lightning strike destroyed much of the mosque in 1481, Sultan Qaitbay rebuilt the east, west and qibla walls.

The Ottoman sultans who controlled Medina from 1517 until World War I also made their mark. Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566) rebuilt the western and eastern walls of the mosque and built the northeastern minaret known as al-Suleymaniyya. He added a new mihrab (al-Ahnaf) next to prophet Muhammad's mihrab (al-Shafi'iyyah) and placed a new dome covered in lead sheets and painted green above the Prophet's house and tomb.

[![Image 15: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286288)

[Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/43714545@N06/)

During the reign of Ottoman Sultan Abdülmecid (1839-1861), the mosque was entirely remodeled with the exception of Muhammad's Tomb, the three mihrabs, the minbar and the Suleymaniyya minaret. The precinct was enlarged to include an ablution area to the north. The prayer hall to the south was doubled in width and covered with small domes equal in size except for domes covering the mihrab area, Bab al-Salam and Muhammad's Tomb. The domes were decorated with Qur'anic verses and lines from Qaṣīda al-Burda (Poem of the Mantle), the famous poem by 13th century Arabic poet [Busiri](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Busiri). The qibla wall was covered with glazed tiles featuring Qur'anic calligraphy. The floors of the prayer hall and the courtyard were paved with marble and red stones and a fifth minaret (al-Majidiyya), was built to the west of the enclosure.

[![Image 16: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2296462)

[Al-Masjid an-Nabawi — Fadhlur Rahman @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/64395656@N07/)

After the foundation of the [Kingdom of Saudi Arabia](https://en.advisor.travel/country/Saudi+Arabia) in 1932, the Mosque of prophet Muhammad underwent several major modifications. In 1951 King Ibn Saud (1932-1953) ordered demolitions around the mosque to make way for new wings to the east and west of the prayer hall, which consisted of [concrete](https://en.advisor.travel/city/concrete) columns with pointed arches. Older columns were reinforced with concrete and braced with [copper](https://en.advisor.travel/city/copper) rings at the top. The Suleymaniyya and Majidiyya minarets were replaced by two minarets in Mamluk revival style. Two additional minarets were erected to the northeast and northwest of the mosque. A library was built along the western wall to house historic Qur'ans and other religious texts.

In 1973 Saudi King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz ordered the construction of temporary shelters to the west of the mosque to accommodate the growing number of worshippers in 1981, the old mosque was surrounded by new prayer areas on these sides, enlarging five times its size.

[![Image 17: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286276)

[بلال الدويك @ WikiCommons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User_talk:%D8%A8%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%84%20%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%8A%D9%83)

The latest renovations took place under King Fahd and have greatly increased the size of the mosque, allowing it to hold a large number of worshippers and pilgrims and adding modern comforts like air conditioning. He also installed twenty seven moving domes at the roof of Masjid Nabawi.

[![Image 18: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286283)

## Description

[Шаблон:Refimprovesect](javascript:; "Шаблон:Refimprovesect (страница не существует)") ]] As it stands today, the Prophet's Mosque has a rectangular plan on two [floors](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Storey) with the Ottoman prayer hall projecting to the south. The main prayer hall occupies the entire first floor. The mosque enclosure is 100 times bigger than the first mosque built by the Prophet and can accommodate more than half a million worshippers.

The Prophet's Mosque has a flat paved roof topped with 24 [dome](https://en.advisor.travel/city/dome)s on square bases. Holes pierced into the base of each dome illuminate the interior. The roof is also used for prayer during peak times, when the 24 domes slide out on metal tracks to shade areas of the roof, creating light wells for the prayer hall. At these times, the courtyard of the Ottoman mosque is also shaded with umbrellas affixed to freestanding columns. The roof is accessed by stairs and escalators. The paved area around the mosque is also used for prayer, equipped with umbrella tents.

[![Image 19: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286287)

[Interior of the Prophet's Mosque, Madinah, Saudi Arabia (1) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/43714545@N06/)

The north facade has three evenly spaced [portico](https://en.advisor.travel/city/portico)s, while the east, west and south facades have two. The walls are composed of a series of windows topped by pointed [arch](https://en.advisor.travel/city/arch)es with black and white voussoirs. There are six peripheral minarets attached to the new extension, and four others frame the Ottoman structure. The mosque is lavishly decorated with polychrome [marble](https://en.advisor.travel/city/marble) and stones. The columns are of white marble with brass capitals supporting slightly pointed arches, built of black and white stones. The column pedestals have ventilation grills that regulate the temperature inside the prayer hall.

[![Image 20: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286280)

[Madinah Al-Munawwarah — neo saed @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/44656211@N02/)

This shiny new Prophet's Mosque contains the older mosque within it. The two sections can be easily distinguished: the older section has many colorful decorations and numerous small pillars; the new section is in gleaming white marble and is completely air-conditioned.

The open courtyard of the mosque can be shaded by folded, umbrella-like canopies, designed by Bodo Rash and Buro Happold[[1]](https://en.advisor.travel/out?u=http%3A%2F%2Fwww.anwary-islam.com%2Fmedina-pic%2Fnabwi-umb_b4.htm)

[![Image 21: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286270)

[DcoetzeeBot @ WikiCommons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User_talk:DcoetzeeBot)

The most notable feature of the Prophet's Mosque is the green "Dome of the Prophet", which rises higher amongst the sea of white domes. This is where the tomb of Muhammad is located; early Muslim leaders Abu Bakr and Umar ibn al-Khattab are buried in an adjacent area as well.

[![Image 22: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/111000)

## Ar-Rawdah an-Nabawiyah

[Шаблон:Unreferenced section](javascript:; "Шаблон:Unreferenced section (страница не существует)")

The heart of the mosque houses a very special but small area named _ar-Rawdah an-Nabawiyah_, which extends from [Muhammad](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Muhammad)'s tomb to his pulpit. [Pilgrim](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Pilgrim)s attempt to visit and pray in ar-Rawdah, for there is a tradition that supplications and prayers uttered here are never rejected. Entrance into _ar-Rawdah_ is not always possible (especially during the Hajj season), as the tiny area can accommodate only a few hundred people. _Ar-Rawdah_ has two small gateways manned by Saudi police officers. The current marble pulpit was constructed by the Ottomans. The original pulpit was much smaller than the current one, and constructed of palm tree wood, not marble. _Ar-Rawdah an-Nabawiyah_ is considered part of [Jannah](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Jannah) (Heaven or [Paradise](https://en.advisor.travel/city/Paradise)).

## Saudi expansion of the Mosque

[Шаблон:Refimprovesect](javascript:; "Шаблон:Refimprovesect (страница не существует)")

[![Image 24: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286275)

[Vkontakte User @ Vkontakte](https://vk.com/photo-4252164_305417454)

The original mosque was not very large, and today the original exists only as a small portion of the larger mosque. From 1925, after Medina surrendered to Ibn Sa'ud, the mosque was gradually expanded until 1955 when extensive renovations were carried out. The latest renovations took place under King Fahd and have greatly increased the size of the mosque, allowing it to hold a large number of worshippers and pilgrims. It is also completely air conditioned and decorated with marble.

The newer and older sections of the mosque are quite distinct. The older section has many colorful decorations and numerous small pillars.

[![Image 25: Bab al-Salam (Gate of Peace), one of the entrances of the Prophet's Mosque in Madinah, Saudi Ar](https://css.advisor.travel/i/grey.gif)](https://en.advisor.travel/photo_ex/2286285)

[Interior of the Prophet's Mosque, Madinah, Saudi Arabia (3) — Prof. Mortel @ Flickr](http://www.flickr.com/photos/43714545@N06/)

The mosque is located in what was traditionally the center of Medina, with many hotels and old markets nearby. It is a major pilgrimage site and many people who perform the Hajj go on to Medina before or after Hajj to visit the mosque.

**Masjid al-Haram** ([Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_language "Arabic language"): المسجد الحرام, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Arabic "Romanization of Arabic"):_al-Masjid al-Ḥarām_, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'The Sacred Mosque'),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-4) also known as the **Great Mosque of Mecca**,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-5) is a [mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque "Mosque") in [Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca "Mecca"), [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), serving as the holiest and most important mosque in [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-7)As of 2026,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit) the Great Mosque is the [largest mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_mosques "List of largest mosques") in the world.

The Great Mosque is considered, alongside the [Quba Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quba_Mosque "Quba Mosque") in [Medina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medina "Medina"), among the earliest mosques in Islam.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-8) According to Islamic scholars, Abraham is seen as having built the _Kaaba_ in [Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca "Mecca"), and consequently its sanctuary, which according to the Muslim view is seen as the first mosque[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-Palmer20163-9) that ever existed.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-12)

It has undergone major renovations and expansions through the years.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-13) It has passed through the control of various [caliphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliphs "Caliphs"), [sultans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sultans_of_the_Ottoman_Empire "List of sultans of the Ottoman Empire") and kings, and is now under the control of the [King of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Saudi_Arabia "King of Saudi Arabia") who is titled the [Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custodian_of_the_Two_Holy_Mosques "Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-14)

It encloses the vicinity of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") in Mecca, in the [western region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz") of the country. It is among the pilgrimage sites associated with the [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj"), which every [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") according to orthodox Islamic belief, must perform at least once in their lives if able. It is also the main site for the performance of ʿ[Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah"), the lesser pilgrimage that can be undertaken any time of the year. The rites of both pilgrimages include [circumambulating the Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawaf "Tawaf") within the mosque. The Great Mosque contains other important sites, such as the [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone"), the [Zamzam Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well"), [Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim"), and the hills of [Safa and Marwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safa_and_Marwa "Safa and Marwa").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-15)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Further information: [Hejaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejaz "Hejaz"), [History of Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Islam "History of Islam"), [History of Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Saudi_Arabia "History of Saudi Arabia"), and [Islamic architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_architecture "Islamic architecture")

In the [pre-Islamic religions of Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_pre-Islamic_Arabia "Religion in pre-Islamic Arabia") -spanning from the [Levant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levant "Levant") to [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen"), [numerous deities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_pre-Islamic_Arabian_deities "List of pre-Islamic Arabian deities") —such as, [Al-Lat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Lat "Al-Lat"), [Dhu al-Khalasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Khalasa "Dhu al-Khalasa"), and [al-Uzza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Uzza "Al-Uzza") (also occasionally referred to as [Chaabou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaabou "Chaabou")), [Dushara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dushara "Dushara"), [Dhu Samawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_Samawi "Dhu Samawi") etc.— were represented by [aniconic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aniconism "Aniconism") cubic stone carvings or by cubic structures regarded as [the abodes of these deities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaabas "Kaabas"); furthermore, the existence of "sacred/haram zones" surrounding these sanctuaries and the widespread use of [the name "Ka'b"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ka'b "Ka'b") to denote such sanctity, is well-established.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-16) Although the cultural heritage of the pagan era was largely eradicated during Islam's struggle to establish [Islamic monotheism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tawhid "Tawhid"), historical research has uncovered traces of some [sanctuaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctuary "Sanctuary") that were significant enough to rival the Kaaba in Mecca; nevertheless, the belief that there has always been only one Kaaba has become deeply ingrained in Muslim literary and religious tradition. Today, the Kaaba and the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca are identified as the direction of prayer; however, an archaeological document found in the [Taif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taif "Taif") region suggests that this view is anachronistic from the perspective of traditional Islamic historiography, as a stone inscription discovered there dates the construction of the Masjid al-Haram to the year 78 AH.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-17) Furthermore, a Quranic verse recounting [Muhammad's night journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra'_and_Mi'raj "Isra' and Mi'raj") —an event often presented today as a miracle— to the [Masjid al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Aqsa "Masjid al-Aqsa") offers clues suggesting that the *Masjid al-Haram* mentioned in the Quran might differ from the one located in Mecca. [Surah Al-Isra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Isra "Al-Isra")[17:1](https://quran.com/17?startingVerse=1):

> Glory be to the One Who took His servant by night from Masjid al-Haram to the [Masjid al-Aqsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Aqsa_Mosque "Al-Aqsa Mosque") whose surroundings We have blessed, so that We may show him some of Our signs. Indeed, He alone is the All-Hearing, All-Seeing

The significance of mosque structures from the early Islamic period that face in different directions continues to be a subject of serious debate between [revisionist historians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revisionist_school_of_Islamic_studies "Revisionist school of Islamic studies") and conservatives.

### Era of Abraham and Ismael

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Era of Abraham and Ismael")]

See also: [Abraham in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam"), [Hagar in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam"), and [Ishmael in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael_in_Islam "Ishmael in Islam")

According to Islamic tradition in the [Quran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran "Quran"), [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam"), together with his son [Ismael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael_in_Islam "Ishmael in Islam"), raised the foundations of a house,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-18) which has been identified by commentators as the Kaaba. According to Islamic tradition, it is said that Allah showed Abraham the exact site, which was previously built by [Adam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_in_Islam "Adam in Islam"), very near to what is now the [Well of Zamzam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Well_of_Zamzam "Well of Zamzam"). After Abraham had built the Kaaba, an angel is said to have brought him the [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone"), a celestial stone that, according to tradition, had fallen from Heaven on the nearby hill [Abu Qubays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Qubays_(mountain) "Abu Qubays (mountain)"). The Black Stone is believed by Islamic scholars to be the only remnant of the original structure made by Abraham.

After placing the Black Stone in the Eastern corner of the Kaaba, Abraham reportedly received a revelation in which God told the aged prophet that he should now go and proclaim the pilgrimage to mankind, so that men may come both from Arabia and from lands far away, on camel and on foot.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-19)

### Era of Muhammad

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Era of Muhammad")]

Main article: [Muhammad in Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_in_Islam "Muhammad in Islam")

Upon Muhammad's [victorious return to Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquest_of_Mecca "Conquest of Mecca") in 630 [CE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Era "Common Era"), he and a number of the [Sahaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahaba "Sahaba") including Ali broke the idols in and around the Kaaba,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-20) similar to what, according to the Quran, Abraham did in his homeland. This ended polytheistic use of the Kaaba, and began monotheistic rule over it and its sanctuary.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-24)

### Rashidun era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rashidun era")]

The mosque has been expanded by [caliph Umar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umar "Umar") in 637 CE by 1,500 m 2, in response to the increasing number of Muslims, its area has reached a total of 3,600 m 2, another expansion was carried out by [caliph Uthman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthman "Uthman") where the covered porticoes have been introduced for the first time.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:7-25)

### Umayyad era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Umayyad era")]

In 682, the ruler of Mecca [Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_Allah_ibn_al-Zubayr "Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr"), who opposed the Umayyads following the death of [Mu'awiya I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu'awiya_I "Mu'awiya I") carried an expansion that increased the total area to 7,465 m 2,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:7-25) and following [the reconquest of Mecca by the Umayyads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Mecca_(692) "Siege of Mecca (692)") in 692, the first major renovation to the mosque took place on the orders of [Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abd_al-Malik_ibn_Marwan "Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-26) Before this renovation, which included the mosque's outer walls being raised, the mosque was a small open area with the Kaaba at the center. By the end of the 8th century, the mosque's old wooden columns had been replaced with marble columns and the wings of the prayer hall had been extended on both sides along with the addition of a [minaret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minaret "Minaret") on the orders of [Al-Walid I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Walid_I "Al-Walid I").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-28)

### Abbasid era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Abbasid era")]

The next expansion of the mosque was sponsored by the [Abbasid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate "Abbasid Caliphate") caliph [al-Mansur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mansur "Al-Mansur") between 754 and 757.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:16-29) This was followed by a major expansion begun by his successor, Caliph [al-Mahdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mahdi "Al-Mahdi"), in 779. This work was completed shortly after him by his successor, Caliph [al-Hadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Hadi "Al-Hadi") (r.785–786),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:6-30) which made the mosque's total area reach 28,000 m 2. This was the largest expansion to the size of the mosque thus far. Two further extensions were completed by caliph [al-Mu'tadid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Mu'tadid "Al-Mu'tadid") in 894–5 and by caliph [al-Muqtadir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Muqtadir "Al-Muqtadir") in 918,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:6-30) but it retained its overall form from this period on until the later [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") renovations.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:16-29)

### Ottoman era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Ottoman era")]

In 1570, [Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Sultan "Ottoman Sultan")[Selim II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selim_II "Selim II") commissioned the chief architect [Mimar Sinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimar_Sinan "Mimar Sinan") to renovate the mosque. This renovation resulted in the replacement of the flat roof with domes decorated with [calligraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calligraphy "Islamic calligraphy") internally, and the placement of new support columns which are acknowledged as the earliest architectural features of the present mosque. These features are the oldest surviving parts of the building.

During heavy rains and flash floods in 1621 and 1629, the walls of the Kaaba and the mosque suffered extensive damage.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-31) In 1629, during the reign of Sultan [Murad IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murad_IV "Murad IV"), the mosque was renovated. In the renovation of the mosque, a new stone arcade was added, three more minarets (bringing the total to seven) were built, and the marble flooring was retiled. This was the unaltered state of the mosque for nearly three centuries, the Ottoman era renovations did not expand the size of the mosque.

### Saudi era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Saudi era")]

#### First Saudi expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: First Saudi expansion")]

The first major renovation under the Saudi kings was done between 1955 and 1976. In this renovation, four more minarets were added, the ceiling was refurnished, and the floor was replaced with artificial stone and marble. The Mas'a gallery (As-Safa and Al-Marwah) is included in the Mosque, via roofing and enclosures. During this renovation many of the historical features built by the Ottomans, particularly the support columns, were [demolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia").

On 20 November 1979, the Great Mosque was [seized by extremist insurgents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Mosque_seizure "Grand Mosque seizure") who called for the overthrow of the Saudi dynasty. They took hostages and in the ensuing siege hundreds were killed. These events came as a shock to the Islamic world, as violence is strictly forbidden within the mosque.

#### Second Saudi expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Second Saudi expansion")]

The second Saudi renovations under [King Fahd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Fahd "King Fahd"), added a new wing and an outdoor prayer area to the mosque. The new wing, which is also for prayers, is reached through the King Fahd Gate. This extension was performed between 1986 and 1994.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-32)

1987 to 2005 saw the building of more minarets, the erecting of a [King's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_Saudi_Arabia "King of Saudi Arabia") residence overlooking the mosque and more prayer area in and around the mosque itself. These developments took place simultaneously with those in [Arafat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Arafat "Mount Arafat"), [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina,_Saudi_Arabia "Mina, Saudi Arabia") and [Muzdalifah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muzdalifah "Muzdalifah"). This extension also added 18 more gates, three domes corresponding in position to each gate and the installation of nearly 500 marble columns. Other modern developments added heated floors, air conditioning, escalators and a drainage system.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In addition, the King Fahd expansion includes 6 dedicated prayer halls for people with disabilities. These halls have ramps to facilitate entry and exit with wheelchairs, as well as dedicated paths and free electric and manual carts for their use.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-33)

#### Third Saudi expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Third Saudi expansion")]

In 2008, the Saudi government under [King Abdullah Ibn Abdulaziz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_of_Saudi_Arabia "Abdullah of Saudi Arabia") announced an expansion[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-34) of the mosque, involving the [expropriation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expropriation "Expropriation") of land to the north and northwest of the mosque covering 300,000 m 2 (3,200,000 sq ft). At that time, the mosque covered an area of 356,800 m 2 (3,841,000 sq ft) including indoor and outdoor praying spaces. 40 billion riyals (US$10.6 billion) was allocated for the expansion project.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-35) In August 2011, the government under [King Abdullah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_of_Saudi_Arabia "Abdullah of Saudi Arabia") announced further details of the expansion. It would cover an area of 400,000 m 2 (4,300,000 ft 2) and accommodate 1.2 million worshippers, including a multi-level extension on the north side of the complex, new stairways and tunnels, a gate named after King Abdullah, and two minarets, bringing the total number of minarets to eleven. The circumambulation areas (Mataf) around the Kaaba would be expanded and all closed spaces receive air conditioning. After completion, it would raise the mosque's capacity from 770,000 to over 2.5 million worshippers.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:3-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:5-37)[His successor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_kings_of_Saudi_Arabia "List of kings of Saudi Arabia"), [King Salman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salman_of_Saudi_Arabia "Salman of Saudi Arabia") launched five megaprojects as part of the overall King Abdullah Expansion Project in July 2015, covering an area of 456,000 m 2 (4,910,000 sq ft). The project was carried out by the [Saudi Binladin Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Binladin_Group "Saudi Binladin Group").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-38) In 2012, the [Abraj Al Bait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraj_Al_Bait "Abraj Al Bait") complex was completed along with the 601-meter-tall (1,972 ft) Makkah Royal Clock Tower. Austrian company Lights of Vienna was hired to complete a 100 million euro order of 4700 chandeliers and light fixtures in 26 sizes in 2013. The chandeliers and light fixtures were installed in the Shamiya Extension of the mosque. Some of the biggest gilded chandeliers were priced at 1 million euros each. The company has since been the provider of additional light fixtures to the mosque and other buildings in Mecca.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-39) In 2025, the lighting for the Mataf extension was completed by Lights of Vienna. The project involved the delivery of 10 different lighting types and a total of around 550 custom-made chandeliers and luminaires, all produced from high-grade stainless steel and gilded with more than 200 kg of 24-karat gold. The project value is approximately €90 million. Part of the new lights was the 7-metre _Al Fath Gate Chandelier_, an octagonal, gold-plated chandelier with a 7-meter diameter and 360,000 lumens of output. All fixtures incorporate high-efficiency LED systems.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-41)

On 11 September 2015, at least 111 people died and 394 were injured [when a crane collapsed onto the mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca_crane_collapse "Mecca crane collapse").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-46) Construction work was suspended after the incident, and remained on hold due to financial issues during the [2010s oil glut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010s_oil_glut "2010s oil glut"). Development was eventually restarted two years later in September 2017.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-47)

#### COVID-19 Pandemic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: COVID-19 Pandemic")]

On 5 March 2020, during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the mosque began to be closed at night and the Umrah pilgrimage was suspended to limit attendance.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-48) The resumption of Umrah service began on 4 October 2020 with the first phase of a gradual resumption that was limited to Saudi citizens and expatriates from within the Kingdom at a rate of 30 percent.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-49) Only 10,000 people were given Hajj visas in 2020 while 60,000 people were given visas in 2021.

## Pilgrimage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Pilgrimage")]

Main articles: [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah")

The Great Mosque is the main setting for the Hajj and Umrah pilgrimages[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-50) that occur in the month of [Dhu al-Hijja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_al-Hijja "Dhu al-Hijja") in the [Islamic calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calendar "Islamic calendar") and at any time of the year, respectively. The Hajj pilgrimage is one of the Pillars of Islam, required of all able-bodied Muslims who can afford the trip. In recent times, over 5 million Muslims perform the Hajj every year.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-51)

## Notable structures

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Notable structures")]

### Kaaba

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Kaaba")]

Main article: [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/The_Kabah_in_the_Grand_Mosque_of_Makkah%2C_Saudi_Arabia_%2852501405646%29.jpg/250px-The_Kabah_in_the_Grand_Mosque_of_Makkah%2C_Saudi_Arabia_%2852501405646%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Kabah_in_the_Grand_Mosque_of_Makkah,_Saudi_Arabia_(52501405646).jpg)

The [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")

The [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") is a [cuboid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuboid "Cuboid")-shaped building in the centre of the Masjid al-Haram and is the [most sacred site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_significant_religious_sites#Islam "List of significant religious sites") in Islam.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-eoi317-52) It is the [qibla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qibla "Qibla")_(direction of prayer)_ for [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") worldwide. It is the focal point of the [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah") rites. The [pilgrims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilgrimage "Pilgrimage") perform the _tawaf_ (circumambulation) around its exterior.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-eoi317-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-54) The [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba")'s fabric covering ([kiswah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiswah "Kiswah")) is replaced annually in a formal ceremony.

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/The_Blackstone.jpg/250px-The_Blackstone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Blackstone.jpg)

The [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone") is seen through a portal in the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba").

The [Black Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Stone "Black Stone") is set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba's external wall. Historically and culturally venerated in Islamic tradition, the stone today exists as several fragments within a silver frame and is a focal point of devotion during _tawaf_.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-57)

### Mataf (Tawaf area)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Mataf (Tawaf area)")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Masjid_al-Haram_2022.jpg/250px-Masjid_al-Haram_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Masjid_al-Haram_2022.jpg)

The Mataf full of worshipers

The mataf is the open, circular, paved area immediately surrounding the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") where _tawaf_ (circumambulation) is performed. Over centuries the mataf has been enlarged and modernised, including multi-level and climate-controlled expansions to accommodate the large and growing numbers of pilgrims that visit during [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and throughout the year.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-Long16-58) Major 20th- and 21st-century Saudi expansion programmes substantially increased the mataf’s capacity.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:3-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:5-37)

### Maqam Ibrahim

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Maqam Ibrahim")]

Main article: [Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim")

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Maqam_Ibrahim%2C_Makkah.jpg/250px-Maqam_Ibrahim%2C_Makkah.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Maqam_Ibrahim,_Makkah.jpg)

The enclosure of [Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim") in _Mataf_ area

[Maqam Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maqam_Ibrahim "Maqam Ibrahim") is a small square stone associated in Islamic tradition with the [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham "Abraham") ([Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_in_Islam "Abraham in Islam")). It is displayed near the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba") under a protective enclosure.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-59) According to Islamic tradition, the [imprint on the stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petrosomatoglyph "Petrosomatoglyph") came from Abraham's feet.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-61) It is the only standing historic structure in the _Mataf_ area out of at least six other, which were removed to clear the area for the circumambulation (_tawaf_).[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-madainmataf-62)

### Safa and Marwa

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Safa and Marwa")]

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Mount_Safa_Mecca.jpg/250px-Mount_Safa_Mecca.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mount_Safa_Mecca.jpg)

Mount Safa

[Safa and Marwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safa_and_Marwa "Safa and Marwa") are two small hills within the mosque precinct, connected by the enclosed al-Mas'a walkway, where pilgrims perform the _saʿī_ ritual during [Hajj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajj "Hajj") and [Umrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umrah "Umrah").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-AtoZ-63) The ritual commemorates [Hājar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam") ([Hagar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar "Hagar")), wife of [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham "Abraham") and mother of [Ismail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ismael_in_Islam "Ismael in Islam"), who ran between the hills searching for water for her infant son.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:0-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:1-65) The area was historically separate but incorporated into Masjid al-Haram during 20th-century expansions.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:3-36)

Mouth-piece of the Zamzam well from the Exhibition of the Two Holy Mosques Architecture Museum[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-Madaintwomosques-66)

The [Zamzam well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamzam_Well "Zamzam Well"), located 20 m (66 ft) east of the [Kaaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaaba "Kaaba"),[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-survey-67) is an ancient groundwater source traditionally linked to [Hājar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagar_in_Islam "Hagar in Islam") and [Ishmael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishmael "Ishmael").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-islamonline-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:22-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-:4-70) Modern engineering has enclosed the well and provides Zamzam water to pilgrims through pumping, bottling and distribution systems.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-71)

## Destruction of heritage sites

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Masjid_al-Haram&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Destruction of heritage sites")]

Main article: [Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destruction_of_early_Islamic_heritage_sites_in_Saudi_Arabia "Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia")

There has been some controversy that the expansion projects of the mosque and Mecca itself are causing harm to early Islamic heritage. Many ancient buildings, some more than a thousand years old, have been demolished to make room for the expansion.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masjid_al-Haram#cite_note-73)
